en: Vālmīki: Rāmāyaṇa, 5. Sundarakāṇḍa 5.001.001a Then, [regarding] Sītā who had been carried off by Rāvaṇa, the crusher of enemies—

He desired to seek out his tracks along the path frequented by wandering minstrels. Then, on the emerald-colored grassy meadows that resembled water in their lushness, the mighty and steadfast one wandered at his pleasure.
Terrifying the twice-born with his chest and uprooting trees, the wise one struck down vast numbers of deer like a full-grown lion;
he was marked by colors as blue, red, madder-red, and lotus-hued, as well as white and black.

It was beautifully adorned with various minerals produced by its own nature, and it was constantly inhabited by yakṣas, kiṃnaras, gandharvas, and serpent-demons who were like gods, all possessing the power to assume any form at will and accompanied by their retinues.
Standing at the base of that excellent mountain, which was filled with the finest of serpents,
that best of monkeys shone like a serpent in a lake.
He [offered salutations] to Sūrya, Mahendra, Pavana, and Svayambhū.
Having offered a respectful salutation with joined palms to all beings, he set his mind on departure.
Facing the east, he made a gesture of reverence with joined palms to the Wind, his own progenitor;
thereupon, the skillful one resolved to travel toward the southern direction.
Observed by the foremost of the monkeys,
he who was resolved upon leaping grew in size for the sake of Rama’s success, like the ocean during the full moons; with his body beyond measure, he desired to cross the sea.
With his two arms and his two feet, he pressed down upon the mountain;
oppressed by the monkey, that immovable peak wavered beautifully for a moment,
shedding all the blossoms from the trees with flowering tops.

Covered on all sides by that fragrant mass of flowers released from the tree, the mountain shone as if it were made entirely of blossoms. And that mountain, being crushed by him of supreme prowess, [was shaken].
Like an elephant in rut, he poured forth water;
being thus oppressed by that mighty one, Mount Mahendra discharged streams of gold, antimony, and silver.
And the mountain released massive rocks together with realgar;
as the mountain was being crushed on all sides,
the creatures dwelling within its caves cried out with distorted voices.
That great roar of the beings, born from the pressure upon the mountain,
filled the earth, the quarters, and the groves.
With their broad heads, marked with clearly visible svastikas, the serpents—
5.001.017c Vamanting the terrible fire, they bit the rocks with their fangs.
5.001.018a Then those great rocks, bitten by those enraged and venomous ones, 5.001.018c Blazed up, ignited by the fire, and shattered into a thousand pieces.

Furthermore, whatever networks of medicinal herbs grew on that mountain were unable to neutralize the poison of the *nāgas*, even though they were antidotes for poison. Thinking, "This mountain is being split asunder by supernatural beings," the ascetics [fled].
Terrified, the Vidyādharas fled from there along with their groups of women,
abandoning the golden seats and vessels located in the drinking hall,
as well as the highly precious bowls and the golden water-pots.
Various kinds of foods to be licked and diverse edibles, as well as many types of meats;
bull-hide shields and swords with golden hilts— [these were offered],
while [the men] wore garlands around their necks, were intoxicated, and were adorned with red flower-garlands and unguents.
With blood-red eyes and lotus-like eyes, they ascended into the sky;
women wearing necklaces, anklets, armlets,
and bracelets stood in the air with their lovers, filled with wonder and smiling.
Displaying their great knowledge, the great seers among the Vidyādharas stood together in the sky and gazed upon the mountain;
then they heard the voices of the sages whose souls were purified.
While the *cāraṇas* and *siddhas* remained in the stainless sky,
this Hanumān, son of the Wind-god and resembling a mountain,
desired to cross the ocean— the abode of sea-monsters— with great speed.
Desiring to perform a difficult task for the sake of Rāma and for the sake of the monkeys,
he wished to reach the far shore of the ocean, which is so hard to attain;
though he was like a mountain, his hair bristled and he trembled.
He let out a great roar, like a massive rain-cloud;
and as he was about to spring up, he tossed his tail— which was thickly covered with hair and coiled in successive rings— just as the king of birds hurls a serpent.
His tail, trailing behind him with great speed,
appeared like a massive serpent being carried away by Garuḍa;
he then stiffened his arms, which resembled great iron bars.
The monkey sat down upon his haunches and clenched his feet;
then the glorious and powerful one drew in his arms and likewise his neck,
as he entered into his own splendor, essence, and valor.
Looking at the path from afar with his eyes directed upward,
he restrained his vital breaths in his heart while gazing into the sky;
that elephant among monkeys firmly planted his feet upon the ground.
Covering his ears and about to leap up, the immensely powerful Hanumān,
the best of monkeys, spoke these words to the other monkeys:
"Just as an arrow released by Rāghava, possessing the speed of the wind..."
Just as he went, so shall I go to Laṅkā, which is protected by Rāvaṇa;
for if I do not see the daughter of Janaka there in Laṅkā,
I shall go with this very same speed to the abode of the gods.
"Even if I do not see Sītā in the third heaven despite my exertions,
I shall bind Rāvaṇa, the king of the rākṣasas, and bring him here;
in every way, having accomplished my purpose, I shall return with Sītā."
"Or I shall bring Laṅkā here, having uprooted it along with Rāvaṇa.
Having spoken thus to the monkeys, Hanumān, the best of monkeys,
being swift and acting without hesitation, then leapt up with great speed.
But as he leaped up with speed, those trees growing on the mountain contracted all their branches and sprang up from every side;
they were trees adorned with flowers, frequented by intoxicated lapwings and bulbuls.
Carrying [the mountain] by the force of his thighs, he traveled through the stainless sky;
uprooted by the force of his thighs, the trees followed the monkey for a moment,
like kinsmen following their own relative who has set out on a long journey.
5.001.044a Sāla trees and other excellent mountains, uprooted by the force of his thighs,
followed Hanumān like soldiers following a lord of the earth.
5.001.045a The monkey was accompanied by many trees with their tops in full bloom.
Hanumān, appearing like a mountain, became a wondrous sight to behold. Then those sturdy trees sank into the salt waters,
as if out of fear of Mahendra, like mountains sinking into the abode of Varuṇa.
Strewn with various flowers, along with sprouts and buds, that monkey,
resembling a cloud, shone like a mountain filled with fireflies.
Released by his force, those trees shed their blossoms.

They fell scattered upon the water like friends who have turned away; that diverse variety of tree blossoms, endowed with lightness, fell into the ocean, stirred up by the wind from the monkey's breath.
With a continuous shower of flowers of various colors, the monkey shone like a rising cloud adorned with flashes of lightning;
by the flowers produced by his speed, the water appeared as if it were solid.
Like the sky filled with rising stars that delight the eye,
his two arms were seen outstretched as he moved through the air,
like two five-headed serpents emerging from a mountain peak.
He appeared as if he were drinking the great ocean with its network of waves;
that great monkey seemed to gaze upon the sky as if he were thirsty for it. As he followed the path of the wind, his form took on the brilliance of lightning.
The two eyes of that leader of the tawny-eyed ones, large and round, shine with a tawny glow like two fires situated upon a mountain;
they appear like the sun and the moon stationed together.
His face, with its copper-colored nose, shone with a copper hue,
like the orb of the sun touched by the twilight;
and his upturned tail, as he leaped, was beautiful to behold.
In the sky, the son of the Wind stood tall like the banner of Śakra;
with his great tail as a halo, the highly wise son of Anila, possessing white tusks, shone like the sun surrounded by a lunar orb.
With his rump, which was copper-red, that great monkey shone like a mountain split open by a vast deposit of red ochre minerals as he leaped across the ocean,
that lion among monkeys.
The wind passing through the mountain clefts roars like a thundercloud;
just as a meteor, having burst forth from the northern sky,
is seen falling with its trail, so too is that elephant among monkeys.
Resembling a flying moth,
the long-limbed monkey shone like a full-grown elephant being girded with a leather strap;
he was magnificent with his body above and his deep shadow below.
Then the monkey was like a ship on the ocean driven by the wind;
whatever region of the sea that great monkey traversed,
each appeared as if possessed by madness due to the force of his limbs.
Striking with his chest the masses of ocean waves that were as high as mountains,
that great monkey, possessing immense speed, leapt forth;
and the powerful wind from the monkey’s movement emerged together with the wind from the clouds.
They caused the ocean of terrifying roar to tremble violently;
dragging along masses of great waves in the salt waters,
they crossed over with immense speed as if counting the billows.
Then, seeing that tiger among monkeys gliding through the sky, the serpents whose home is the ocean thought him to be Suparṇa. He was ten yojanas wide and thirty yojanas long.
The shadow of that lion among monkeys appeared even more beautiful upon the water;
like a row of dense white clouds following the son of the Wind,
that shadow shone forth, spread wide across the salt ocean.
Seeing that monkey leaping so swiftly at that time,
the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas rained down showers of flowers.
Indeed, the sun did not scorch that lord of monkeys as he was leaping.
And then the Wind-god attended him for the sake of accomplishing Rāma’s purpose.
As he was leaping through the sky, the sages praised him,
and the gods and Gandharvas sang, extolling the one of great luster.
The nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gods, and birds offered praise upon seeing the best of monkeys,
Hanumān, suddenly free from fatigue as he leaped through the sky.
While that tiger among monkeys, Hanumān, was thus leaping across it, [the ocean appeared].
Desiring to honor the Ikṣvāku lineage, Sāgara reflected:
"If I do not provide assistance to Hanumān, the lord of monkeys,
I shall become subject to the reproach of all who wish to speak."
"I was raised by Sagara, the lord of the Ikṣvākus;
and this minister of the Ikṣvākus ought not to come to ruin.
Therefore, I must act in such a way that the monkey may find rest."

"Having rested the remainder [of his journey] upon me, he will cross over in comfort. Having formed this virtuous resolve, the ocean spoke to Maināka, the best of mountains, who has a golden navel and is hidden within the waters.

"O best of mountains, you have been stationed here by the king of the gods as a barrier against the hosts of Asuras dwelling in the depths of Pātāla. You shall serve as the check for these beings of known prowess when they seek to rise up once again."
You stand blocking the entrance to the immeasurable netherworld;
your power can expand upward, downward, and across like a mountain.
Therefore, I urge you: arise, O best of mountains!

"This very tiger among monkeys, the heroic Hanumān, who performs formidable deeds, is passing over you in the sky, having leaped up for the sake of Rāma’s mission. I must provide assistance to him, who acts on behalf of the Ikṣvāku lineage."

"The Ikṣvākus are worthy of my worship, but they are even more worthy of your worship. Perform this service for us; let no duty of ours be neglected. A duty left undone provokes the anger of the virtuous."
"Rise up from the water; let this monkey remain upon you.
He is our guest and worthy of honor, O best of leapers, possessing the great luster of refined gold and served by gods and gandharvas."

"Having rested upon you, Hanumān will then proceed with what remains. Considering the compassion of the descendant of Kakutstha, the exile of Maithilī, and the exhaustion of the lord of monkeys, you ought to rise."
5.001.089a Hearing [the roar] of the salt waters, Maināka, whose navel is gold,
5.001.089c quickly rose up from the water, covered with great trees and creepers.
5.001.090a Having pierced through the ocean water, he then stood towering high above.
Just as the sun with its blazing rays pierces through the clouds,
[so he shone] with peaks made of gold, frequented by *kiṃnaras* and great serpents,
resembling the rising sun as if they were scraping the very sky.
5.001.092 With its rising peaks made of Jāmbūnada gold,
the sky, which resembled the gleam of weapons, came to possess the luster of gold.
5.001.093 With its shining peaks composed of refined gold, they were radiant with their own inherent light.
That best of mountains became like a hundred suns. Seeing him risen and standing before him without attachment in the midst of the salt waters, Hanumān concluded, "This is an obstacle."
That great monkey of immense speed struck down that exceedingly lofty [mountain] with his chest, just as the wind strikes down a cloud. Then,
that best of mountains was felled by that monkey.
Perceiving the speed of that monkey, he rejoiced and exulted. As the heroic monkey stood poised in the sky,
the mountain, delighted and with a joyful heart, addressed these words to him.
5.001.097e Assuming a human form, you have stood upon my summit;
5.001.098a you have performed this difficult task, O best of monkeys.
5.001.098c Having alighted upon my peaks, rest as you please.
"The ocean was nourished by those born in the lineage of Rāghava;
therefore, that sea honors you who are devoted to the welfare of Rāma. To repay a favor is this eternal law."
Seeking recompense for that, he deserves honor from you;
it was on your account that I was urged by him out of great respect,
and this monkey has leaped even a hundred yojanas.
"Having rested upon your ridges, let him proceed with what remains.
"Wait, O tiger among monkeys; having rested upon me, you may go.
Here is much fragrant, delicious root, bulb, and fruit."
"O best of monkeys, having tasted this and rested, you shall proceed. O chief of monkeys, we too indeed have a connection with you—
one renowned throughout the three worlds for its possession of great virtues."
"O son of the Wind, among those monkeys who are swift and leaping,
I consider you, O elephant among monkeys, to be the foremost.
For even an ordinary person, when he is a guest, is worthy of honor by one who possesses discernment."
By one who desires to know the Dharma, how much more so by one such as you? For you, O elephant among monkeys, are the son of the high-souled Māruti, the best of gods, and are equal to him in speed.
"O knower of dharma, when you are honored, the Wind-god receives honor as well.
Therefore, you are worthy of my worship; hear now the reason for this.
O dear one, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, the mountains possessed wings."
5.001.108c They too departed in all directions, possessing the speed of Garuḍa and the wind.
5.001.109a Then, when they had set out, the hosts of gods along with the ṛṣis 5.001.109c and all living beings were seized by fear, apprehensive of their fall.

Then the thousand-eyed Śatakratu, enraged, cut off the wings of the mountains by the thousands here and there with his thunderbolt. Raising his thunderbolt, the king of the gods approached me in a fury.

5.001.111c Then I was suddenly cast forth by that great-souled Śvasana; 5.001.112a And I was thrown into this salt-water, O best of monkeys; 5.001.112c But my wings were protected and I remained whole, being guarded by your father.
"Therefore, I honor you, for the Wind-god is worthy of my respect. O chief of monkeys, this alliance between us is indeed of great merit.
Now that this matter concerning the ocean and myself has come to such a pass,"
"O great monkey, you ought to grant me joy with a joyful mind. O best of monkeys, dispel my fatigue and accept this honor;
value my affection highly, for I am delighted by the sight of you."
Thus addressed, the best of monkeys spoke to that preeminent mountain:
"I am pleased; hospitality has been rendered. Let this anger be laid aside. The time for my task is pressing, and the day is passing away."
"I have given my promise that I must not stop midway. Having said this, the bull among monkeys, the valiant one, touched the mountain with his hand and entered the sky, as if laughing.
5.001.119a Beheld with great respect by both the mountain and the ocean,
5.001.119c and honored with appropriate blessings, the son of the Wind-god 5.001.120a then leaped high into the air, leaving behind the mountain and the great sea.
Having set out upon his father’s path, he traveled through the stainless sky;
ascending even higher, the son of the Wind-god continued through the cloudless firmament while gazing back at that mountain.
Seeing that second most difficult feat of Hanumān,
all the gods, the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis praised him;
and the deities present there were filled with joy at his deed.
And Vāsava, the thousand-eyed one,
spoke these words with a voice faltering from joy to the wise Sunābha,
that best of mountains, for he himself was the lord of Śacī.
"O Hiraṇyanābha, lord of mountains, I am greatly pleased with you. I grant you freedom from fear; stay here, gentle one, as you please.
You have rendered great assistance to the valiant Hanumān."
"Traveling at a pace of a hundred *yojanas* while remaining fearless even in the face of danger—
this is indeed the monkey who goes as the messenger of Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
By showing me such hospitality, you have truly satisfied me."
Then that best of mountains attained immense joy upon seeing Śatakratu, the lord of the gods, fully gratified. Having been granted his boon, that mountain remained steadfast at that time.
And in a mere moment, Hanumān crossed the ocean.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis,
spoke to Surasā, the mother of the Nāgas, who was radiant like the sun.
"This glorious son of the Wind-god, named Hanumān, is leaping over the ocean; you must create an obstacle for him for a moment,
assuming an extremely terrible rakshasa form resembling a mountain."
Making his face tawny-eyed, with fangs bared and reaching to the sky, he said:
"We wish to know his strength and further his prowess; he will either conquer you by some stratagem or fall into despair."
Thus addressed and honored by the deities, that goddess Surasā, assuming a Rākṣasa form— deformed, misshapen, and terrifying to all— stood in the midst of the ocean.
Turning toward Hanumān as he was floating along, he spoke these words:
"O bull among monkeys, you have been ordained as my food by the lords;
I shall devour you—enter this mouth of mine!"
Thus addressed by Surasā, the illustrious bull among monkeys, with joined palms and a joyful countenance, spoke these words:
"The son of Daśaratha named Rāma has entered the Daṇḍaka forest."
Together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and his wife Vaidehī, he was intent upon this task and had established a deep enmity with the rākṣasas; yet, while he was thus engaged,
his illustrious wife Sītā was abducted by Rāvaṇa.
"I am a messenger going to her presence by Rama's command.
You, who dwell within his domain, ought to provide assistance to Rama.
Or else, having seen Maithilī and Rama, whose actions are effortless,"
"I shall come to your mouth; I promise this truly to you.
Having been addressed thus by Hanumān, Surasā, who can assume any form at will, replied:
"No one may pass me; this is my boon."
Thus addressed by Surasā, the bull among monkeys became enraged and said,
"Make your mouth wide enough so that you may swallow me. Having spoken thus to Surasā, he grew ten *yojanas* in length in his anger.
At that time, Hanumān became ten yojanas in width.
Seeing him, who resembled a cloud and was ten yojanas long,
Surasā also opened her mouth to a length of twenty yojanas.
Then Hanumān, filled with rage, became thirty yojanas in length;
Surasā likewise opened her mouth forty yojanas wide,
and the heroic Hanumān grew to be fifty yojanas in height.
Surasā made her mouth sixty *yojanas* wide;
likewise, the heroic Hanumān, seventy *yojanas* in height,
made Surasā’s mouth eighty *yojanas* wide.
Hanumān, who resembled a mountain and was ninety yojanas high,
caused Surasā to open her mouth to a width of one hundred yojanas. Seeing that gaping mouth, the intelligent son of the Wind-god [acted].
With his long tongue, which was most terrible and like that of a hell-being, he tasted [the blood].
Then, contracting his own body like a cloud,
Hanumān, the son of the Wind, in that very moment became the size of a thumb.
5.001.152a Having swiftly entered that mouth and emerged again with great speed, 5.001.152c the illustrious one, stationed in the intermediate space, spoke these words:
5.001.153a "I have indeed entered your mouth; O daughter of Dakṣa, salutations be unto you!"
"I shall go where Vaidehī is; let your word come true. Seeing him released from her mouth like the moon from the mouth of Rāhu, the goddess Surasā assumed her own form and spoke to the monkey.
"O best of monkeys, O gentle one, go at your ease for the accomplishment of our purpose;
and bring back Vaidehī to be reunited with the high-souled Rāghava.
Having seen that third exceedingly difficult feat of Hanumān, [Rāma said:]...
"Excellent! Excellent! the beings then praised Hari. Approaching the unassailable ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, he entered the sky and went forth with speed like Garuḍa.
Frequented by clouds and birds,
inhabited by masters of the Kaiśika style, and served by Airāvata,
it is frequented by those who ride upon lions, elephants, tigers, birds, and serpents.
It was adorned with descending celestial chariots (vimānas) that were stainless and well-decorated;
it was graced by fires whose impact was like thunderbolts and lightning,
and it was beautified by highly fortunate ones who had performed meritorious deeds and conquered heaven.
[The sky] where the oblation is constantly carried by the one of variegated luster (Agni),
adorned with planets, constellations, the moon, the sun, and hosts of stars,
and crowded with throngs of great sages, gandharvas, nāgas, and yakṣas.
In that secluded, pure, and all-pervading space, frequented by Viśvāvasu;
trodden by the elephant of the king of gods; auspicious, the path of the moon and sun; and spread out as a canopy for the world of living beings, fashioned by Brahmā.
In that place frequented many times by the foremost hosts of Vidyādharas,
the great clouds being dragged along by the monkey shone brightly as he entered the masses of clouds and emerged from them again and again.
Then, as he was entering and emerging like the moon appearing during the rainy season,
the Rākṣasī named Siṃhikā, who could assume any form at will, saw him floating and thought to herself: "He has grown large."
"Today, after a long time, I shall be satiated;
for this great being has finally come under my power after a long wait.
Having reflected thus in her mind, she cast her shadow upon him.
When his shadow had been captured, the monkey thought:
"I have been suddenly overwhelmed, my prowess rendered as if crippled,
like a great ship in the ocean by a contrary wind."
Then, looking sideways, upwards, and downwards,
the monkey beheld that great being risen from the salt waters—
the creature of wondrous appearance of which the king of monkeys had spoken.
"Capturing the shadow, this is of great power; there is no doubt about this.
Having understood that Simhika according to the true nature of the matter, the wise monkey increased his body to a massive size, like a rain-cloud in the monsoon.
Beholding the body of that great monkey growing larger,
she opened her mouth wide until it resembled the sky above the netherworld.
Then he beheld her vast and distorted face.

The wise and mighty monkey, whose body was as firm as a thunderbolt, observed her body alone and her vital organs; then, repeatedly contracting his own form, he leapt out from within her wide-open mouth.
5.001.176a The Siddhas and Cāraṇas saw him plunging into her mouth,
5.001.176c being swallowed like the full moon on the day of conjunction by Rāhu.
5.001.177a Then, having torn at his vital organs with his sharp claws, the monkey—
Then, with the speed of thought and the prowess of his stride, he leapt up with force. Seeing that Siṃhikā had been swiftly slain by the monkey and was fallen,
the beings who roam the sky spoke to that bull among monkeys.
"A formidable deed has been accomplished today; a great being has been slain by you.
Accomplish your desired purpose, O best of leapers, remaining unharmed!
O Lord of Monkeys, he whose four [limbs] are like yours—"
Possessing fortitude, vision, intelligence, and skill, he did not falter in his tasks.
Honored by them as one worthy of worship, having accomplished his purpose,
the monkey entered the sky like the eater of serpents (Garuḍa).
Having reached the far shore on all sides and looking about everywhere,
he saw a line of forests at the end of a hundred yojanas;
and even as he was descending, he beheld it adorned with various trees.
The best of monkeys beheld the island and the groves of Mount Malaya;
he gazed upon the ocean, the marshlands along the sea, the trees growing in those coastal swamps,
and even the faces of the wives of the ocean.
Beholding himself with his own self as resembling a massive cloud,
as if obstructing the very sky, the wise one formed this thought:
"Upon seeing the growth of my body and my great speed, the Rākṣasas will surely [be terrified]."
"The great monkey thought, 'They might feel curiosity toward me.
Then, contracting his body which resembled a mountain,
he returned to his natural form like a self-possessed man free from delusion."
Assuming various beautiful forms,
he reached the far shore of the ocean,
a form impossible for others to attain.
Having examined his own self and scrutinized the matter,
he then descended upon a prosperous peak of Mount Lamba, which was adorned with various summits.
5.001.189c Accompanied by Ketaka, Uddālaka, and Nālikera;
that great-souled one was like the peak of a massive mountain.
5.001.190a He [crossed] the ocean, which was filled with Dānavas and Pannagas;
Having then displayed his prowess by force against the great ocean garlanded with massive waves, he alighted upon its shore and beheld Laṅkā, which was like Amarāvatī.
Having crossed the unassailable ocean, the mighty one,
composed in mind, beheld Laṅkā situated upon the peak of Mount Trikūṭa.
Then, the heroic one was showered with a rain of flowers released from the trees.
Drenched by the rain, he stood there shining like a tree made of flowers. Having crossed a hundred yojanas despite his supreme prowess,
that glorious monkey neither sighed nor experienced any exhaustion.
"I could stride even many hundreds of yojanas;
how much more so the measured end of the ocean, which is but a hundred yojanas?
He is the best among the valiant and the most excellent among those who leap."
Moving with great speed, he crossed the great ocean and went to Laṅkā; he passed through lush green meadows, fragrant forests,
and regions abounding in springs and mountains.
The radiant Hanumān, the bull among monkeys, traversed mountains shrouded by trees and rows of blossoming forests. Standing upon that mountain,
he beheld various woods and groves.
5.002.008c And from the mountain peak, the son of the Wind beheld that Laṅkā;
5.002.009a Sarala trees, Karṇikāras, and Kharjūra trees in full bloom,
5.002.009c as well as Priyālas, Muculindas, Kuṭajas, and Ketakas.
Priyaṅgu trees full of fragrance, nīpas, and likewise saptacchadas;
asanas, kovidāras, and karavīras in bloom;
those weighed down by the burden of flowers, as well as those still in bud.
He saw trees crowded with birds, their tops shaken by the wind;
ponds filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and abounding in lotuses and water-lilies; various delightful pleasure-groves and diverse reservoirs of water.
The elephant among monkeys beheld delightful gardens, continuous with various trees that blossomed and bore fruit in every season;
and having reached Laṅkā, which was protected by Rāvaṇa, he, endowed with splendor, looked upon it.
It was adorned with moats filled with lotuses and water-lilies,
well-guarded by Rāvaṇa for the purpose of protecting Sītā,
and surrounded on all sides by Rākṣasas bearing formidable bows.
That great city was beautiful, enclosed by a golden wall,
crowded with hundreds of watchtowers, and adorned with garlands of flags and banners;
it was further embellished with divine golden archways variegated by rows of creepers.
Hanumān beheld Laṅkā like a city of the gods in the sky; standing upon the mountain peak with its auspicious white mansions,
that glorious monkey saw the city as if it were moving through the air.
Hanumān beheld that city, protected by the lord of the Rākṣasas and constructed by Viśvakarman, appearing as if it were floating in the sky;
it was filled with terrible Rākṣasas, like Bhogavatī is filled with serpents.
It was inconceivable, well-constructed, and magnificent, inhabited in ancient times by Kubera;
it was guarded by many brave fanged Rākṣasas with spears and battle-axes in their hands, and even by terrible venomous serpents.

Having reached the northern gate, the monkey reflected upon the city, which had embankments and ramparts for its hips, vast waters for its fresh garment, *śataghnī* engines and spikes for the ends of its hair, and watchtowers for its earrings.

Resembling the peak of Mount Kailāsa, it seemed to scrape the sky; with its towering, magnificent palaces, it appeared to support the very heavens. And having observed its great fortifications and the surrounding ocean, he—
The monkey thought of his formidable enemy Rāvaṇa:
"Even if the monkeys come here, they will be rendered useless;
for Laṅkā cannot be conquered in battle even by the gods."
"But having reached this uneven and difficult-to-traverse Laṅkā, protected by Rāvaṇa, what will that mighty-armed Rāghava do? No opportunity for conciliation is found among the Rākṣasas."
Neither through gift-giving, nor through sowing dissension, nor indeed through battle is a way seen for these four high-souled monkeys:
the son of Vālin, Nīla, myself, and the wise King.
"As long as I do not know whether Vaidehī lives or not,
I shall reflect upon that very matter once I have seen the daughter of Janaka.
Then that elephant among monkeys reflected for a moment.
Standing upon that mountain peak, intent on the success of Rāma, [Hanumān thought:
"In this form, it is not possible for me to enter the city of the Rākṣasas,
which is guarded by cruel and powerful demons."
The Rākṣasas are fierce in power, of great heroism, and strong;
yet all of them must be deceived by me as I search for Jānakī.
By means of a form that is both visible and invisible, I shall enter the city of Laṅkā at night.
"The time has come for me to enter and accomplish my great task," Hanumān thought, sighing repeatedly upon seeing that city, which was so impregnable even to the gods and asuras.
"By what means might I see Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka,
without being seen by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas? How may the mission of the self-knowing Rāma not be destroyed?"
"May I see the daughter of Janaka alone with me in a secluded place. Even when a purpose has been accomplished, it may perish if it is obstructed by adverse time and place,
just as darkness vanishes upon the rising of the sun when it encounters a confused messenger."

Even when the intellect has reached a certainty regarding what is beneficial and what is harmful, it does not shine [if it acts wrongly], for messengers who consider themselves wise ruin undertakings.
How might the task not perish? How might there be no distress?
"How might my leaping across the ocean not be in vain?
For if I am seen by the Rākṣasas, this mission of Rāma— who knows his own self and desires the ruin of Rāvaṇa— will become futile."
5.002.041a For it is not possible to remain anywhere unknown to the rākṣasas,
5.002.041c even in the form of a rākṣasa, much less in any other form. 5.002.042a It is my opinion that even the wind cannot move about here unobserved.
For there is nothing unknown to these most powerful Rākṣasas. If I remain here concealed in my own form,
I shall meet with destruction and my husband’s purpose will be lost.
Therefore, having assumed my own form and become small in stature during the night,
I shall fly toward Laṅkā for the sake of accomplishing Rāghava’s purpose;
I will enter Rāvaṇa’s city at night, which is so difficult to approach.
"Searching through the entire palace, I shall find the daughter of Janaka. Thinking thus, the heroic monkey Hanumān, eager for the sight of Vaidehī, then waited for the setting of the sun.
Having become the size of a spotted deer, Hanumān, a marvel to behold,
the heroic one, leaped up quickly at the time of dusk and entered the beautiful city with its well-laid-out great highways.

He beheld that great city, spread with rows of palaces, featuring pillars of gold and silver and lattices made of refined gold, resembling a city of the Gandharvas; it was adorned with buildings of seven and eight stories.
Those dwellings of the rākṣasas shone there with floors filled with crystal, adorned with gold, variegated with cat’s-eye gems, and decorated with nets of pearls.
The golden and variegated archways of the rākṣasas illuminated Laṅkā, which was adorned on every side. Having beheld that inconceivable Laṅkā of wondrous form, the great monkey—
He was both despondent and joyful, longing for the sight of Vaidehī.
He beheld [the city] adorned with rows of lofty, pale-white palaces,
featuring gateways with lattices of precious gold.
[He saw] that city protected by the arms of Rāvaṇa, filled with illustrious ones,
and crowded with night-stalkers of fearsome strength;
even the moon seemed to act as his companion.
Shining as he stands in the midst of the hosts of stars, spreading the canopy of moonlight over the world,
the sun of many thousands of rays rises.
That hero among monkeys beheld the moon rising and shining forth, with the luster of a conch shell and the color of milk and lotus stalks.
Standing firm with courage on that long peak, which resembled a hanging cloud, the wise Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, remained there like a swan floating upon a lake.
At night, the great being, that elephant among monkeys, entered Laṅkā—
the city protected by Rāvaṇa, abounding in delightful groves and waters,
and adorned with palaces resembling autumnal clouds.
It possessed a resonance like the ocean and was fanned by the ocean breezes;
it was well-guarded by a robust army, just like Viṭapāvatī,
with beautiful arches and turrets and white gates and portals.
It was like the auspicious Bhogavatī, protected by the movements of serpents;
it was filled with clouds flashing with lightning and frequented by celestial paths,
resounding with fierce winds like Indra’s Amarāvatī.
Having reached that city, which was enclosed by a great wall of gold and adorned with banners resounding with the tinkling of networks of small bells,
he approached the wall suddenly and with joy.
With his heart filled with wonder, he gazed upon the city on all sides,
with gates made of gold and altars fashioned from lapis lazuli,
adorned with jewels, crystal, and pearls, and featuring floors inlaid with precious gems.
With turrets of refined gold, white and pure as silver,
with stairways of lapis lazuli and floors of crystal, these auspicious mansions,
complete with beautiful courtyards, seemed as if they had leapt into the sky.
Resounding with the cries of cranes and peacocks and frequented by royal swans,
it echoed on all sides with the sounds of musical instruments and ornaments;
then, having beheld that city which was like the Vasvokasārā, [he entered].
Hanumān, the monkey, rejoiced as Laṅkā seemed to spring up like the sky.
Beholding that auspicious city of the lord of the Rākṣasas, Laṅkā—
unsurpassed and endowed with prosperity— the valiant one reflected upon it.

5.003.014 This city cannot be overcome by force by anyone else, as it is protected by the forces of Rāvaṇa bearing uplifted weapons. 5.003.015 Nor can it be overcome by Kumuda, Aṅgada, or even by Suṣeṇa, the great monkey.
This land shall be renowned as belonging to Mainda and Dvivida; it shall be the domain of Vivasvat’s son Hari, of Kuśaparvan,
of Ṛkṣa, of Ketumāla, and of me as well.
Having observed the prowess of Rāghava and the valor of Lakṣmaṇa, O mighty-armed one, the monkey became filled with joy. [He beheld] that city,
adorned with garments of jewels and possessing treasuries as its earrings.

That great monkey beheld the city of the lord of the Rākṣasas, which was as prosperous as a woman adorned with ornaments whose breasts are mechanical engines; it was a city where darkness had vanished due to the lamps and the brilliance of its great mansions.
Endowed with courage, the son of the Wind-god entered during the night;
he took to the great highway, which was adorned with pearls and flowers,
and preceded by the sounds of musical instruments accompanied by laughter and loud shouts.
With houses resembling adamantine hooks and adorned with adamantine lattices, the lovely city shone like the sky with clouds;
at that time, Laṅkā blazed forth with the auspicious dwellings of the hosts of Rākṣasas.
[He saw] it with variegated [palaces] resembling white clouds, arranged in the form of lotuses and svastikas,
and also with *vardhamāna* houses well-distributed on all sides; [the king],
who brings benefit to the lord of monkeys, [beheld] that city adorned with wonderful garlands and ornaments.
Wandering for the sake of Rāghava, the illustrious one saw [them] and rejoiced;
he heard the sweet singing of women, enriched with intoxication, adorned with notes from the three registers of the voice, like that of the Apsarases in heaven.
He heard the sound of girdles and the tinkling of anklets,
as well as the noise of footsteps on staircases within the mansions of the great-souled one;
and here and there he heard the sounds of clapping and the shouts of warriors.
He saw Yātudhānas intent upon their private Vedic recitations,
as well as Rākṣasas roaring while engaged in the praise of Rāvaṇa;
and he beheld a vast army of Rākṣasas stationed, blocking the royal highway.
In the central grove, he saw many spies of the Rākṣasa—
some initiated with sacred vows, some with matted hair, some shaven-headed, and others clothed in cow-hides; they carried handfuls of *darbha* grass as weapons and used fire-pits as their arms.
Some held mallets and hammers in their hands, while others carried staffs as weapons;
some had but one eye or many ears, and some had pendulous, dangling breasts.
They were likewise formidable, with distorted faces, hideous, and dwarfish.
[He saw] archers and swordsmen, those armed with *śataghnīs* and maces,
and those with excellent iron clubs in their hands, resplendent in variegated armor—
neither too stout nor too lean, neither too tall nor too short.

That great monkey beheld those who were deformed, those of many forms, and those of beautiful form and great splendor; some bearing spears, trees, and weapons, others wielding *paṭṭiśas* and thunderbolts, and still others with slings and nooses in their hands.

The monkey saw a middle guard of one hundred thousand men, composed and vigilant, who were wearing garlands, anointed with unguents, adorned with excellent ornaments, wielding sharp spears, and possessing great strength like those armed with thunderbolts.
That great monkey beheld the city, which was completely surrounded by walls;
it was divine, resembling heaven itself, resounding with celestial sounds,
echoing with the neighing of horses, and likewise filled with the tinkling of ornaments.
Adorned with chariots, vehicles, and celestial palaces, as well as auspicious elephants and horses,
and with four-tusked tuskers resembling masses of white clouds,
the city’s beautiful gates were graced by intoxicated beasts and birds.
The monkey entered the well-guarded palace of the lord of the Rākṣasas. Then he saw the sun, which had reached the meridian, casting forth a vast canopy of moonlight.
The wise one beheld the radiant one in the sky,
wandering like an intoxicated bull in a pen,
destroying the sins of the world.
And he beheld the moon, the cool-rayed one, approaching, augmenting the great ocean and illuminating all living beings.
That splendor which shines on earth while residing on Mount Mandara,
likewise at the onset of night while residing in the ocean,
and similarly upon the waters while residing in the lotus;
She shone like a swan perched upon a silver cage,
or like a lion dwelling within a cave of Mount Mandara, seated there amidst the lovely moon.
Just as a hero mounted upon a proud elephant,
so too did the moon shine while stationed in the sky;
it stood like a bull with sharp horns.
Like a great mountain with lofty white peaks,
like an elephant with tusks bound in gold,
the moon shines forth with its horns fully rounded.
His faults were destroyed by the rising of the moon of wisdom;
his faults regarding the consumption of flesh by Rākṣasas had increased; and the fault of his mind was impelled by the delightful Rāmā.
The divine evening, illuminating heaven, has arrived;
the sounds of lutes, pleasing to the ear, have begun;
and women of virtuous conduct sleep with their husbands.
And likewise, the night-prowlers,
engaged in most wonderful and fierce activities,
were intoxicated, heedless, and agitated.
The wise monkey beheld those households, crowded with chariots, horses, and auspicious seats, and filled with the splendor of heroes.
They insult one another excessively;
they brandish their thick arms;
they utter intoxicated ravings.
The intoxicated ones revile one another;
the rākṣasas strike at chests;
and they cast their limbs about their beloveds.
He saw lovely women conversing with one another,
while others there were sleeping again; likewise,
he saw great elephants trumpeting.
And with those well-honored and truly virtuous heroes sighing deeply,
the lake shone as if with hissing serpents.
Those who prioritize intelligence, those with pleasing names,
those full of faith, the foremost in the world,
and those of various kinds with pleasing names.
In that city he saw Yātudhānas; seeing them so handsome, endowed with various qualities corresponding to his own qualities, he rejoiced.
He saw some of them shining and beautiful, while others were again deformed;
then there were those worthy of boons and possessed of perfectly pure natures.
There he saw their women, possessed of great majesty, whose hearts were attached to their beloveds and their drinks,
and who were as radiant as stars.
He saw some women blazing with beauty yet veiled in modesty, like those embraced by their lovers at the hour of midnight, or as if enveloped in joy.
Just as birds are embraced by flowers,
others again sat upon the terraces of the palace, seated comfortably in the arms of their beloveds.
The wise one saw those women, beloved of their husbands, devoted to dharma, and settled in their homes, yet overcome by passion—
unveiled, with complexions like streaks of gold.
Some were of the highest excellence, with a complexion like refined gold;
others again had a complexion like the moon,
their beautiful limbs and complexions having been abandoned by their beloveds.
Then, having obtained those beloved objects pleasing to the mind, the women,
filled with great joy and beholding them, were exceedingly delighted in their homes.
That hero among the monkeys beheld those beautiful women,
their faces radiant as the moon,
with rows of curved eyes and lashes and beautiful lines of eyes.
And he beheld garlands of ornaments,
as beautiful as garlands of lightning;
yet he did not see Sītā, who was most noble-born.
On the royal road, he beheld a slender woman of noble birth, well-born like a creeper in full bloom, who had given birth while standing there.
Established upon the eternal path,
she whose eyes were fixed on Rāma was possessed by love;
her husband’s mind had entered into her glorious being.
She who was always more distinguished than even the most excellent women,
who was formerly adorned with a neck-ornament of the finest gold worthy of the best, now suffers from the heat, her throat choked with flowing tears.
With well-formed eyelashes and a lovely voice,
she was like a peahen wandering in the forest, or like the crescent of the moon with its faintly visible markings.
Like a streak of gold covered in dust,
like a scar from an arrow that has healed over,
or like a line of clouds dispersed by the wind.
Not seeing Sītā, the wife of Rāma, the lord of men and best among speakers,
he became stricken with grief after a long time.
Moving slowly like a monkey,
wandering at will among the bowers, that monkey, who could assume any form at will, traversed Laṅkā with great agility.
Then the fortunate one reached the residence of the lord of the rākṣasas,
which was surrounded by a radiant wall the color of the sun,
and guarded by fearsome rākṣasas like a great forest by lions.
Gazing at the palace, that elephant among monkeys shone brilliantly;
it was adorned with variegated archways set with silver and decorated with gold,
and surrounded by diverse courtyards and beautiful gates.
It was attended by great elephant-drivers mounted on elephants, by heroes free from fatigue,
and by irresistible horses moving in chariots;
[it was adorned] with armor made of the skins of lions and tigers, and with ivory, gold, and silver.
It was always traversed by various chariots making resonant sounds;
it was strewn with many jewels and contained the most excellent seats and vessels;
it was the dwelling place of great chariot-warriors and the great seat of the great chariot-warriors.
It was filled on all sides with various thousands of most magnificent deer and birds visible to the eye,
and it was well-protected by disciplined frontier guards and *rakṣas* demons.
The residence of the Lord of the Rākṣasas was filled on all sides with excellent women of the foremost rank; it was a jewel of a place where joyful maidens resided,
and with the tinkling of their exquisite ornaments, it produced a sound like the roar of the ocean.
That [palace], endowed with royal virtues, was adorned with the finest choice sandalwood;
it resounded with the beating of kettledrums and clay drums, and was made resonant with the blare of conchs.
It was constantly worshipped, offered sacrifices on festival days, and was always honored by the rākṣasas.
That great monkey beheld a vast mansion, as deep as the ocean and resonant like the ocean, filled with great jewels and crowded with many people.
Resplendent in its form and crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
that great monkey considered it truly the ornament of Laṅkā.
The vanara went from house to house among the Rākṣasas and through the gardens.
Looking about without fear, he moved through the palaces;
then, leaping with great speed from the residence of Prahasta,
the valiant one flew to another house, that of Mahāpārśva.
Then that great monkey leapt to the residence of Kumbhakarṇa, which resembled a cloud, and likewise to that of Vibhīṣaṇa,
as well as to those of Mahodara and Virūpākṣa.
That great monkey leapt to the abode of Vidyujjihva and likewise to that of Vidyutmālī; he also leapt to the abode of Vajradaṃṣṭra,
as well as to those of Śuka of great speed and the wise Sāraṇa.
Thus the leader of the monkey hosts went to the dwelling of Indrajit; the leader of the monkey hosts went to the dwellings of Jambumālī and Sumālī,
as well as to the abode of Raśmiketu and likewise that of Sūryaśatru.
The son of the Wind-god [Hanumān] visited the abodes of Dhūmrākṣa and Sampāti, as well as those of Bhīma—
who was like lightning— Ghana, Vighana,
Śukanābha, Vaktra, Śaṭha, and Vikaṭa.
Of the Rākṣasa Hrasvakarṇa, Daṃṣṭra, and Romaśa;
of Yuddhonmatta, Matta, Dhvajagrīva, and Nādina; and likewise of Vidyujjihva, Indrajihva, and Hastimukha.
Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, of great renown, proceeded step by step through those various magnificent palaces belonging to Karāla, Piśāca, and Śoṇitākṣa.
That great monkey beheld the supernatural power of those powerful beings;
having passed beyond all their dwellings on every side,
the illustrious one then reached the residence of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Wandering about, that best of monkeys, a tiger among monkeys, beheld the female Rākṣasas lying beside Rāvaṇa— beings with distorted eyes,
holding spears and mallets in their hands, and capable of wielding javelins.
In the palace of that lord of the Rākṣasas, he beheld various troops of elephants—
red, white, black, and even tawny ones— all possessed of great speed,
noble birth, and perfect form, capable of crushing the elephants of enemies.
In that house, he saw elephants equal to Airāvata in battle, stationed at the tips of their trunks, ready to slay the enemy forces;
they were like pouring clouds and like mountains discharging water.
Resounding with the roar of thunderclouds and invincible by enemies in battle,
there were a thousand chariot-divisions there, adorned with gold,
covered with golden nets, and resembling the rising sun.
In the residence of Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
that monkey, the son of the Wind-god, beheld palanquins of various forms,
as well as wonderful bowers of creepers and variegated picture galleries.
In the residence of Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, he saw other pleasure-houses, even wooden mountain-cottages, as well as the delightful chamber of Kāma and the daytime quarters.
He beheld that supreme palace, which resembled the surface of Mount Mandara, was crowded with peacock perches, and was strewn with flagstaffs;
it contained an infinite heap of jewels and a multitude of treasures on every side.
With its domestic tasks firmly established by wise overseers, that house shone like the abode of Bhūtapati;
and with the brilliance of the gems and the splendor of Rāvaṇa,
that mansion then gleamed like the sun with its rays.
The leader of the monkey hosts beheld couches and seats made entirely of Jāmbūnada gold, as well as brilliant vessels;
they were filled with jeweled containers moistened with honey and spirituous liquors.
It was as delightful and spacious as the abode of Kubera;
it resounded with the tinkling of anklets, the ringing of waist-bands,
and the rhythmic beating of drums.
Hanumān entered that great mansion, which was filled with clusters of palaces, crowded with hundreds of excellent women, and possessed well-arranged courtyards.
That powerful one beheld the entire network of chambers.
With its network of gold and inlaid lapis lazuli,
it was like a vast mass of clouds in the rainy season,
entwined with lightning and filled with flocks of birds.
And there were various halls for the dwellings,
as well as principal halls for conchs, weapons, and bows—
captivating and spacious.
He beheld moon-chambers upon the mountain-like mansions, houses resplendent with various treasures,
and highly honored even by gods and asuras.
Free from all defects,
the monkey beheld those [palaces] acquired by his own strength, which had been constructed with great effort.
He beheld the mansions of the Lord of Laṅkā upon the surface of the earth, which surpassed all others in excellence, appearing as if they had been fashioned by Maya himself.
Then he beheld [the mountain], which had the form of a towering cloud,
enchanting and beautiful with its golden appearance, resembling the sovereign power of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
For that most excellent house, of incomparable form,
was like heaven scattered upon the surface of the earth,
blazing with splendor and strewn with many jewels.
It was strewn with various kinds of flowers like the peak of a mountain covered in dust,
and it shone as if with the presence of the most excellent women.
Like a cloud being honored by flashes of lightning,
or like a celestial chariot being drawn by the finest swans, that vehicle of the virtuous was endowed with splendor in the sky.
He beheld the mountain peak, variegated with many minerals,
and the sky, adorned with planets and the moon,
and further embellished by clouds arranged in patterns.
The jewel of a celestial palace, variegated with many gems,
was fashioned; the earth was made filled with ranges of mountains,
and the mountains were made covered with canopies of trees.
The trees were fashioned full of canopies of blossoms;
the flowers were fashioned complete with filaments and petals;
and the dwellings were made white.
Likewise, there were lotus ponds with beautiful blossoms,
and furthermore, lotuses with their filaments;
as well as auspicious and variegated groves.
It was named Puṣpāhvaya,
resplendent and increasing with the radiance of jewels,
towering even above the most excellent dwellings.
There the great monkey saw a magnificent celestial palace,
with birds made of beryl, and likewise birds made of silver and coral.
And there were variegated serpents with diverse treasures,
as well as auspicious horses with limbs true to their noble breed,
possessing wings like coral and gold.
With their curved wings gracefully bent,
these birds with beautiful faces and fine wings appear like the very wings of Kāma manifest.
And the elephants being yoked had beautiful trunks;
they held lotuses with their filaments and were adorned with lotus-leaf ornaments on their trunks.
And the queen was made to have beautiful hands.
"Thus, having approached that beautiful house, Lakṣmī herself, lotus-handed,
was as if filled with wonder at that dwelling which was as lovely as a mountain."
And again, that supremely fragrant and beautiful [place] was like a mountain with lovely caves at the end of winter;
then that monkey, having approached her who was thus honored, [beheld her].
Wandering through the city protected by the arms of the ten-faced one,
he did not see that daughter of Janaka, who was highly honored,
yet deeply distressed, and held fast by the force of her husband’s virtues.
Then,

as he beheld the daughter of Janaka— who was herself of purified soul, of perfected self, and walking the excellent path— the mind of him whose own soul was likewise cultivated became exceedingly sorrowful.

Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, beheld in the center of that supreme abode of the great-souled one who possesses keen vision and wanders with discernment— a vast and extensive, most excellent palace.
That palace of the lord of the Rākṣasas was half a yojana in width and one yojana in length, crowded with many mansions;
yet he continued searching for Sītā, the princess of Videha, who possessed long eyes.
Hanumān, the slayer of enemies, moved about everywhere;
he saw it surrounded by elephants with four tusks as well as those with three,
crowded yet unconfined, guarded by those with weapons raised.
Rāvaṇa’s residence was filled with Rākṣasa women who were his wives,
and with princesses whom he had carried off by force;
it was like the ocean, teeming with crocodiles and sea-monsters, and crowded with timingila fish and large fish.
Agitated by the force of the wind like the ocean by serpents—
whatever splendor resided in Vaiśravaṇa and whatever splendor was in Indra, whose vehicle is the green horse,
all that was ever-present and never-failing in the house of Rāvaṇa.
Whatever prosperity belongs to King Kubera, Yama, and Varuṇa— such prosperity, or even superior to it, exists here in the houses of the Rākṣasa.
And situated in the middle of that palace is another well-constructed residence.

The son of the Wind-god beheld the celestial chariot named Puṣpaka, adorned with every kind of jewel, which had been fashioned by Viśvakarman in heaven for the sake of Brahmā; it was crowded with many turrets.
That which Kubera obtained from the Grandfather through supreme asceticism,
the Lord of the Rākṣasas obtained by conquering Kubera with his own might.
[He traveled] in vehicles yoked with deer, made of silver and gold, and swift as thought.
It was built up with the fruits of virtuous deeds, as if ablaze with splendor upon its pillars;
it was adorned on all sides with gabled chambers of auspicious form that, resembling Mount Meru and Mandara, seemed to scrape the very sky.
Resembling a blazing sun, it was well-constructed by Viśvakarman;
it was provided with golden staircases and beautiful, excellent altars,
and was equipped with latticed windows made of gold and crystal.
The great monkey ascended the divine Puṣpaka chariot, which had a platform made of the finest sapphire and emerald gems;
standing there, he then smelled the fragrance arising from drinks, snacks, and foods.

Smelling that divine, pervasive fragrance, as if it were a beautiful wind, that scent— as if a kinsman calling to his dearest kin— seemed to say to that Great Being, "Come this way," toward where Rāvaṇa was located.
Then, having set out, he beheld that great and auspicious hall,
which was as pleasing to Rāvaṇa’s mind as a beautiful woman;
it was adorned with jeweled staircases and resplendent with golden lattices.
Its floor was covered with crystal, its wall-pilasters were set between ivory columns, and it was adorned with pearls, corals, silver,
and gold, as well as many pillars embellished with precious gems.
With pillars that were smooth, straight, exceedingly tall, and beautifully adorned on all sides,
it seemed as if it were about to ascend to heaven upon its lofty wings;
it was covered with a great rug marked with the signs of the earth.
Like the vast earth, garlanded with kingdoms and houses,
resounding with the cries of intoxicated birds, perfumed with divine fragrances,
furnished with the most excellent carpets, and inhabited by the lord of the rākṣasas.
She was smoky with the incense of agallochum, yet stainless and white as a swan;
she was variegated with offerings of flowers, possessing a radiant luster like that of a dappled cow.
She produced delight for the mind and brought clarity even to the complexion.
She, who destroys sorrow and is divine, was like the very source of prosperity;
then, protected by Rāvaṇa, she gratified her five senses with the five most excellent objects of the senses, just as a mother does for her children.
"This must be heaven, this must be the world of the gods, this must be the city of Indra;
or perhaps this is supreme spiritual perfection (siddhi)," so thought the son of the Wind-god.
As he reflected thus, he beheld golden lamps there.
She thought herself ablaze with the light of the lamps, the splendor of Rāvaṇa, and the radiance of her ornaments— like great rogues who have defeated swindlers at dice.
Then he saw a thousand excellent women, adorned with garments and garlands of various colors, seated upon carpets;
it was at the turn of midnight, and they were all overcome by the power of drink and sleep.
Having ceased his play at night, he then slept soundly;
as he lay thus asleep, he shone forth with his inner ornaments silenced,
like a vast forest of lotuses where the swans and bees are silent.
The son of the Wind beheld the faces of those beautiful women, their teeth concealed and their eyes closed,
yet fragrant as lotuses that had opened at the end of the night.
Then, with their petals closed as if at night,
these lotus-faces shone; surely bees intoxicated with passion seek them out again and again, as if they were full-blown lotuses.
Thus the illustrious great monkey reflected;
for he considered those [lakes] to be equal in quality to the lotus-born ones.
That hall of his shone brightly, adorned by those women.
Like the autumnal sky, serene and adorned with stars,
the lord of the Rākṣasas shone, surrounded by them,
just as the glorious moon is encompassed by the stars.
5.007.039a Those stars that fall from the sky, enveloped by the remnants of their merit—
5.007.039c Hari then thought that all of them had gathered here.
5.007.040a They were clearly visible like great stars of auspicious radiance.
The radiance, complexion, and grace of the women there shone forth; their heavy,
thick garlands were displaced and their excellent ornaments scattered,
as their minds were overcome by sleep during the times of drinking and revelry.

Some of those excellent women had their forehead-marks smudged, some had their anklets jingling out of place, and some had their necklaces slipped from their sides. Others had their faces covered by their necklaces, while still others had their garments disarrayed.
With their waist-bands and cords disarrayed, they were like young mares that had been driven hard;
others, wearing beautiful earrings, with their garlands broken and crushed,
were like flowering creepers trampled by lordly elephants in the great forest.
And the magnificent necklaces of some women, shining like rays of moonlight,
lay sleeping upon their breasts like swans;
and on others, the lapis lazuli beads appeared like kādamba birds.
And the golden threads upon others became like ruddy geese;
crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and adorned by ruddy geese,
they shone like rivers with their hips as if they were sandy banks.
Resembling networks of tinkling bells, with vast golden lotuses as their substance, those women— having passion for their crocodiles and fame for their banks— appeared like sleeping rivers.
They rested upon the soft limbs and the tips of the breasts of some.
The rows of ornaments became like beautiful ornaments themselves;
and the hems of the garments of some, stirred by the breath from their mouths,
were repeatedly tossed upward above their faces.
5.007.051a Those wives of radiant splendor, like uplifted banners,
shone at the base of the faces of those women of various colors and gold.
5.007.052a And there, the earrings of some of them, possessing auspicious luster, swayed to and fro.
Through contact with the breath from the mouths of those beautiful women,
that scent of sugar-wine— naturally fragrant and pleasant—
was then wafted by their exhalations and served Rāvaṇa.
Some of Rāvaṇa’s wives, suspecting them to be the faces of Rāvaṇa himself,
repeatedly smelled the faces of their co-wives;
for those excellent women were utterly infatuated with Rāvaṇa.
Lacking independence, they then did only what was pleasing to their co-wives;
placing their arms one upon another,
those women, adorned with bracelets and wearing beautiful garments, lay down there.
One woman rested her chest against another’s, while yet another clasped her arms around her; another rested her lap against one woman’s, and yet another her arms against hers.
They leaned upon one another’s thighs, sides, hips, and backs.
With their limbs intertwined, following the influence of intoxication and affection,
those slender-waisted women, delighted by the touch of one another’s bodies,
all fell asleep there with their arms entwined.
For that row of women was indeed strung together by the thread of their arms;
like a garland woven on a string with intoxicated bees,
it shone like a cluster of flowering creepers in the month of Mādhava when stirred by the wind.
With their garlands intertwined with one another and their clusters of flowers closely joined,
their beautiful necks entwined and swarming with bees from one another,
that grove of women belonging to Rāvaṇa was like a forest in full bloom.
Even though they were well-adorned, it was impossible at that time to distinguish the ornaments, garments, and garlands of those women;
for while Rāvaṇa lay there in deep repose, those women of diverse splendor remained indistinguishable.
Blazing golden lamps seemed as if they were gazing with unblinking eyes;
the women of the royal sages, ancestors, Daityas, and Gandharvas,
as well as the daughters of the Rākṣasas, fell under the sway of desire for him.
Therein, no woman was taken by force;
she was won through the quality of his heroic prowess.
She desired no other man, nor had she belonged to another before.
Except for the daughter of Janaka, who is worthy of the best,
there is no one of low birth, nor of inferior form; none who is lacking in courtesy, nor devoid of proper conduct.
His wife was not lacking in virtue,
nor was she unlovely to her beloved;
yet the mind of the lord of monkeys became troubled.
Since such is this lawful wife of Rāghava,
compared to these wives of the king of the rākṣasas,
it was indeed well-born for him, O one of virtuous intellect.
And again, appearing distressed, he thought:
"Sītā is surely distinguished by her virtues;
therefore, this high-souled one has acted toward her in such a way."
Alas, what a cruel and ignoble deed!
There, Hanumān beheld a principal couch, divine in appearance, made of crystal and adorned with jewels, as he looked about.
And in one part of that place, he saw a white umbrella, adorned with the finest garlands and resembling the lord of the stars (the moon),
being fanned on all sides by hands holding yak-tail whisks.
It was graced with various perfumes and incensed with excellent incense;
it was spread with the finest coverlets and lined with woolen skins,
and it was adorned all around with strings of choice garlands.
Upon him [he saw] one resembling a cloud, with blazing, excellent earrings,
red eyes, mighty arms, and clad in garments of great silver;
his limbs were anointed with fragrant red sandalwood paste.
Like a cloud in the sky reddened by twilight and streaked with lightning,
he was beautiful, able to assume any form at will, and adorned with divine ornaments;
rich with trees, forests, and shrubs, he resembled Mount Mandara while it lay asleep.

The great monkey saw him resting after his night’s play, adorned with excellent ornaments— beloved by the daughters of the rākṣasas and bringing happiness to the rākṣasas— and he saw him even as he lay there, having finished drinking.
Approaching the heroic Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, who was sleeping upon his sun-bright bed and sighing like a serpent, that best of monkeys,
overcome with extreme agitation, drew back as if terrified.
Then, having reached the ascent and taken his place upon another altar,
the great monkey beheld the tiger among rākṣasas lying asleep. The excellent bed of the sleeping lord of the rākṣasas shone with splendor.
When Gandhahastin had fallen asleep at the great spring,
he saw the two outstretched arms of that high-souled lord of the Rākṣasas, adorned with golden bracelets and resembling the banners of Indra.
Their broad shoulders bore scars from being gored by the tips of Airāvata’s tusks; they were scarred by the thunderbolt and circled by Viṣṇu’s discus.
Their thick, symmetrical, well-formed shoulders met together, endowed with great strength.
His thumbs and nails were auspiciously marked, and his fingers and palms were well-defined;
his arms were joined together, shaped like iron clubs, rounded,
and resembling the trunks of elephants, appearing like two five-headed serpents when stretched out upon the white bed.
Anointed with the most excellent sandalwood paste— cool as rabbit's blood,
fragrant, and highly refined— and beautifully adorned, they were massaged by the finest women and treated with the most sublime perfumes.
That monkey saw his two arms resting upon the bed, resounding with the cries of yakṣas, pannagas, gandharvas, gods,
and dānavas; they lay there like two great, enraged serpents asleep within Mount Mandara.
With those two fully developed arms, the lord of the Rākṣasas shone like Mount Mandara with its two peaks,
fragrant with mango and *puṃnāga* trees and joined by the finest *bakula*.
Accompanied by the flavors of refined food and preceded by the scent of drink,
a great exhalation issued from the mouth of that lion among Rākṣasas as he lay there, as if filling the entire house.
His face was radiant with earrings and adorned by a displaced crown that shone with gold variegated with pearls and gems;
likewise, he was graced by a necklace smeared with red sandalwood paste.
He was resplendent with a chest that was thick, broad,
and expansive; his eyes were blood-red from wounds, and he was well-encased in a discarded white linen garment and a costly, superior yellow robe.
Resembling a heap of black gram, sighing like a serpent,
he was like an elephant fast asleep on the vast waters of the Ganges;
[he was surrounded] by four golden lamps blazing in the four directions.
With all his limbs illuminated like a cloud by flashes of lightning,
he saw at the feet of that great-souled lord of the Rākṣasas,
who was accompanied by his beloved wives, those very wives themselves within the house.
The leader of the monkey hosts beheld women whose faces shone like the moon, adorned with excellent earrings, wearing unfading garlands and ornaments;
they were skilled in dance and music, and rested upon the arms of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
The monkey saw them seated there, wearing excellent ornaments;
he beheld the earrings made of refined gold and the armlets upon the women, which were set with diamonds and lapis lazuli at their edges.
With their beautiful faces, which resembled the moon and were adorned with graceful earrings,
that celestial chariot shone like the sky filled with clusters of stars.
Those wives of the lord of the Rākṣasas were weary from intoxication and exertion.
In various places, those slender-waisted women were fast asleep.
One was clearly visible, fast asleep while embracing her lute,
like a lotus plant from a great river clinging to a boat as it drifts away.
Another dark-eyed, passionate woman, with a madduka drum tucked under her arm, shone as she slept like a mother tenderly toward her young son.
And another woman of beautiful limbs and lovely breasts lay sleeping, pressing a paṭaha drum against her.
5.008.036c Having found her lover after a long time, as if embracing him,
a certain lotus-eyed woman— 5.008.037a a beautiful lady who had fallen under the power of sleep— fell asleep while embracing his shoulder, like a passionate woman with her beloved.
Another, with limbs resembling gold— soft, plump, and beautiful—
was fast asleep with her eyes heavy with intoxication, pressing against a mṛdaṅga drum;
that slender-waisted woman had the instrument resting between her arms and at her side.

5.008.039c Another blameless woman, exhausted by the intoxication [of music], slept with her drum; 5.008.040a another, having taken up her *ḍiṇḍima* drum, likewise remained clinging to it as she slept,
like a passionate woman embracing a young calf.

A certain lotus-eyed woman, intoxicated with passion, lay fast asleep after pressing her arms against the *āḍambara* (the headboard). Another beautiful woman shone as she slept, having cast aside her water-jar.
In spring, like a garland variegated with flowers and freshly groomed, a certain woman—
overcome by the power of sleep— fell asleep while embracing with both her hands her breasts, which resembled golden jars.
Another lotus-eyed woman with a face like the full moon,
that fair-hipped lady, lay fast asleep, overwhelmed by intoxication, embracing another woman;
and excellent women were embracing various musical instruments.
Having pressed their lovers with their breasts, those amorous women slept as if they were embracing them; there, upon a beautiful couch set aside in a secluded spot,
that monkey beheld another woman endowed with perfect beauty lying asleep.
She was exquisitely adorned with ornaments set with pearls and gems; she seemed to embellish that supreme palace with her own splendor—
Gaurī, possessing a golden complexion, the beloved mistress of the inner apartments.

There, the monkey saw Mandodarī lying down, possessed of a beautiful form. Seeing her adorned, the mighty-armed son of the Wind-god reflected that she must be Sītā because of her perfection of beauty and youth.
Filled with great joy, the leader of the monkey hosts rejoiced;
he clapped his hands, kissed his tail,
rejoiced, played, sang, and moved about.
Climbing the pillars, he leaped down to the ground,
demonstrating his own nature as a monkey; then, shaking off that state of mind, he remained composed.
5.009.001 And the great monkey turned his thoughts once more toward Sītā:
5.009.002 "Separated from Rāma, that passionate lady cannot possibly sleep;
she is not able to eat, nor to adorn herself, nor even to partake of drink."
Thinking, "There is no other man to attend upon, even if he were the lord of the gods—
for indeed, there is no one equal to Rāma even among the thirty deities," he wandered through the drinking grounds, certain that she was someone else.
Some were exhausted by playing, others likewise by singing;
some were worn out by dancing, and others were overcome by drinking. They remained seated upon drums, mṛdaṅgas, and stools.
Likewise, other women lay upon the finest carpets;
they were accompanied by a thousand adorned ladies,
skilled in conversation regarding beauty and capable of speaking with meaningful songs.
The leader of the monkey host, who was skilled in place and time and spoke with reasoned words, beheld [the city] where they were fast asleep, having been lulled by their pleasure;
in the midst of them, the mighty-armed lord of the Rākṣasas shone resplendent.
Like a bull in the midst of a great and preeminent herd of cows,
that lord of the Rākṣasas shone as he himself was surrounded by them,
like a great elephant roaming through a forest encircled by female elephants.
In the palace of that lord of the rākṣasas, the tiger among monkeys beheld a drinking hall endowed with every object of desire,
where deer, buffaloes, and boars were laid out in portions.
There, on the drinking grounds, he saw meats laid out;
and in large golden vessels,
he saw half-eaten peacocks as well as cocks, O tiger among monkeys.
Hanumān observed wild boars and rhinoceroses mixed with curd and sauvarcala salt, as well as porcupines, deer,
and peacocks; he also saw various prepared kṛkara birds and half-eaten cakora birds.
Buffaloes, single-horned animals, and goats prepared for sacrifice;
various kinds of foods to be licked, drunk, and eaten;
and diverse *rāga-ṣāḍavas* distinguished by sour and salty flavors.
Strewn with necklaces, anklets, and armlets of great value cast aside,
and scattered with drinking vessels and various fruits,
the earth, having been offered these floral tributes, manifests even greater splendor.
With beds and seats arranged here and there, so well-fitted together,
the drinking hall appeared as if ablaze even without a fire;
it was filled with various kinds of excellent foods prepared with diverse refinements.
In the drinking halls, various divine and pleasing liquors were served separately, including those mixed with meat prepared by skilled cooks, as well as *surā* made from grain,
sugar-based spirits (*śarkarāsava*), honey-wine (*mādhvīka*), and spirits distilled from flowers and fruits (*puṣpāsava* and *phalāsava*).
The ground shone, strewn with various types of fragrant powders, each distinct from the other, and covered with many scattered garlands;
it was also adorned with golden water-pitchers and vessels made of crystal.
It was surrounded by other water-jars made of Jāmbūnada gold;
and there the monkey beheld an abundance of the finest drink in both silver and golden jars.
That great monkey saw vessels made of gold, others of gems, and some of silver, all filled with *śīdhu* liquor;
in some places there were only half-remnants, while in others it had been drunk entirely away.
In some places he saw drinks that had not been drunk at all;
in some places various kinds of foods, and in some places drinks distributed in portions;
and in some places seeing remnants of food, he indeed wandered about.
In some places there were broken jars, in others overturned pots;
in some places the waters were mingled with garlands and fruits. Furthermore, there were many empty beds belonging to women here.
5.009.026c Some excellent women slept while embracing one another; 5.009.027a and some woman, having snatched away the garment of another and embraced her, lay there asleep,
that helpless woman overcome by the power of sleep.
By the breath of their sighing, their garments and the garlands upon their bodies did not flutter excessively, as if they had encountered only a gentle breeze.
And [there was the scent] of cool sandalwood and of sweet-flavored wine.
There, the wind blew in many ways, carrying the diverse fragrances of various garlands and flowers;
it was intensified by the scents of bathing powders, sandalwood, and incense.
Then a fragrant scent wafted through the Puṣpaka chariot. There in that abode of the Rākṣasa, some excellent women were dark-complexioned and fair, while others had limbs the color of gold.
Because they were under the power of sleep and stupefied by passion,
the appearance of those lotus-like women was exactly like that of sleeping lotus plants.
In this way, the monkey [beheld] the entire inner apartment of Rāvaṇa without exception.
The one of great majesty beheld them, yet he did not see Jānakī. As that great monkey gazed upon those women,
he fell into deep anxiety, apprehensive of violating righteousness.
To gaze upon another man's wife while she is asleep within the inner apartments—
this will surely cause a great violation of my dharma;
for my sight has never before been directed toward the wives of others.
And here I have seen this taking of another's wife;
then another thought arose in that wise man,
whose mind was fixed on a single point and who perceived the certainty of what must be done.
"Granted, I have seen all the wives of Rāvaṇa with confidence;
yet, not even the slightest perturbation arises in my mind.
For the mind is the cause that sets all the senses in motion."
In both auspicious and inauspicious circumstances, that [truth] is well-established for me:
indeed, Vaidehī cannot be sought out by me anywhere else than among women;
for in the course of a thorough search, women are always to be found among women.
5.009.041a One must search for a being in that very womb from which it was born. 5.009.041c It is not possible to search for a lost woman among female deer.
5.009.042a Therefore, this has been searched by me with a pure mind thus far.
The courageous Hanumān beheld Rāvaṇa’s inner apartments and the lakes, yet Janakī was not to be seen; though he looked among the daughters of the gods, the Gandharvas,
and the Nāgas, he did not see Jānakī at all.
Not seeing her there, yet beholding other excellent women,
the heroic monkey then withdrew and began to reflect.
That vanara was in the middle of that palace;
Eager for a sight of Sītā, he went to the vine-arbors, the painted chambers, and the night-quarters,
yet he did not see that lady of lovely appearance.
Then that great monkey thought:
"Not seeing that beloved of the joy of the Raghus, surely Sītā must be dying, for she does not appear before me."
As he searched, the young Maithilī came into his sight— she who was devoted solely to the preservation of her own virtue, guarded by that foremost of Rākṣasas.
Surely she, who stood upon the supreme path of the noble ones, must have been slain by this man of truly wicked deeds—
she who was once of beautiful form, yet now disfigured, deformed, and lusterless.
Beholding those wives of the Rākṣasa king, who had large mouths and long, misshapen appearances,
