the daughter of the lord of Janaka was overcome with fear.
Having failed to see Sītā and having exhausted my manly efforts,
and having spent a long time with the monkeys,
I have no way to remain in the presence of Sugrīva.
The powerful monkey, who wields a most severe rod of punishment,
has searched the entire inner apartment and seen Rāvaṇa’s women;
yet the virtuous Sītā is not to be seen, and my labor has been in vain.
"What indeed will all the monkeys say to me when we have gathered together after my departure?
O hero, having gone there, tell us what was done by you.
Not having seen that daughter of Janaka, what shall I say?"
5.010.008c They will surely resort to fasting unto death when time has passed.
5.010.009a What will the aged Jāmbavān and Aṅgada say, and what will the assembled monkeys say, who have reached the far shore of the ocean?
5.010.010a Perseverance is the root of prosperity; perseverance is the highest happiness. 5.010.010c I shall search further in places where no search has yet been made.
5.010.011a For perseverance always impels one toward the attainment of all goals.
"He makes fruitful whatever action a living being performs.
Therefore, I shall exert my highest effort without despondency;
I will search through the lands ruled by Rāvaṇa that have not yet been seen."
They constructed drinking halls, as well as flower-houses,
picture galleries, and further, various pleasure-houses;
they also built inner garden paths and palatial mansions in every direction.
Having reflected thus, he began to search once more—
among underground chambers, shrines, houses, and even small inner apartments—
flying up, falling down, standing still, and moving again here and there.
Opening doors and battering down panels,
entering and rushing out, falling down and springing up,
that great monkey roamed through every available space.

Not even a space the size of four fingers was found in that inner apartment of Rāvaṇa’s harem which the monkey did not enter. He traversed the streets within the ramparts and the platforms situated near the shrines.
He beheld chasms and lotus-pools; everything was surveyed by him.
There he saw Rākṣasa women of various forms, misshapen and deformed, but not that daughter of Janaka.

Hanumān beheld there the most excellent women of the Vidyādharas, peerless in beauty in the world; yet he did not see the one who brings joy to Rāghava. He also saw daughters of the Nāgas with beautiful limbs and faces resembling the full moon.
Hanumān saw her there, but not Sītā of the slender waist; rather,
he saw that the daughters of the Nāgas had been forcibly seized by the lord of the Rākṣasas after he had overwhelmed them,
but that daughter of Janaka was not there.
Seeing her, yet seeing other excellent women as well,
the mighty-armed Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, despaired.
He reflected upon the exertion of the lords of the monkeys and their leaping across the ocean.
Seeing it all in vain, the son of the Wind-god again fell into deep reflection.
Then Hanumān, the son of Māruta, having descended from the celestial chariot,
was overcome with anxiety as his mind was stricken by grief.
Having leaped from the palace onto the wall, Hanūmān, the leader of the monkey hosts, became as swift as lightning amidst the clouds. Having circled around Rāvaṇa’s residences, Hanūmān—
Not having seen Jānakī Sītā, the monkey spoke these words:
"Lanka has been searched extensively by me while performing what is pleasing to Rāma;
yet I do not see Vaidehī Sītā, who is beautiful in all her limbs."
5.011.004a Pools, ponds, lakes, and likewise rivers; 5.011.004c streams, marshy forest edges, and inaccessible mountains—
I have searched the entire earth, yet I do not see Jānakī.

5.011.005a Here, Sītā was described by Saṃpāti, the king of vultures, as being in the abode of Rāvaṇa; yet, I do not see her. 5.011.006a Is she indeed Sītā, the princess of Videha, the daughter of Janaka from Mithilā?
Helpless, she might wait upon Rāvaṇa, that man of evil conduct;
or, as the Rākṣasa flies away swiftly taking Sītā,
she might fall in mid-air, terrified by the arrows of Rāma.
Or rather, as she was being carried away along the path frequented by the Siddhas,
I believe the noble lady’s heart must have failed her upon beholding the ocean,
while it was also being crushed by Rāvaṇa’s thighs and his arms.
I believe that noble lady of large eyes has given up her life; surely,
as she was then stepping higher and higher over the ocean,
Janaka’s daughter fell into the sea while struggling.
"Or has that wretched Rāvaṇa, while she was protecting her own virtue, devoured the poor Sītā who has no protector? Or else,
has that dark-eyed woman been taken by the wives of the lord of the Rākṣasas?"

Though she herself was innocent, she will have been devoured by those of wicked intent. Meditating on Rāma’s face— which resembles the full moon and has eyes like lotus petals— that miserable woman has met her death.
"Alas Rāma! Alas Lakṣmaṇa! and "Alas Ayodhyā!"—thus lamenting profusely, the princess of Mithilā will lay down her body.
Or rather, I believe she has been cast into the dwelling of Rāvaṇa.
"Surely she laments softly like a female śārikā bird confined in a cage;
born in the family of Janaka, the slender-waisted wife of Rāma—
how could that lotus-petal-eyed woman fall under the power of Rāvaṇa?"
Whether she has perished, been lost, or died—the daughter of Janaka—it is not fitting to inform Rāma, her beloved husband.
If it were reported, there would be harm; if it were not reported, there would be harm.
"How indeed should this be done? It appears difficult to me. Now that the matter has reached this state, what would be appropriate and timely?
Thus Hanumān reflected further, deliberating upon his thoughts.
5.011.020a If I depart from here for the city of the lord of monkeys without having seen Sītā, 5.011.020c then what purpose will there be for my manly effort?
5.011.021a This leaping of mine across the ocean will have been in vain.
The entry into Laṅkā and the sighting of the Rākṣasas;
what indeed will Sugrīva say, or the assembled monkeys,
when those two sons of Daśaratha have reached Kiṣkindhā?
"But if, having gone to the descendant of Kakutstha, I speak this most unpleasant news—
that Sītā has not been seen by me— then they will give up their lives.
[It would be] harsh, dreadful, cruel, sharp, and a tormentor of the senses."
Having heard those harsh words spoken on account of Sītā, he will cease to exist.
But seeing him fallen into such distress, his mind set upon death,
the wise Lakṣmaṇa, who is deeply devoted to him, will likewise cease to exist.
Hearing that his two brothers have perished, Bharata too will die;
and seeing Bharata dead, Śatrughna will not survive. Then, beholding their sons dead, the mothers will cease to exist.
Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and Kaikeyī— of this there is no doubt—
and Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, who is grateful and true to his promise,
will likewise give up their lives upon seeing Rāma in such a state.
Dejected, distressed, miserable, joyless, and wretched, Rumā—
tormented by grief for her husband and emaciated by sorrow caused by Vālin’s son— will give up her life.
When the king has met his death, even Tārā will cease to exist; with the destruction of her parents and the calamity that has befallen Sugrīva,
why would Prince Aṅgada continue to cling to life?
Overwhelmed by grief born of their lord’s absence, those forest-dwellers will strike their own heads with their palms and fists.
[They should be pacified] with conciliation, gifts, and honorable praise.
Cherished by the king of monkeys, these vanaras shall give up their lives;
no longer will those elephant-like monkeys gather together to enjoy their play in the forests, upon the mountains, or in the caves.
Afflicted by the calamity that has befallen their master,
they will fall from mountain peaks, or gather together in rugged places; they will take poison, or hang themselves, or enter into fire.
"Then the monkeys will practice fasting and take up arms;
I believe there will be a terrible lamentation when I have departed,
as well as the destruction of the Ikṣvāku lineage and the destruction of the forest-dwellers."
Therefore, I shall not go from here to the city of Kiṣkindhā;
for I am unable to face Sugrīva without Maithilī. While I remain here and do not depart, those two righteous-souled great chariot-warriors [will surely act].
5.011.039c Out of hope, those two and the wise forest-dwellers will sustain themselves.

5.011.040a Taking only what is placed in my hand, taking only what is placed in my mouth, self-restrained and dwelling at the foot of trees, 5.011.040c I shall become a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) until I have seen the daughter of Janaka.
"In a region on the coastal marshlands of the ocean, abundant in roots, fruits, and water,
I shall prepare a funeral pyre and enter the kindled fire born of the fire-drills; or else, remaining seated in the proper manner, I shall accomplish the goal of the ascetic."
"Crows and beasts of prey will devour my body;
this too is a departure witnessed by the seers—such is my thought. I shall enter the waters completely if I do not see Jānakī."

With its well-grown roots, fortunate, garlanded with fame, and glorious— this long-standing hope of mine has been shattered by my not seeing Sītā. I shall become an ascetic, self-restrained, dwelling at the foot of a tree.
"I shall not return from here without having seen that dark-eyed lady.
If I return from here without having found Sītā,
Aṅgada will no longer exist along with all the monkeys."
"There are many evils in death; while living, one attains what is auspicious.
Therefore, I shall preserve my life; for when one lives, reunion is certain.
Thus he repeatedly bore this manifold sorrow in his mind.
At that time, that elephant among monkeys did not find the end of his grief:
"I shall slay Rāvaṇa, the ten-necked one of great strength;
let Sītā have been abducted at will—it shall be avenged."
"Or else, having lifted him up high above the ocean,
I shall present him to Rāma like an animal to Paśupati. Thus he fell into such thoughts, failing to find Sītā.
Overwhelmed by grief and meditation, the monkey reflected:
"As long as I do not see the illustrious Sītā, the wife of Rāma,
I shall search this city of Laṅkā again and again."
"If I bring Rāma here on the word of Saṃpāti,
Rāghava, not seeing his wife, might consume all the monkeys with his wrath.
Therefore, I shall remain right here, restrained in my senses and restricted in my food."
5.011.054c Let not all those men and monkeys perish on my account.
5.011.055a This great Aśoka grove with its many large trees— 5.011.055c I shall go there, for it has not yet been searched by me.
Having paid homage to the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, as well as the Aśvins and the Maruts, I shall depart, increasing the grief of the Rākṣasas;
and having conquered the Rākṣasas, I shall [rescue] the goddess who brings joy to the Ikṣvāku lineage.
"I shall bestow it upon Rāma, the ascetic, according to his accomplishment.
Having meditated for a moment, his senses bound by anxiety,
the mighty-armed Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, arose.
Homage be to Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa,
and to that goddess, the daughter of Janaka;
homage be to Rudra, Indra, Yama, and Vāyu.
"Salutations be to the moon, the sun, and the hosts of winds!
Having paid homage to them and to Sugrīva, Māruti surveyed all the directions and [beheld] the Aśoka grove."
Having first gone mentally to the auspicious Aśoka grove,
the monkey, son of the Wind, reflected further:
"This forest-thicket will surely be heavily guarded by Rākṣasas."
The Aśoka grove, conditioned by all formative forces (*saṃskāra*), must be contemplated; guards have surely been stationed here to protect the trees,
and even the Blessed One, the soul of all, does not blow with excessive turbulence.

5.011.064a This account of myself and of Rāvaṇa for the sake of Rāma has been told by me in brief. 5.011.064c May the gods, together with the hosts of ṛṣis, here bring about my success. 5.011.065a May the self-existent Lord Brahmā and the gods likewise grant it to me.
Agni and Vāyu, Puruhūta the wielder of the thunderbolt,
Varuṇa with noose in hand, as well as Soma and the Ādityas,
the two high-souled Aśvins, and all the Maruts— these have attained perfection.
"May all beings grant me success, and he who is the lord of beings, and those others who are unseen and move along the path.
That [fruit] which has a prominent nose, white teeth, and is free from blemish— "
When indeed shall I behold that noble lady’s face, with its pure smile and eyes like lotus petals, its appearance resembling the serene Lord of Stars?
By that base, sinful man of cruel deeds,
wearing a most dreadful and disguised appearance, that helpless, ascetic woman was overcome by force.
"How might she come within the range of my vision this very day?
Having reflected thus for a moment and having perceived her with his mind,
he of great splendor leaped over the wall of that residence.
With all his limbs thrilled with joy, that great monkey, standing upon the rampart,
beheld various trees with flowering tops at the onset of spring:
*sāla* trees, *aśoka* trees, and *bhavya* and *campaka* trees in full bloom.
[He saw] *uddālaka* trees, *nāgavṛkṣa* trees, mangoes, and even *kapimukha* trees;
then, like an iron arrow released from a bowstring, he leapt across the grove of trees, which was covered with mango orchards and entwined by hundreds of creepers.
Having entered that variegated grove, which resounded with the cries of birds and was surrounded on all sides by trees of silver and gold,
he beheld that wonderful forest filled with flocks of birds and herds of deer.
The monkey Hanumān beheld her, who resembled the rising sun,
surrounded by various kinds of trees laden with flowers and fruits,
and constantly frequented by intoxicated cuckoos and *bhṛṅgarāja* birds.
In that time when the people were overjoyed and the place was filled with beasts and birds,
[he wandered] through the grove resounding with intoxicated peacocks and teeming with various flocks of birds,
searching for the blameless princess of noble form.
The monkey awakened the birds sleeping peacefully;
as the flocks of birds flew up, their wings struck the *sāla* trees,
which released showers of flowers of many colors and various kinds.
5.012.011a Strewn with flowers, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, shone resplendent;
5.012.011c like a mountain made of blossoms in the midst of the Aśoka grove.
5.012.012a [They saw] the monkey situated within the thicket of trees, leaping toward all directions.
Seeing all these beings, they thought, "Spring has arrived.
Covered with various kinds of flowers fallen from the trees,
the earth there shone like an adorned young woman.
Then, violently shaken by the forceful monkey, those swift trees released various kinds of flowers;
their leafy crests were stripped away, and their trees were shorn of blossoms and fruit.
5.012.015c Like defeated rogues who have cast off their clothes and ornaments,
5.012.016a those excellent trees, shaken by the swift Hanumān,
5.012.016c quickly shed their flowers, leaves, and fruits, though they were once so full of blossoms.
Deprived of their flocks of birds, those trees became mere trunks; all the trees were stripped bare, as if shaken down by a violent wind.
They appeared like a young woman with disheveled hair and her cosmetic pigments rubbed away.
With her beautiful teeth and lips crushed, mangled by claws and teeth,
and likewise trampled by tails, hands, and feet,
the Aśoka grove became a place where the noble trees were utterly broken.
The monkey swiftly tore apart the garlands of great creepers,
just as the wind scatters masses of clouds over the Vindhya mountains during the rainy season.
There, he [trampled] delightful floors made of jewels and silver.
Thus, as the monkey roamed over the lands of gold,
he beheld ponds of various shapes filled with the finest water,
provided here and there with costly staircases made of jewels.
With sands of pearls and coral, with pavements inlaid within crystal,
they were adorned by variegated golden trees growing along their banks;
they possessed groves of blooming lotuses and water-lilies and resounded with the cries of ruddy geese.
Resounding with the cries of water-fowl and the calls of birds, and made vocal by swans and cranes,
they were adorned on all sides by long rivers lined with trees,
which were auspicious and possessed waters like nectar.
Covered by hundreds of creepers and overspread with *santānaka* trees,
the forests were filled with various shrubs and interspersed with *karavīra* flowers.
Then [he saw] the mountain, resembling a mass of clouds, with its peaks towering high.

The tiger among monkeys beheld that delightful mountain in the world, which was adorned with various peaks, surrounded on all sides by summits, covered with stone dwellings, and filled with diverse trees.
And from that mountain, the monkey beheld a river falling down,
like a beloved woman leaping from the lap of her lover;
it was adorned by trees whose tips had fallen into the water.
The great monkey saw her, like an angry woman being restrained by her dear kinsmen, with her waters turned back once more,
appearing like a beloved wife who has returned to her lover in a gracious mood.
Not far from there, Hanumān, the tiger among monkeys and son of the Wind-god, beheld lotus ponds filled with various flocks of birds. He also saw an artificial pool brimming with cool water.
With stairs made of the finest jewels and beautified by sand of pearls,
it possessed a variegated and wonderful forest filled with various herds of deer;
and it was adorned with immense palaces constructed by Viśvakarman.
It was adorned on all sides with both natural and artificial groves. Whatever trees were there, laden with flowers and fruits,
all had parasols and lamps, and all possessed pedestals made of gold.
That great monkey saw a single golden *śiṃśupā* tree, covered with many spreading creepers and many leaves;
he also beheld portions of the ground, as well as pits and springs.
He beheld other golden trees resembling crests of fire;
by the radiance of those trees, the heroic great monkey then thought, "I am made of gold," like Mount Meru.
Seeing that [palace], fanned by the wind with its clusters of golden trees and resounding with the tinkling of hundreds of small bells, he was filled with wonder; it was beautiful,
with its tips in full bloom and its young shoots and sprouts fresh.
Having climbed that *śiṃśapā* tree, which was thick with foliage, I, possessed of great speed, shall see from here Vaidehī, who longs for the sight of Rāma and is wandering here and there by chance,
afflicted with grief.
And this Aśoka grove of the evil-minded one is exceedingly beautiful,
adorned with Campaka, sandalwood, and Bakula trees;
and here is this lovely lotus pond, frequented by flocks of birds.
5.012.043c Surely this Jānakī, the queen of Rāma, will come here.
5.012.044a O Rāma, that queen of Rāma, ever beloved by the descendant of Raghu,
5.012.044c skilled in wandering through the forest, surely Jānakī will come.
Or rather, that fawn-eyed woman, who is well-acquainted with this forest,
will come here to the woods, emaciated by her constant thoughts of Rāma;
for that lovely-eyed queen is consumed by the grief of separation from Rāma.
Constantly delighting in dwelling in the forest, she will come to roam the woods; indeed, in the past, she always longed for the life of forest-dwellers—
she who was the beloved wife of Rāma and the virtuous daughter of Janaka.
"With her mind fixed on the time of twilight, the dark-complexioned Jānakī will surely arrive;
for that woman of excellent complexion has come to this river of auspicious waters for the sake of the twilight rites. And this beautiful Aśoka grove is truly worthy of her."

5.012.049c She who is the auspicious wife of the lord of the earth, equal to Rāma— 5.012.050a if that queen, whose face resembles the lord of the stars, is still alive, 5.012.050c she will certainly come to this river of auspicious waters.
Having thus reflected, the high-souled Hanumān,
while awaiting the wife of the lord of men and observing everything, beheld it all.
Hidden within that thick foliage of well-flowered trees,
staying there, looking about, and searching for Maithilī,
he gazed upon the entire earth.
Adorned with creepers and trees, endowed everywhere with divine fragrances and flavors, and beautified on all sides, he beheld that grove,
which resembled the Nandana garden and was filled with beasts and birds.
It was crowded with mansions and palaces, filled with the warbling of cuckoos,
and adorned with ponds containing golden water-lilies and lotuses; it was provided with many seats and carpets, and contained tens of thousands of multi-storied houses.

Standing there, the son of the Wind beheld the splendor of the blossoming *aśoka* trees, which possessed the radiance of the rising sun, like a blazing fire, surrounded by lovely trees bearing flowers of every season and laden with fruit.
With hundreds of variegated flower-ornaments falling away, it was as if the birds were repeatedly stripping the branches of their leaves;
with those *aśoka* trees, which destroy all sorrow, covered in flowers from the very roots.
With *karṇikāra* trees laden with an excessive weight of flowers as if touching the earth,
and with *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom,
that region was, as it were, set ablaze on all sides by their radiance.
Puṃnāgas, saptaparṇas, campakas, and uddālakas—
many of these, with their roots well-developed and in full bloom, shone brilliantly;
some were like refined gold, while others resembled the flames of fire.
There, thousands of *aśoka* trees were like black collyrium.
That various garden was like the wondrous Caitraratha grove in Nandana;
it was inconceivable, as if transcending all bounds, divine, delightful, and endowed with splendor.
It was like a second sky filled with hosts of flowers and stars,
variegated by hundreds of flower-jewels like a fifth ocean;
it was densely covered with trees fragrant with honey that bore blossoms of every season.
With the various cries of herds of deer and birds, the garden was delightful; it wafted many fragrances, was holy-scented and enchanting,
rich in aroma like the king of mountains, a second Gandhamādana.
In that Aśoka grove,
the bull among monkeys saw nearby a magnificent temple-palace,
white as Kailāsa, standing in the center upon a thousand pillars.
With stairs made of coral and altars of refined gold,
it seemed to steal away the eyes and to blaze with splendor;
pure and lofty in its stature, it appeared as if scraping the very sky.
Then he beheld her, clad in soiled garments and surrounded by ogresses— emaciated by fasting, miserable, sighing again and again,
yet as stainless as the crescent of the moon at the beginning of the bright fortnight.
With a form barely visible, she possessed a beautiful radiance,
like a flame of fire enveloped in a web of smoke; she was clad in a single, worn upper garment of yellow silk.
She was like a lotus pond covered in mud, devoid of ornaments, and stripped of its lotuses;
she was ashamed, tormented by grief, withered, and distressed,
like the star Rohiṇī afflicted by the planet Mars.
With her face filled with tears, miserable and emaciated from fasting, she was dejected,
devoted to sorrowful meditation, and perpetually surrendered to suffering;
not seeing her beloved kin, she saw only the host of ogresses.
Like a doe separated from her herd and surrounded by a pack of dogs, she was pursued by a single braid of hair as dark as a blue serpent;
though worthy of happiness, she was tormented by suffering and had long been the victim of calamities.
Beholding that large-eyed woman, who was exceedingly soiled and emaciated,
he reasoned that she was Sītā based on supporting grounds:
"She must have been carried away at that time by that Rākṣasa who can assume any form at will."
For this lady is indeed exactly as she was seen;
with a face like the full moon, beautiful eyebrows, and lovely rounded breasts,
this goddess makes all the quarters of the sky free from darkness by her radiance.
Her hair was dark blue, her lips were like the bimba fruit, and she possessed a slender waist and a graceful gait; Sītā, with eyes like lotus petals, was like Rati, the consort of Manmatha,
beloved by the entire world and possessing a radiance like that of the full moon.
Seated on the ground with her beautiful body, she appeared like a self-restrained female ascetic;
filled with heavy sighs, the timid woman did not shine, being enveloped by a vast web of grief like the consort of a serpent-king.
Like a flame of fire entangled in a web of smoke, like prosperity that has become doubtful through memory, like fallen fortune,
like faith frustrated, and like hope thwarted— [she appeared].
Like an accomplishment marred by obstacles, like an intellect clouded by impurity;
like fame fallen through false slander;
she was pained by the obstruction caused by Rāma and emaciated by the abduction of her husband by the Rākṣasa.
She was gazing here and there at her weak,
fawn-eyed [husband] with a face lacking serenity— its dark eyes and lashes filled with tears of water— and sighing again and again.
Covered in dirt and mud, miserable, and unadorned though worthy of ornaments— like the radiance of the moon obscured by dark clouds—
his mind wavered repeatedly as he gazed upon Sītā.
Through the lack of application to the sacred scriptures, as if his knowledge were lax,
Hanumān recognized Sītā with difficulty, unadorned,
like speech that has lost its original meaning due to a lack of grammatical refinement.
Beholding that large-eyed, blameless princess,
he reasoned that she was Sītā, establishing it through various grounds; for he recalled those very features of Vaidehī’s limbs which Rāma had previously described.
He observed those networks of ornaments adorning his limbs;
he saw well-fashioned earrings and well-proportioned cheek-ornaments,
as well as various jewels and coral set in his hands.
"Because they have been joined for so long, these [trees] are dark and possess such a configuration;
I believe these are indeed those which Rāma described.
Among them, I do not perceive those that were missing."
5.013.042c Those [garments] of hers that were not lost are these very ones, without a doubt.
5.013.043a That beautiful yellow garment, shining like a golden band, having slipped off, 5.013.043c was then seen by the monkeys caught upon the mountain, serving as her upper robe.
And these preeminent ornaments, resounding and magnificent, were seen upon the surface of the earth, cast away by her alone;
yet this garment, because it has been worn for so long, is exceedingly soiled.
For indeed, her complexion and her splendor are surely just like those of the other;
this beloved queen of Rāma, whose limbs are the color of gold,
though she has vanished from sight, does not vanish from his mind.
This is she for whose sake Rāma is tormented by four things:
by compassion, by kindness, by grief, and by love.
Out of compassion he thinks, "A woman has been lost," and out of kindness, "She has sought refuge [with me]."
"Because of grief that his wife was lost and because of passion for his beloved, he [searched].
Just as this goddess possesses beauty and the perfection of every limb and member, so too does Rāma; this dark-eyed woman is his."
The mind of this goddess is fixed upon him, and his upon her;
therefore she, and that righteous-souled one, continue to live for even a moment.
Rāma performs a difficult task in that he maintains this woman of intoxicating beauty.
"Without Sītā, the mighty-armed one does not live even for a moment.
Having thus seen Sītā, the son of the Wind-god was filled with joy;
he went mentally to Rāma and praised that lord.
Having praised Sītā, who was worthy of praise, that bull among monkeys,
as well as Rāma, who is delightful in his virtues, again became lost in thought. Having meditated for a moment, his eyes were clouded with tears.
5.014.002c Relying upon Sītā, the radiant Hanumān lamented:

5.014.003a "She who was the beloved of his preceptor, Lakṣmaṇa—who is himself humble toward his elders—is now worthy of honor; yet even Sītā is afflicted by grief, for time is indeed difficult to overcome."
Knowing the resolve of Rāma and the wise Lakṣmaṇa,
the queen was not greatly agitated, like the Gaṅgā at the arrival of the rainy season;
she was one whose character, age, and conduct were equal [to theirs], and whose lineage and auspicious marks were likewise equal.
"Rāghava deserves Vaidehī, and she, the dark-eyed one,
deserves him. Having seen her, who shone like fresh gold and was like Śrī, the beloved of the world,
she went to Rāma in her mind and spoke these words:
For the sake of this large-eyed lady, the mighty Vālin was slain;
Kabandha, who equaled Rāvaṇa in valor, was struck down;
and Virādha, a Rākṣasa of terrifying prowess, was killed in battle.
In the forest, Rāma, exerting his prowess like Mahendra against Śambara,
slew fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds at Janasthāna with arrows resembling tongues of fire.
Khara was slain in battle, and Triśiras was struck down,
as was the highly energetic Dūṣaṇa, by Rāma, the knower of the self; likewise,
the sovereignty over the monkeys, which had been protected by Vālin, was won— a sovereignty difficult to attain.
On her account, Sugrīva attained the honor of the world;
for her sake, I crossed the glorious ocean, the lord of rivers and streams, and this city was surveyed by me for the sake of this large-eyed lady.
5.014.013a Even if Rāma were to overturn the earth bounded by the ocean,
5.014.013c and even the entire world for her sake— it is my firm conviction that this alone is right.
5.014.014a Whether it be sovereignty over the three worlds, or Sītā, the daughter of Janaka.

The entire sovereignty of the three worlds would not equal even a fraction of Sītā. She is that very daughter of the high-souled Janaka, the King of Mithilā, who is devoted to righteousness and firm in her vows toward her husband.
Having burst through the earth in a field furrowed by the tip of a plow, she rose up,
strewn with auspicious soil from the field that resembled the pollen of lotuses—
[the soil] of one who was valiant, of noble character, and who never retreated in battles.
"This is the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha, the illustrious eldest wife of King Rāma—
himself a knower of dharma, grateful, and self-realized. This is that beloved wife who has now fallen under the power of the rākṣasa."
Having renounced all luxuries out of the strength of her love for her husband,
she entered the desolate forest without considering her sufferings,
content with fruits and roots and devoted to serving her husband.
She who experiences the highest joy even in the forest as if she were in a palace— she,
this lady with limbs the color of gold, who always speaks with a gentle smile, though undeserving of such misfortunes, endures this torment.
"Rāghava desires to see her, who is endowed with such perfection of virtue,
just as a thirsty man longs for a drinking fountain that has been despoiled by Rāvaṇa. Surely, upon regaining her, Rāghava will attain great joy."
Like a king fallen from his kingdom who has regained the earth,
she— though abandoned by the enjoyments of desire and deprived of her kinsmen—
sustains her own body, longing for reunion with him.

She does not see these ogresses, nor these trees laden with flowers and fruit; surely, with her heart fixed on one point, she beholds only Rāma. For a husband is indeed a woman’s supreme ornament, even more so than any physical adornment.
For she, though worthy of splendor, does not shine when deprived of him;
Lord Rāma performs a difficult feat in that, though separated from her,
he maintains his body and does not perish from grief.
Seeing her— whose hair-ends are black, whose eyes resemble a hundred-petaled lotus, who deserves happiness yet is now suffering— even my mind is pained.
Her eyes are like lotuses, and she possesses the patience of the earth.
She who was protected by Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa is now being guarded at the foot of a tree by ogresses with distorted eyes.
Like a lotus pond struck by frost, her beauty vanished;
oppressed by a succession of calamities,
she was like a female cakravāka bird separated from her mate.
The daughter of Janaka has fallen into a miserable state;
for these aśoka trees, with their branches bent down by flowers, truly produce intense grief in her.
With the departure of the snow, the sun, its rays now mild, has risen with its many thousands of beams;
having reflected on this matter, the monkey—
Thinking, "This is Sītā," his mind firmly settled upon her,
that powerful and swift bull among monkeys took refuge in that tree and sat down.
Then the stainless moon himself, shining like a cluster of white water-lilies, ascended the pure sky like a swan entering blue water; he,
of spotless radiance, seemed to offer assistance with his own light.
The moon served the son of the Wind with its cool rays.
Then he beheld Sītā, whose face resembled the full moon,
appearing as if weighed down by a burden of grief, like a boat laden with cargo upon the waters.
Desiring to see Vaidehī, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god,
beheld nearby several Rākṣasa women of terrifying appearance:
one with a single eye, one with a single ear, and another whose ears served as a covering for her head.
Some were earless, some had spike-like ears, and some had nostrils that puffed out from their heads; some had oversized upper bodies, some had thin and long necks,
some had disheveled hair, some were hairless, and others wore blankets of hair.
With long ears and foreheads, with pendulous bellies and breasts, with long lips,
long chins,
long faces, and long knees; likewise short, tall, hunchbacked, misshapen, and dwarfish.
She was formidable, with disheveled garments, tawny eyes, and a distorted face; she was accompanied by women who were deformed,
tawny, dark-complexioned, wrathful, and fond of quarreling,
bearing great spears, mallets, and hammers of black iron.
Some had the faces of boars, deer, tigers, buffaloes, goats, and jackals;
others had the feet of elephants, camels, and horses, while still others had their heads buried in their chests.
Some had but one hand and one foot, and some had ears like those of donkeys or horses.

Some had ears like those of cows, others like those of elephants, and still others like those of monkeys; some were noseless, some had oversized noses, some had crooked noses, and some were entirely without nostrils;
some had noses resembling those of elephants, while others had nostrils that seemed to protrude from their foreheads.
5.015.013 They had feet like elephants' feet, massive feet, cow's feet, and feet with tufts of hair; 5.015.013c they had excessively large heads and necks, and excessively large breasts and bellies;
5.015.014a they had excessively large mouths and eyes, as well as long tongues and nails.
5.015.014c Those with the faces of goats, elephants, cows, and pigs; 5.015.015a And those with the faces of horses, camels, and donkeys— terrible-looking Rākṣasīs,
holding spears and mallets in their hands, wrathful, and fond of quarreling.
The Rākṣasīs— Karālā and Dhūmrakeśī, with their distorted faces—
were constantly drinking liquor; they were always fond of meat and wine,
their limbs smeared with flesh and blood, and they fed upon flesh and blood.
The best of monkeys beheld those women, whose sight caused one's hair to stand on end; they were seated around the trunk of a great tree, surrounding that lord of the forest.
And beneath it, he saw that blameless princess, the queen.
The illustrious Hanumān beheld the daughter of Janaka,
lusterless, tormented by grief, her hair disheveled with filth— like a star whose merit is exhausted, fallen from the heavens to the earth.
Rich in her reputation for virtuous conduct, yet miserable at the sight of her husband; deprived of her finest ornaments, yet adorned by her love for her husband;
confined by the lord of the Rākṣasas, and separated from her kinsmen.
Like a female elephant confined in a herd and held captive by a lion;
like the crescent moon at the end of the rainy season, veiled by autumnal clouds;
her form distressed from lack of touch, like a lute left unplayed.
Sītā, devoted to her husband’s welfare, was now unrightfully held in the power of the Rākṣasas;
she was immersed in an ocean of grief in the midst of the Aśoka grove,
surrounded there by those women like the star Rohiṇī surrounded by the planets.
Hanumān beheld the goddess like a creeper devoid of flowers;
her limbs were smeared with filth, yet she was adorned by her very form—
like a lotus stalk covered in mud, she both shone and did not shine.
The monkey Hanumān beheld that beautiful woman, a fawn-eyed lady, covered by a soiled and worn garment;
though her face was dejected, she remained undaunted by the splendor of her husband’s majesty.
Having seen Sītā, whose eyes were dark and who was protected by her own virtue,
Hanumān beheld that woman with eyes like those of a young deer,
looking about in all directions like a frightened fawn.
As if burning the leaf-bearing trees with her sighs,
like a mass of sorrows or a rising wave of misery— emaciated, yet with well-proportioned limbs, she was no longer adorned by ornaments.
Beholding Maithilī, the son of the Wind-god experienced incomparable joy;
and seeing that woman with intoxicating eyes, Hanumān shed tears born of delight and there paid homage to Rāghava.

Having paid homage to Rāma and to Lakṣmaṇa, the valiant Hanumān, thrilled at the sight of Sītā, remained concealed. As he thus gazed upon the forest with its trees in full bloom, [he continued his search].
And as he searched for the princess of Videha, a small portion of the night remained;
at the end of the night, he heard the Vedic chants of the Brahmarākṣasas— those who were learned in the Vedas with their six auxiliary limbs and performers of the most excellent sacrifices.

Then, by the sounds of auspicious musical instruments that were pleasing to the ear, the mighty-armed and exceedingly powerful Ten-necked one was awakened. Having awakened at the proper time, the lord of the Rākṣasas, who was possessed of great splendor, [arose].
Wearing garlands and garments that had slipped from him, he thought only of Vaidehī; intensely obsessed with her and fierce with passion,
that Rākṣasa was unable to conceal his desire within himself.
Adorned with all ornaments and possessing unsurpassed splendor, he beheld that city,
which was frequented by various trees bearing all kinds of flowers and fruits,
and surrounded by lotus ponds beautified by diverse blossoms.
He beheld the paths, most wonderful and variegated with birds that were ever-intoxicated,
surrounded by various artificial deer that were captivating to the sight, and adorned with archways of jewels and gold.
He entered the Aśoka grove itself, which was filled with various herds of deer, strewn with fallen fruits, and lined with dense trees;
and about a hundred women followed him as he walked.

5.016.010c Like Mahendra’s son Paulastya, the women of the gods and gandharvas— 5.016.011a some women there took up golden lamps; others held yak-tail whisks in their hands, and still others held palm-leaf fans.

5.016.012 Some carried water in golden jars before them; others, taking up curved blades and swords, followed behind. 5.016.013 A certain beautiful woman carried a jewel-encrusted vessel filled with drink.
Then, with her right hand,
Dakṣiṇā took hold of the golden-staffed parasol, which resembled a royal swan and possessed the luster of the full moon; taking it up, she followed behind him.

The excellent wives of Rāvaṇa, their eyes clouded by sleep and intoxication, followed their heroic husband like streaks of lightning following a rain-cloud. Then there arose the sound of girdles and the tinkling of anklets.
That monkey, the son of the Wind-god, heard the voices of the most excellent women;
then the monkey Hanumān beheld him, whose deeds were incomparable and whose strength and prowess were inconceivable, as he arrived at the gateway.
It was illuminated on all sides by many lamps filled with fragrant oil and held before him;
he was possessed by lust, pride, and intoxication, his long, copper-hued eyes were squinting.
He was like Kandarpa himself standing before one with his bow cast aside,
gracefully trailing that supreme, stainless garment— which resembled the foam of churned nectar—
now released yet still clinging to his armlet.
Hidden within the leafy branches and densely covered by leaves and flowers,
he began to observe him as he drew near;
and looking out from there, that elephant among monkeys beheld him.
Surrounded by those beautiful and excellent women of Rāvaṇa’s, who were endowed with beauty and youth,
the highly illustrious king entered that pleasure grove resounding with the cries of deer and birds.
Intoxicated, adorned with various ornaments, with spike-like ears and great strength—
by him, the son of Viśravas, the lord of the Rākṣasas, was seen,
surrounded by exquisite women as the moon is by the stars.
The great monkey of immense splendor beheld that radiant being;
reflecting, "This is the mighty-armed Rāvaṇa," the exceedingly energetic Hanumān, son of the Wind, leapt down.
5.016.027 Even though he possessed fierce energy, Hanumān was shaken by that power; clinging within the secret fold of her garment, he remained concealed.
5.016.028 He [beheld] her, whose ends of hair were dark, who had beautiful hips and firm breasts.
Desiring to see her who had dark-cornered eyes, Rāvaṇa approached.
At that very time, the blameless princess,
endowed with beauty and youth and adorned with the finest ornaments, [was there].
Then, upon merely seeing Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, Vaidehī—
she of the beautiful hips— trembled like a plantain tree in a gale;
she covered her abdomen with her thighs and her breasts with her arms.
Seated there, the large-eyed woman of excellent complexion was weeping.
Then the ten-necked Rāvaṇa beheld Vaidehī, guarded by a host of rākṣasīs—
miserable and afflicted with grief, like a ship sinking in the ocean.
She sat upon the bare ground, firm in her vows,
like a branch of a great tree severed and fallen to the earth—
her limbs smeared with dust though worthy of ornaments, left unadorned though she deserved to be adorned.
She was approaching the presence of Rāma, that lion among kings who knows the self,
as if traveling by means of her mental longings yoked to the horses of her resolve;
she was alone, withering away, weeping, and wholly devoted to meditation and grief.
Not seeing an end to her suffering, Rāma’s devoted wife was writhing like the consort of a serpent-king possessed by a spell,
or like Rohiṇī eclipsed by the comet-like planet Ketu.

Born into a family of virtuous conduct, well-behaved and righteous, she has undergone a refinement like one born into a base family; she is like great fame that has declined, or like faith that has been insulted.
Like wisdom utterly exhausted, like hope frustrated; like a future ruined, like a command repudiated; like a radiant quarter of the sky at the wrong time, like a ritual offering snatched away.
Like a lotus pond devastated, like an army whose heroes have been slain;
like radiance destroyed by ascetic heat, like a river that has run dry;
like a sacrificial altar defiled, like the flame of a fire extinguished.
Like a full-moon night when the lunar orb is seized by Rāhu,
like a lotus pond whose leaves and blossoms have been torn away, its birds terrified,
and which has been trampled by the trunks of elephants— thus was she agitated.
Afflicted with grief for her husband, she was like a dried-up river whose waters have been drained; deprived of all adornment, she was like a night in the dark fortnight;
delicate and of well-formed limbs, she was accustomed to the gem-studded inner chambers.
Like a lotus stalk recently uprooted being scorched by the heat,
like a female elephant separated from the leader of the herd, sighing and afflicted by great sorrow as she clings to a pillar for support.
She was effortlessly adorned by a single, long,
dark braid, like the earth graced at the end of the rainy season by a dark line of forest.
Through fasting, grief, meditation, and fear, [she appeared as if]...
Exhausted, emaciated, and dejected, she had taken little food and was rich in asceticism;
with palms joined like a goddess, she, afflicted by grief,
was entreating the supreme descendant of Raghu for the defeat of the Ten-necked one.
Beholding the blameless Maithilī weeping— her beautiful eyelashes and long, white eyes copper-red— with her heart utterly devoted to Rāma;
Rāvaṇa sought to entice her for his own destruction; he addressed that wretched, joyless, and ascetic woman,
who was surrounded by her attendants, with sweet words full of artful gestures.
"Seeing me, O lady with thighs like an elephant's trunk, you wish to hide your breasts and belly out of fear, as if wishing to make yourself invisible.
I desire you, O large-eyed one; honor me, my dear."
O Sītā, you who are endowed with the excellence of every limb and are enchanting to all the world—
here there are no humans or Rākṣasas capable of changing their form at will;
let the fear arising from me depart from you.
"O timid one, this is undoubtedly the inherent duty of Rākṣasas in every respect:
either approaching the wives of others or carrying them off by force.
Yet, O Maithilī, even though you are unwilling, I shall not touch you."
"Let desire act upon my body according to its will, as it pleases.
O Queen, you must not feel fear here; trust in me, my dear. Love me with your whole heart; do not remain thus consumed by grief."
A single braid, sleeping on the ground, meditation, soiled garments,
and fasting at the improper time— these are not suitable for you.
Nor are these various garlands, sandalwood, and aloe-woods.
O Maithilī, having obtained me, you shall receive various garments, divine ornaments, costly drinks, vehicles, and couches, as well as song, dance, and instrumental music.
"You are a jewel among women; do not be thus. Adorn your limbs! Having obtained me, O lady of beautiful form, how could you be unworthy?
This lovely youth of yours is passing away."
5.018.012c That which has passed away does not return, like the swift current of waters.
5.018.013a Having fashioned you, I believe that Creator of All, the Maker of Forms, has desisted;
5.018.013c for there is no other likeness of form like yours, O lady of auspicious appearance.
"O Vaidehī, endowed with such beauty and youth,
what man— even the Grandfather Brahmā himself— could withstand you once he has encountered you?
O lady whose face resembles the cool-rayed moon, whatever limb of yours I behold,"
"O lady of broad hips, my gaze is fixed upon you alone.
O Maithilī, become my wife; cast aside this delusion.
Become my chief queen among many excellent women."

"O timid one, all those jewels which I have brought away after plundering them from the worlds, as well as this kingdom and myself, [I offer] to you. Having conquered the entire earth, garlanded with various cities,"
"O playful one, for your sake I shall bestow [this] upon the people of Janaka.
I see no one else in this world who would be a match for me;
behold my great prowess, which is without rival in combat."
"Time and again in battle, the gods and asuras have been broken by me, their banners crushed; they are unable to stand against my ranks.
Choose now, and let the finest cosmetic preparation be prepared for you."
"Let these radiant ornaments be fastened upon your limbs;
I see your form well-adorned with these decorations. O lady of lovely countenance, you are truly graced by these ornaments through your own grace."
"Enjoy pleasures as you desire, drink, O timid one, and rejoice;
give away the earth or wealth as you wish. Revel with confidence in me and command me boldly."
"Because of my power, while you sport, let your kinsmen also sport. Behold my prosperity, O blessed lady, my splendor, and my fame!
What will you do with Rāma, O fortunate one, who wears garments of bark?"
"Rāma has renounced victory; his glory is gone, and he dwells in the forest.
Observing vows and sleeping upon the bare ground, I suspect he may even be dead.
For indeed, O Vaidehī, Rāma will not find it possible to see you."
Like moonlight shrouded by dark clouds preceded by cranes,
Raghava shall not be able to take you from my hand,
any more than Hiraṇyakaśipu could reclaim the fame that had passed into the hands of Indra.
"O lady of lovely smiles, lovely teeth, and lovely eyes, O playful one,
you steal my heart, O timid one, just as a Garuda seizes a serpent. You,
though clad in soiled silk, slender, and even unadorned— "
Having seen her, I find no pleasure in my own wives. O Jānakī, exercise sovereignty over all these women who dwell in the inner apartments and are endowed with every virtue.
"O lady with dark-tipped hair, for mine are the women who are the most excellent in the three worlds;
they shall attend upon you, just as the Apsarases attend upon Śrī.
O fair-browed one, whatever jewels and riches belong to Vaiśravaṇa—"
"O lady of beautiful hips, enjoy those worlds, and me as well, according to your pleasure.
O Queen, neither in ascetic power, nor in strength, nor in valor, nor in wealth, nor even in splendor or fame, is Rāma equal to me."
"Drink, sport, delight, and enjoy pleasures; I bestow upon you heaps of wealth and the earth itself. O lovely woman, revel with me as you please."
And let your kinsmen gather together upon you and sport,
amidst the groves on the seashore filled with clusters of flowering trees and swarms of bees.
"O timid one, with your limbs adorned by a necklace of pure gold, roam the forests with me.
Having heard those words of that fierce Rākṣasa, Sītā—
Afflicted and speaking in a piteous tone, she slowly replied with these sorrowful words;
Sītā, distressed by grief, weeping, trembling, and emaciated,
that woman of noble form and devoted to her husband thought only of her lord.
Placing a blade of grass between them, she of the pure smile replied:
"Turn your mind away from me; let your mind be set upon your own kin. It is not fitting for you to solicit me, any more than it is for a doer of evil to seek spiritual perfection."

"Having been born into a great lineage and having entered a virtuous family, it is not right for me— a devoted wife— to perform such a contemptible act. Having spoken thus to Rāvaṇa, the illustrious Vaidehī—
Turning her back on the Rākṣasa, she spoke these words once more:
"I am not a suitable wife for you, being as I am the wife of another. Behold righteousness; practice virtue with excellence."
"O night-stalker, as your own wife is to be protected, so are the wives of others;
making yourself the analogy, take delight in your own wives. One who is dissatisfied with his own wife, fickle, and of unsteady senses [brings ruin upon himself]."
Those who possess a deceitful intellect bring about their own ruin through the wives of others.
Whether the virtuous exist here or do not, or whether you do not follow the virtuous— you, whose soul is led astray by falsehood, have rejected the beneficial words spoken by the wise.
5.019.010a Having encountered a king who has not disciplined his soul and is devoted to misconduct, 5.019.010c prosperous kingdoms and cities perish.
5.019.011a Likewise, this Laṅkā, teeming with a multitude of jewels, having encountered you, [is in peril].
"Because of your single transgression, O Rāvaṇa, you who are short-sighted, shall before long perish, being struck down by your own deeds;
for all living beings rejoice at the destruction of one who performs evil actions."

5.019.013a Thus will people, treated with contempt, speak of you, a doer of evil deeds: 5.019.013c "By good fortune this fierce man has met with such a calamity"—thus they will rejoice. 5.019.014a I cannot be enticed by power or by wealth.
"I am not different from Rāghava, just as radiance is not different from the sun.
Having rested upon the honored arm of that Lord of the World,
how indeed could I ever rest upon the arm of anyone else?"
"I am the lawful wife of that very lord of the earth,
like sacred knowledge belongs to a self-realized Brahmin who has performed his ritual ablutions.
O Rāvaṇa, it is right that you unite me, who am so distressed, with Rāma."

O bull among men, by one who desires to secure a proper place for himself, who wishes to make a suitable alliance with a friend like a female elephant with her mate in the forest, and who does not desire a terrible slaughter, that bull among men, Rāma, must be befriended.
One might avoid a hurled thunderbolt, and one might long avoid Death himself;
but that Rāghava, the Lord of the World, when enraged, will not spare one such as you. You shall hear the great sound of Rāma’s bow.
Like the roar of a thunderbolt released by Śatakratu,
arrows marked with the signs of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa will swiftly descend here, well-jointed and with flaming tips like serpents.
Slaying the Rākṣasas on all sides within this city, those birds with feathers like herons will descend so densely that no passage remains;
for he, the great Rāma-Garuḍa, shall destroy the great serpents that are the lords of the Rākṣasas.

He will snatch me away from you with speed, like Vainateya snatching up serpents; my husband, the subduer of enemies, will quickly carry me off from you, just as Viṣṇu took the radiant sovereignty from the Asuras in three strides.
5.019.025a Janasthāna, the place of slaughter, where the host of rākṣasas has been slain—
5.019.025c this evil deed was indeed committed by you, O Rākṣasa, while being powerless.
5.019.026a Having entered the empty hermitage of those two lions among men, [you acted thus].
"O lowest of men, you have carried her away while her two brothers were within range. Indeed,
having caught the scent of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, it is not possible for you to stand before their sight, just as a dog cannot stand before two tigers."
In your struggle with those two, the seizing of both arms will be as unstable as the subduing of Vṛtra’s single arm by the two arms of Indra.
That Rāma, my protector, together with the son of Sumitrā, will soon [be here].
Like the sun drinking up a small amount of water with its rays, he will take away our lives with his arrows—
whether he has gone to the mountain that is Kubera’s abode,
or has entered the assembly hall of King Varuṇa.
"Without a doubt, you shall not escape the son of Daśaratha,
like a great tree struck down by time when hit by a thunderbolt.
Having heard these harsh words of Sītā, the lord of the Rākṣasas—
Then he spoke these unpleasant words to Sītā, who was so pleasing to behold:
"To the very extent that a man is conciliatory and submissive toward women, to that same extent he is treated with contempt;
and to the very extent that he speaks kindly, to that same extent he is disregarded."
"The desire that has arisen within me for you restrains my anger,
just as a skilled charioteer restrains galloping horses on their path. Indeed,
it is said that men are bound by whatever object their desire finds attractive."
"5.020.004c Compassion and affection indeed arise toward that person;
5.020.005a for this reason, O lovely-faced one, I do not have her killed— though she deserves death and deserves contempt, being devoted to a false ascetic life."
"O Maithilī, for every single harsh word that you speak to me, a terrible death is deserved by you.
Having spoken thus to Vaidehī, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas— "
Filled with rage and agitation, he spoke these further words to Sītā:
"Two months must be observed by you as the deadline I have set;
after that, O woman of excellent complexion, you shall ascend my bed."

"But after two months, since I do not desire you as my husband, they will begin to prepare you in the kitchen for my morning meal. Seeing Jānakī being thus threatened by the lord of the Rākṣasas, [he spoke].
Those large-eyed daughters of the gods and gandharvas were filled with grief;
some with various gestures of their lips, and others with their eyes and faces,
they comforted Sītā, who had been threatened by that rākṣasa.
Comforted by them, Sītā addressed Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
with words for her own welfare, which were full of pride born from her conduct and valor: "Surely there is no person whatsoever who stands in your best interest."
5.020.013c He who does not restrain you from this censurable deed—
5.020.014a for who else in the three worlds, other than you, would even in thought desire me, the wife of one whose soul is dharma, as Śacī is to the Lord of Śacī?
"O lowest of Rākṣasas, you have spoken evil words regarding the wife of Rāma, who possesses immeasurable splendor; where can you go to escape the retribution for that?
It is like the prideful elephant and the hare meeting together in the forest."
5.020.016c Thus Rāma is like an elephant, while you, O base one, are considered as a hare.
5.020.017a You, who insult the lord of the Ikṣvākus here, do you not feel shame? For you have not yet come within the range of his vision.
"These eyes of yours are cruel, deformed, and tawny-black;
why have they not fallen to the ground, you who look upon me with such ignoble intent? [Why did they not fall] upon the wife of that righteous-souled one, and the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha?"
O wicked one, why does your tongue not wither away as you speak thus to me? Yet,
because Rāma gave no command and out of respect for the preservation of my ascetic power,
O Ten-necked One, I do not reduce you to ashes with my fiery energy, though you deserve to be turned to ash.
"I cannot be taken away from that wise Rāma;
there is no doubt that destiny has been ordained for your destruction.
[This was said] by the heroic brother of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), who is endowed with great forces."
"Having set aside Rāma, why indeed have you committed this theft of a wife?
Hearing these words of Sītā, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas,
rolled his cruel eyes and glared at the daughter of Janaka.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with mighty arms and a broad neck,
possessing the gait and courage of a lion, glorious, with a flaming tongue and fierce eyes, his high crown swaying, tall in stature, and adorned with variegated garlands and unguents.
Wearing red garlands and garments, adorned with ornaments of refined gold,
he was well-girded by a great waist-cord and a single-strand belt,
like Mount Mandara encircled by the serpent at the churning for the nectar of immortality.
Adorned with two earrings having the hue of the rising sun,
he resembled a mountain with two *aśoka* trees bearing red shoots and blossoms;
looking toward Vaidehī, his eyes were bloodshot with rage.
Hissing like a serpent, Rāvaṇa said to Sītā:
"O you who are devoted to a vow, I shall destroy you today— though you are possessed of misconduct and devoid of purpose— just as the sun destroys the twilight with its splendor."
Having spoken thus to Maithilī, King Rāvaṇa, the terror of his enemies,
then commanded all the rākṣasīs of fearsome appearance—
those with one eye, those with one ear, and likewise those whose ears served as veils.
Gokarṇī, Hastikarṇī, Lambakarṇī, and Akarṇikā; Hastipadī, Śvapadī, Gopadī, and Pādacūlikā;
Ekākṣī, Ekapādī, Pṛthupādī, and Apādikā.
With heads and necks of excessive size, with breasts and bellies of excessive size;
with mouths and eyes of excessive size, with long tongues, or no tongues at all;
without noses, with faces like lions, faces like cows, and faces like pigs.
"O Rākṣasīs, all of you assemble quickly and act in such a way that Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, shall swiftly come under my control—
using methods both direct and indirect, and through conciliation, gifts, and sowing dissension."
"Bring back the princess of Videha by the raising of your staff!
Having thus commanded them again and again, the lord of the Rākṣasas,
his soul overwhelmed by lust and anger, threatened Jānakī.
Then, having quickly approached, the rākṣasī Dhānyamālinī embraced the Ten-necked One and spoke these words:
"Sport with me, O Great King; what use have you for this Sītā?"
"The body of one who desires a woman who does not desire him is tormented;
but for one who desires a woman who desires him, there is beautiful joy.
Having been addressed thus by the Rākṣasī, the powerful one then leapt up.
He entered his residence, which shone with the brilliance of the blazing sun;
then those daughters of the gods, Gandharvas,
and Nāgas surrounded the Ten-necked one and entered that most excellent palace.
Having threatened Maithilī, who remained steadfastly devoted to dharma and was trembling, Rāvaṇa—
deluded by passion— abandoned Sītā.
Having spoken thus to Maithilī, King Rāvaṇa, the terror of his enemies, gave instructions to all the rākṣasīs and then entered his own radiant palace.
When the lord of the Rākṣasas had departed and returned once more to the inner apartments,
those Rākṣasa women of terrifying form rushed toward Sītā.
Then, having approached Sītā, the Rākṣasa women were overcome with rage.
5.021.003c With extremely harsh words, they spoke thus to Vaidehī:
5.021.004a "O Sītā, do you not hold in high regard the status of being the wife of the great-souled Rāvaṇa, the descendant of Pulastya, the ten-necked one, the most excellent?"
Then a rākṣasī named Ekajaṭā, her eyes copper-red with rage, addressed Sītā— whose waist was as slender as the palm of a hand— and spoke these words:
"The fourth among the six Prajāpatis is the one who [created] the Prajāpatis..."
The mind-born son of Brahmā is renowned as Pulastya. The mind-born son of Pulastya was the radiant great seer named Viśravas, who possessed a splendor equal to that of Prajāpati.
"O large-eyed one, his son is Rāvaṇa, the one who makes his enemies cry out;
you ought to become the wife of that lord of the Rākṣasas. Why do you not agree to the words spoken by me, O lady of beautiful limbs?"
Then a Rākṣasī named Harijaṭā spoke these words,
her eyes like those of a cat, rolling them in rage:
"By him the thirty-three gods and the king of the gods were conquered."
"You ought to become the wife of that lord of the Rākṣasas—
he who is exalted by his prowess, a hero who never retreats in battles,
powerful and endowed with valor; why would you not obtain the status of his wife?"
"Leaving behind his beloved and highly esteemed wife, the mighty King Rāvaṇa will come to you, O illustrious lady, who are the most distinguished among all [his wives],
amidst a thousand women adorned with various jewels."
"Abandoning the inner apartments, Rāvaṇa will come to you. He,
by whom the gods, nāgas, gandharvas, and dānavas have been repeatedly defeated in battle, has now approached your side."
"O base woman, for what reason do you not desire to be the wife of that high-souled Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, who possesses every prosperity—
for him before whom the sun does not burn out of fear, and before whom the wind [bows]?"

O lady with long-cornered eyes, he does not even blow; why then do you not remain by his side? At his mere will, O fair-browed one, the trees shed a rain of flowers, the mountains yield water, and the clouds pour forth rain.
"O beautiful lady, why do you not set your mind upon becoming the wife of Rāvaṇa, that king of kings and sovereign of the Nairṛtas?
O Goddess, O beautiful lady, I have told you the truth; it is well said."
"Accept my words, O sweet-smiling one; otherwise, you shall cease to exist.
Then, approaching Sītā, those hideous-faced Rākṣasa women—harsh women themselves—spoke these harsh and unpleasant words.

"Sītā, why do you not consent to dwell within the inner apartments— which are enchanting to all beings and provided with costly couches? Being a human woman, do you hold the status of wife to a mere mortal in such high regard?"
"5.022.003c Withdraw your mind from Rāma; you shall never [be happy].
5.022.004a You are a human woman, O beautiful one, yet you desire that human Rāma, 5.022.004c who has fallen from his kingdom, whose purpose is unfulfilled, and who is despondent, O blameless one."
Having heard the words of the rākṣasīs, Sītā, whose eyes resemble lotuses,
spoke these words with her eyes filled with tears:
"That which you have all spoken together is loathsome to the world."
5.022.006c This sinful speech does not take root in my mind.
5.022.007a A human woman ought not to become the wife of a Rākṣasa. 5.022.007c You may all eat me at your pleasure, but I will not do your bidding.

"Whether he be wretched or deprived of his kingdom, he who is my husband is my teacher. Hearing Sītā's words, the Rākṣasīs, overwhelmed with rage and urged on by Rāvaṇa, reviled her with harsh speech.
5.022.009a Hidden and silent within the *śiṃśapā* tree, Hanumān,
the monkey, heard those rākṣasīs threatening Sītā. 5.022.010a Approaching her from all sides, they surrounded her as she trembled in agitation.
They repeatedly licked their blazing, protruding lips;
and, seizing their battle-axes with great fury, they cried out:
"She does not deserve Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, as her husband!"
5.022.012a Being threatened by those fearsome ogresses, that lady of beautiful countenance,
5.022.012c wiping away her tears, approached that *śiṃśapā* tree.
5.022.013a Then Sītā, surrounded by the ogresses, [reached] that *śiṃśapā* tree.
Having approached, the large-eyed woman stood there, overwhelmed with grief.
Those terrifying Rākṣasa women surrounded her on all sides and threatened her as she stood emaciated, with a dejected face, and wearing soiled garments.
Then a Rākṣasī named Vinatā, of terrifying appearance,
with a fierce mien, formidable and with a sunken belly, spoke to her:
"Sītā, this much display of affection for your husband is sufficient."
"5.022.016c Everywhere, O blessed lady, excessive action leads to calamity.
5.022.017a I am well-pleased; may it be well with you; you have fulfilled your human duty.
5.022.017c But now, O Maithilī, act upon my words, which I speak for your own welfare."
"Accept Rāvaṇa as your husband, the lord of all the rākṣasas—
he who is valiant and handsome like Vāsava, the lord of the gods;
he who is generous, self-sacrificing, and speaks kindly to everyone."
"Abandoning the wretched human Rāma, take refuge with Rāvaṇa! O Vaidehī, anointed with divine unguents and adorned with divine ornaments,
from this day forward, become the sovereign of all the worlds."
"5.022.020e O Agni, Svāhā! Just as the goddess Śacī is to Indra, O beautiful one, [so am I to you]. 5.022.021a What use have you for Rāma, O Vaidehī, that wretched man whose life is spent?
5.022.022a If you do not act upon these words spoken by me,"
"In this very moment, we shall all devour you!
Then another, named Vikaṭā, with her breasts hanging down,
raised her fist and, roaring in anger, spoke to Sītā.

O Maithilī, many improper words have been endured by you from me out of compassion and gentleness, O evil-minded one; yet you do not act upon our beneficial advice, which is offered in accordance with the demands of the time.
5.022.025a You have been brought to the far shore of the ocean, which is difficult for others to reach;
5.022.025c and you have entered the formidable inner apartments of Rāvaṇa, O Maithilī.
5.022.026a Confined within Rāvaṇa’s house, you have been well-guarded by us.
"Even Purandara himself would not be able to protect you;
therefore, O Maithilī, follow my words, for I speak for your own welfare. Enough with this shedding of tears; cast off this useless grief."
"O Sītā, partake in love and joy; abandon this constant state of dejection. Play with the king of the rākṣasas as you please.
For you know, O timid one, that the youth of women is transient."
"Until that time has passed, enjoy happiness;
O lady with intoxicating eyes, wander together with the king of the rākṣasas through delightful gardens and mountain groves."
"Seven thousand women shall remain under your command, O beautiful one;
accept Rāvaṇa as your husband, the lord of all the rākṣasas.
Or else, O Maithilī, I shall tear out your heart and devour it."
"If you do not carry out my spoken word exactly as it was told,
then the Rākṣasī named Caṇḍodarī, of cruel appearance,
brandishing a great trident, shall speak these words."

5.022.034a Seeing this woman with eyes like those of a deer, her breasts trembling with fear, abducted by Rāvaṇa, a great longing arose within me. 5.022.035a [I felt as if] my liver and spleen were being crushed, along with my heart and its very attachments.
"Even her entrails and her head—I intend to devour them.
Then the rākṣasī named Praghasā spoke these words:
"Let us crush the throat of this cruel woman; why do we sit idle?"
"Then let it be reported to the king that this human woman is dead;
there is no doubt about this—he will say, 'Let her be eaten.
Then the Rākṣasī named Ajāmukhī spoke these words:"
"Having slaughtered them all, then make them into equal portions of *pīluka* meat.
Let us divide them all; discord does not please me.
Let drink be brought quickly, along with many various garlands."
Then a Rākṣasī named Śūrpaṇakhā spoke these words:
"What Ajāmukhī has said is indeed pleasing to me.
Let wine, which destroys all sorrow, be brought quickly."
"Having obtained human flesh, let us dance at Nikumbhilā!"—
being thus threatened by those most terrible rākṣasīs, Sītā, who resembled the daughter of a god, abandoned her fortitude and wept.
5.023.001 While those ungentle Rākṣasīs were thus speaking many harsh and cruel words, the daughter of Janaka wept.
5.023.002 Thus addressed by the Rākṣasīs, the high-minded Vaidehī—
Extremely terrified, she spoke with a voice faltering with tears:
"A human woman ought not to become the wife of a *rākṣasa*.
You may all eat me as you wish, but I will not do your bidding."
5.023.004a Surrounded by those rākṣasīs, Sītā, who resembled the daughter of a god,
5.023.004c found no peace, being afflicted by grief and threatened by Rāvaṇa. 5.023.005a Sītā trembled excessively, as if her very limbs were dissolving within herself.
Like a doe strayed from the herd in the forest, tormented by wolves,
she clung to a large, flowering branch of an *aśoka* tree;
with her heart broken by grief, she brooded over her husband.
5.023.007a Bathing her swelling breasts with the streams of tears from her eyes, 5.023.007c she brooded over her grief and found no end to it then.
5.023.008a Trembling, she fell down like a plantain tree in a violent wind.
Terrified by the rākṣasīs, her face turned pale. As Sītā trembled, her long and broad braid was seen quivering like a crawling serpent.
Sighing, afflicted by suffering, her consciousness overwhelmed by grief, the distressed Maithilī shed tears and lamented:
"O Rāma! she cried out in her pain, and again, "O Lakṣmaṇa!"
"Alas, my mother-in-law Kausalyā! Alas, Sumitrā!"—O noble lady, this worldly proverb uttered by the wise is true:
death is difficult to attain for either a woman or a man at an improper time.
5.023.013a Where I am tormented here by these cruel ogresses,
5.023.013c I live, though separated from Rāma, in misery even for a single moment. 5.023.014a This woman of little merit, miserable and protectorless, shall perish like one who has no refuge.
Like a full ship in the middle of the ocean struck by the force of the winds,
not seeing my husband and having fallen under the power of the Rākṣasīs,
I am indeed sinking with grief like a riverbank eroded by the water.
"Blessed are those who behold my lord, whose eyes are like lotus petals, who walks with the stride of a lion, who is grateful and speaks kindly. For me,
however, deprived in every way of that Rāma who knows his own self— "

Having tasted something like fierce poison, my life is now difficult to sustain. What kind of sin must I have committed in a previous body that I am now experiencing this terrible and most dreadful suffering?
"Overwhelmed by great sorrow, I wish to give up my life;
yet, while I am being guarded by the ogresses, Rāma cannot be reached by me. Fie upon this human condition! Fie upon dependence on others!"
"It is not possible to abandon life by one's own will.
Speaking thus, with her face covered in streaming tears, the daughter of Janaka,
the young woman, lowered her face and began to lament.
Like one insane, like one intoxicated, like one whose mind is deranged, she grieved;
like a young mare turned back, she writhed upon the ground because of the Rakshasa, who could assume any form at will, having attacked the vigilant Raghava.
5.024.003c Having been violently overpowered by Rāvaṇa, I was brought here while crying out;
5.024.004a having fallen under the power of the rākṣasīs and being treated most cruelly,
5.024.004c reflecting on this and afflicted by great sorrow, I have no desire to live.
5.024.005a Indeed, I have no need for life, nor for wealth, nor for ornaments,
5.024.005c while dwelling in the midst of ogresses without Rāma, the great chariot-warrior.
5.024.006a Shame on me, ignoble and unchaste, that I am deprived of him!
"I shall protect my life for even a moment, though it be a sinful life;
yet what faith have I in life or in happiness without that beloved husband,
the speaker of kind words, who was dear to the earth bounded by the oceans?"
"Let my body be torn apart or even devoured; I shall cast it aside. Yet, deprived of my beloved, I cannot endure this suffering for long.
I would not touch that night-stalker even with my left foot."
How could I ever desire Rāvaṇa, who is so utterly contemptible? He does not recognize his own rejection, nor himself, nor his own lineage—
he who, by his cruel nature, desires to solicit me.
Whether cut, split, divided, or cast into a blazing fire, I shall not serve Rāvaṇa; what is the use of your long-winded lamentation?
Rāghava is renowned, wise, grateful, and compassionate.

"Though he is of virtuous conduct, I suspect he has become pitiless due to the exhaustion of my good fortune. Why does he not come to me— he by whom alone the fourteen thousand rākṣasas in Janasthāna were destroyed?"
"I have been imprisoned by Rāvaṇa, a rākṣasa of little prowess;
yet my husband is truly capable of slaying Rāvaṇa in combat—
he who [slew] Virādha, that bull among rākṣasas, in the Daṇḍaka forest."
Slain by Rāma in battle, why does he not come to me? Granted, this Laṅkā in the midst of the ocean is difficult to assail;
yet there exists no obstruction to the path of Rāghava’s arrows.

"What indeed could be the reason that Rāma, of firm prowess, does not come to the rescue of his beloved wife who has been carried off by the Rākṣasa? I suspect that the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa does not know that I am staying here."
For even though he was powerful, he endured that assault despite knowing it;
yet that king of vultures, who had learned that I was abducted and would have reported it to Rāghava,
was struck down by Rāvaṇa in battle.

A great deed was performed by Jaṭāyu, though he was old, when he came to my aid while standing in single combat against Rāvaṇa. If that descendant of Raghu knew that I am staying here, [he would come].
Today, filled with rage, he could rid the world of Rākṣasas with his arrows;
he could demolish the city of Laṅkā and dry up the great ocean,
and he could destroy the fame and the name of the base Rāvaṇa.

Then, in every house of the rākṣasa women whose protectors have been slain, there will be weeping just as I am now; of this there is no doubt. Having searched through Laṅkā, Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, will deal with the rākṣasas.
For no enemy seen by those two can live for even a moment;
soon this Laṅkā, its paths choked with the smoke of funeral pyres and crowded with circles of vultures, will become like a cremation ground.
"In a very short time, I shall surely attain my heart's desire. This ill-omened departure portends the reversal of all your fortunes.
For such inauspicious signs as these are seen here in Laṅkā."
In a very short time, Laṅkā shall have its splendor destroyed. Indeed, once the wicked Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, is slain, this invincible city will surely wither away like a widowed woman.

And the city of Laṅkā, though once abundant with festivals for the Puṣya constellation, will become like a woman whose husband has perished— bereft of her lord and filled with Rākṣasas. Surely, in every house, the daughters of the Rākṣasas will be weeping.

In no time at all, I shall hear here the cries of those afflicted by sorrow; for the city of Laṅkā— shrouded in darkness, its light extinguished, and its foremost Rākṣasas slain— shall become utterly consumed by the arrows of Rāma.
If only that heroic Rāma, whose eyes are red at the corners, knew that I am currently staying in the residence of Rāvaṇa!
But by this cruel and base Rāvaṇa, I have been [held].
The time has now arrived for that which was ordained as the agreement.
For those Nairṛtas who commit evil deeds and do not know what ought not to be done,
a great calamity shall indeed arise from unrighteousness at this very moment.
"These flesh-eating Rākṣasas do not understand righteousness;
surely this Rākṣasa will prepare me for his morning meal.
How shall I fare without him, whose appearance is so dear?"
Not seeing Rāma, whose eyes were red at the corners, she was deeply distressed:
"If there were anyone here today who could give me poison,
I would quickly see the god Vaivasvata [the Lord of Death] without my husband."
Rāma, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, does not know that I am alive;
for if those two knew, they would certainly not cease their search for me on this earth. Surely, it is because of my grief alone that the heroic elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa [has come to this state].
Having cast off his body upon the surface of the earth, he has gone from here to the world of the gods.
Blessed are the gods, along with the gandharvas, the siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis,
who behold my lord Rāma, whose eyes are like lotuses.

5.024.040 Or rather, for the sake of that wise royal sage Rāma, who desires righteousness and is the Supreme Soul, I—his wife—would not be pleased by seeing him; there is no affection for one who does not behold [the beloved].
5.024.041 Affection exists for one who sees; it does not exist for one who does not see.
The ungrateful may destroy [all], but Rāma will not destroy [us]. Do I lack any virtues, or has my good fortune indeed been exhausted,
that I, Sītā, a woman worthy of the best, am now separated from Rāma?

"It is better for me to die than to live deprived of that great-souled Rāma— of him whose conduct is untainted, who is heroic, and the destroyer of his enemies. Or perhaps those two have laid down their weapons and are subsisting on roots and fruits in the forest."
For those two brothers, the best of men, were wandering as forest-dwellers;
or perhaps those two heroic brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, have been slain by deceit by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas.
5.024.046a Since time has come to this, I desire death in every way; 5.024.046c yet death is not ordained for me, even though I remain in this suffering.
5.024.047a Truly blessed are the great-souled sages who are esteemed for their truthfulness.
5.024.047c Those highly fortunate ones who have conquered their own selves have neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant.
5.024.048a From the pleasant no suffering arises, and from the unpleasant there is no greater fear.
5.024.048c Salutations to those great-souled ones who are indeed liberated from both.
