"Abandoned here by my beloved Rāma, who knows his own self, I shall give up my life now that I have fallen under the power of the wicked Rāvaṇa. When Sītā had spoken thus so terribly, the rākṣasīs were overcome with rage.
Some went to report that to the powerful Rāvaṇa;
then, approaching Sītā, the Rākṣasa women of terrible appearance spoke again these harsh words, consistent in their intent and aimed at her ruin.
"Come now, O ignoble Sītā, you who are fixed in evil resolve!
These Rākṣasīs shall devour this flesh of yours at their pleasure.
Having seen Sītā then threatened by those ignoble women, [he spoke thus].
The aged Rākṣasī Trijaṭā, as she lay there, spoke these words:
"O ignoble ones, eat yourselves; you shall not devour Sītā—the beloved daughter of Janaka and the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha."
"For today I have seen a dream, terrible and hair-raising,
portending the destruction of the Rākṣasas and the welfare of her husband.
When Trijaṭā had spoken thus, the Rākṣasa women were overcome with rage.
5.025.007c All of them, being terrified, spoke these words to Trijaṭā:
5.025.008a "Tell us, what kind of person was seen by you in this dream during the night?
5.025.009a Having heard those words emerging from the mouths of the rākṣasīs, [she replied:]
At that time, Rāghava spoke these words concerning Trijaṭā’s dream:
"Mounting himself upon a divine palanquin made of ivory that travels through the air, yoked to a thousand horses..."
5.025.011a And today in a dream, I saw Sītā clothed in white garments; 5.025.011c she was stationed upon a white mountain surrounded by the ocean;
5.025.011e Sītā was united with Rāma, just as radiance is united with the sun.
And I saw Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, mounted upon a great elephant resembling a mountain with four tusks, as he moved about;
then those two tigers among men shone with their own splendor.
Wearing white garlands and garments, they stood beside Jānakī. Then,
at the summit of that mountain, Jānakī took her place upon the shoulder of the elephant, who was held by her husband as he remained suspended in the air.
5.025.015a Then, leaping up from her husband’s lap, the lotus-eyed lady,
5.025.015c rubbing the moon and the sun with both her hands, was seen by me.
5.025.016a Thereupon, that best of elephants was mounted by those two princes.
Standing above Laṅkā with the large-eyed Sītā, he himself,
wearing white garlands and garments, was joined by Lakṣmaṇa in a chariot yoked to eight white bulls.
5.025.017e Together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and his wife Sītā,
5.025.018a Rāvaṇa has today fallen from the Puṣpaka chariot to the earth. 5.025.018c Again, he was seen by the woman with a plough in his hand— shaven-headed and clad in black garments.
Adorned with red garlands and unguents, he set out in a chariot yoked with donkeys toward the southern quarter and entered a lake of mud. There,
a woman dressed in red garments bound the ten-necked one by the throat.
Kālī, her limbs smeared with mud, drags toward the southern direction;
the ten-necked Rāvaṇa proceeds on a boar, Indrajit on a porpoise,
and Kumbhakarṇa on a camel as they depart for the southern quarter.
A great assembly has taken place, resounding with the sounds of singing and musical instruments,
as the Rākṣasas— wearing red garlands and red garments— drink.
And here is the lovely city of Laṅkā, crowded with horses and chariots.
5.025.023c They were seen fallen into the ocean, with the city gates and archways shattered.
5.025.024a Having drunk oil, all the Rākṣasa women in Laṅkā— now rough with ashes— began to dance and laugh with loud voices.
5.025.025 These Kumbhakarṇa and all the other preeminent rākṣasas, having taken red garments, have entered a pool of cow dung. 5.025.026 Depart! Perish! Rāghava will recover Sītā.
Filled with supreme indignation, he will surely cause him to be slain along with all the rākṣasas;
for Rāghava will not tolerate his beloved and highly esteemed wife— who has followed him into forest exile— even if she were merely rebuked or threatened.
"Enough of these cruel words from you; let only words of consolation be spoken. We shall entreat Vaidehī, for this is what pleases me—she who, though suffering, has had such a dream revealed to her."
5.025.029c Released from many sufferings, she shall attain unsurpassed joy. 5.025.030a Even though she has been reviled, you should entreat her; O rākṣasīs, what is the use of further speech?
5.025.030c For a terrible danger from Rāghava has now arrived for the rākṣasas.
"For Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, is indeed pleased by my prostration;
she is fully capable of protecting us from this great danger from the rākṣasīs. Moreover, I do not perceive anything amiss in this large-eyed lady."
"Even though there is no sign of contradiction in her limbs,
nor even the slightest mark, I suspect that this misfortune has arisen merely from a defect in her shadow—
this queen who does not deserve such suffering, now standing in the sky."
"I perceive the accomplishment of Vaidehī’s purpose at hand—
the destruction of the lord of the rākṣasas and the victory of Rāghava. This omen is a great source of joy for her to hear."
Her wide eye, like a lotus petal, is seen to be throbbing;
moreover,
her right arm— though she is not naturally right-handed— is suddenly trembling, O Vaidehī.
Her left thigh, peerless and resembling the trunk of a female elephant,
seems to tremble as if to indicate that Rāghava stands before her;
and a bird has entered its dwelling in the branch.
Again and again speaking words of supreme consolation, uttering greetings of welcome,
he urged them on repeatedly as if filled with joy.
Having heard those words of Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, which were so unpleasant, Sītā— afflicted by that which was disagreeable to her— trembled with fear like one in the depths of a forest.
That timid elephant princess, seized by a lion and situated in the midst of the rākṣasīs,
was severely threatened by Rāvaṇa’s words.
Abandoned in the middle of a desolate wilderness,
Sītā lamented like a young girl; "Truly indeed," she said, "they say this in the world:"
"The virtuous say that untimely death does not exist,
yet here I am, being thus reviled,
living on for even a moment, though I am devoid of merit."
Deprived of happiness and filled with much suffering,
this heart of mine must surely be firm, since it does not shatter into a thousand pieces today.
Like a mountain peak struck by a thunderbolt,
there is certainly no fault of mine in this; I am surely to be slain by this one of unpleasant appearance.
5.026.005c Nor can I bestow my affection upon him, just as a twice-born man cannot impart a mantra to one who is not twice-born. 5.026.006a Surely this ignoble man will soon [consume] my limbs;
When that Lord of the World has not yet arrived, the King of the Rākṣasas will cut him with sharp weapons,
like a surgeon cutting a fetus from a womb.
"Alas, this is suffering for me, who am already sorrowful:
that he will not come near for two months, like a man bound and condemned to death at the end of the night."
Like a thief guilty of an offense against the king, [he cried out]: "Alas Rāma! Alas Lakṣmaṇa! Alas Sumitrā!
Alas Rāma's mother, along with my own mother!"
"5.026.008c Thus I, of little fortune, am perishing; like a ship in the great ocean driven by a deluded wind.
5.026.009a While [the deer] was carrying off the two swift horses;"
O sons of the lord of men, those two have surely been slain on my account by their very being,
like two bull-siṃhas struck by a bolt of lightning.
Surely that time was when he, assuming the form of a deer,
lusted after me, unfortunate as I am, at which moment I, foolish as I was, let go of my noble husband.
[He saw] Rāma’s younger brother and Lakṣmaṇa before him:
"O Rāma, you who are devoted to truth, long-armed one!
O you whose face resembles the full moon!"
"Alas! You do not realize that I am dear and beneficial to the world of living beings, yet I am to be slain by the Rākṣasas.
This devotion to no other deity and this forbearance—"
My sleeping on the ground, my observance of dharma, and my devotion to my husband— all this is as fruitless for me as a kindness shown to ungrateful men.
"Truly, this dharma practiced by me has been in vain;
likewise, this state of being a devoted wife is useless,
since I do not see you, emaciated and pale."
Deprived of union with you, she has lost all hope, having strictly fulfilled her father’s command; yet you have returned from the forest, having completed your vow.
"I think you, having achieved your purpose and being free from fear, will take your pleasure with large-eyed women;
but as for me, O Rāma, I have conceived a desire for you."
Having long fixed my heart on destruction and having practiced ascetic vows and penances in vain, I shall now cast them aside; fie upon this life of mine, so lacking in fortune!
"I would sooner quickly give up my life by means of poison or even a sharp weapon; yet,
there is no one who can provide me with poison."
Then Sītā, tormented by grief and reflecting in many ways within the dwelling of the Rākṣasa,
took hold of her braid and began to tie it.
"Having quickly bound my hair with this knot,
I shall go to the abode of Yama.
Having lamented thus in many ways, Sītā—
Constantly remembering Rāma with her whole being,
trembling and with a parched mouth,
she reached that best of flowering trees.
Then she, soft-limbed in every part,
approached and took hold of a branch of that tree while she was deeply reflecting upon Rāma.
Then, for the lady of auspicious limbs, there were many causes for grief regarding her own lineage and Rāmānuja—
causes that had been suppressed by her fortitude and were renowned throughout the world.
Then omens appeared,
which had previously been observed as signs of success;
[they saw] that faultless Tathāgatī, who was thus distressed.
To her, who was devoid of joy and whose mind was deeply distressed,
auspicious omens presented themselves,
just as dependents approach a man graced with prosperity.
The single eye of that fair-haired woman— beautiful, lovely, with curved lashes, surrounded by lashes like a lotus, and with a large black pupil and a white sclera— throbbed.
His arm was like a lotus struck by a fish, slightly reddened, beautiful, curved, thick, and rounded;
it was worthy of the most precious black aloe and sandalwood.
Inhabited by her beloved, who was unsurpassed,
the lovely woman trembled after a long time;
and her full breasts were like the trunks of lordly elephants.
As those two thighs of hers pressed together, her well-formed right thigh throbbed again,
signaling that Rāma was standing before her.
Furthermore, the beautiful garment of that pure-eyed woman, whose teeth were like the tips of mountain peaks, was the color of gold, as if slightly soiled by dust.
With these signs and others, the fair-browed woman of lovely limbs, who was already being awakened by perfected sages of old, felt her body begin to tremble slightly.
Like a seed withered by wind and sun that has perished, he was restored to life by the rain;
her lips, moreover, were like the bimba fruit.
With beautiful eyes, eyebrows, and hair, and with curved eyelashes, his face shone with white,
pure teeth like the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu.
Free from sorrow, with weariness dispelled, her fever stilled and her spirit awakened by joy,
that noble lady shone with a face as bright as the moon in its white phase.
Just as the night [is illuminated] by the risen moon,
the valiant Hanumān also heard everything in its true essence—
the words of Sītā, Trijaṭā, and the threats of the rākṣasīs.
Beholding that queen, who was like a goddess in the Nandana grove,
the monkey then fell into many kinds of reflections:
"How shall these many thousands and tens of thousands of monkeys..."

"She was sought for in all directions; now she has been found by me. Through a well-employed spy moving in secret, I have observed the enemy's strength, and this very thing has been scrutinized by me."
5.028.005 This specific nature of the Rākṣasas, this city,
and the power of this lord of the Rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa, have been observed.
5.028.006 It is fitting for that immeasurable one who is compassionate toward all living beings.
5.028.006c To console my wife, who longs for the sight of her husband, 5.028.007a I shall comfort her, whose face resembles the full moon,
5.028.007c who has not known such sorrow before and who finds no end to her grief.
For if I were to depart without having consoled this queen, whose mind is stricken by grief, my departure would be a transgression. For once I have gone there, this illustrious princess—

Finding no means of rescue, Jānakī might give up her life. Furthermore, it is right that I should console that mighty-armed one, whose face resembles the full moon and who is longing for the sight of Sītā.
"It is impossible to speak face-to-face with these night-stalkers;
indeed, how should I act now that I have fallen into such distress?
For if I am not comforted by you during this remainder of the night,"
5.028.012c There is no doubt at all that she will give up her life.
5.028.013a And if Rāma should ask me, "What words did Sītā say to me? 5.028.013c what could I possibly say to him, having failed to speak with that woman of slender waist?
If I depart from here in haste without Sītā’s message,
the descendant of Kakutstha might consume me with his fierce gaze in his anger; yet,
if I were to inform my lord for the sake of Rāma...
The arrival of him and his army will be in vain;
however, having found an opportunity while stationed here among the rākṣasīs,
I shall gradually console this woman who is overwhelmed with grief.
"For I am indeed very small in stature, and especially so as a monkey;
yet I shall utter speech here in refined Sanskrit.
If I were to deliver such refined speech, one would think me a twice-born brahmin."
Thinking me to be Rāvaṇa, Sītā will become terrified. Indeed, I must certainly speak meaningful human words; otherwise, this blameless woman cannot be comforted by me.
5.028.020a Seeing my form and likewise hearing my speech, this Jānakī,
who was previously terrified by the rākṣasas, will again fall into terror.
5.028.021a Then, overcome with fear, that high-minded woman will raise a cry.
Though she knew Rāvaṇa could assume any form at will, the large-eyed lady [remained there].
And when Sītā made a sound, the terrible host of rākṣasīs,
bearing various weapons and resembling Death itself, suddenly gathered together.
Then, surrounding me on all sides, those with distorted faces will exert their full strength in an effort to capture or kill me.
[I shall resort to] the branches, twigs, and trunks of the noble trees.
Seeing me running about in this manner, they would become filled with fear and apprehension;
and beholding my form as I range through the great forest,
those hideous-faced rākṣasīs would be struck with terror.
Then the rākṣasa women,
appointed by the lord of the rākṣasas to his residence, should summon the rākṣasas as well.
With spears, arrows, swords, and various weapons in their hands, they [should call them forth].
In this conflict, they might fall upon us with force, causing great agitation; yet, though I am enraged and am dispersing the army of the rākṣasas on all sides,
I am unable to reach the further shore of the great ocean.

"Or many swift-acting men might leap up and seize me; then this woman would have her purpose unfulfilled, and my own capture would occur. Furthermore, those who delight in violence might even harm this daughter of Janaka."
Then this mission of Rāma and Sugrīva would fail,
for Jānaki dwells here in a place surrounded by the ocean, hidden and with paths lost amidst these rākṣasas.
Whether I am slain or captured by the *rākṣasas* in battle,
I see no other helper for Rāma in accomplishing his task.
And even upon reflection, I do not see any monkey who, once I am killed, could succeed.
"I could leap across the great ocean, though it be a hundred yojanas wide;
indeed, I am capable of slaying even thousands of rākṣasas.
Yet, I shall not be able to reach the further shore of the great ocean."
"Warfare is full of falsehoods, and uncertainty does not appeal to me. What wise man would exchange a certain task for one that is uncertain?
For there would be a great fault in my speaking with Sītā."
If she is not addressed, Vaidehī will give up her life;
and even purposes already accomplished perish when they encounter a messenger who is incompetent due to the conflict of time and place, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Even a firm judgment regarding what is beneficial and what is harmful does not shine if it is reached by those who merely imagine themselves to be wise; for such messengers ruin the tasks at hand.
How might the task not perish? How might there be no confusion?
"How might my leaping across the ocean not be in vain?
How indeed can he hear my words and yet not be terrified?"—
having reflected thus, the wise Hanumān formed a plan.
"By praising Rāma, whose actions are effortless and who is our own kinsman,
I shall not cause distress to her, whose mind is fixed on him. [I shall speak] of Rāma, the most excellent of the Ikṣvākus, who knows his own self."
Offering auspicious words endowed with righteousness,
I shall cause all of them to be heard while speaking sweet speech;
I shall arrange everything in such a way that she will indeed have faith.
Thus, that high-souled one,
gazing upon the consort of the lord of the world,
spoke these many kinds of sweet and truthful words.
Standing within the branches of the tree, the great monkey Hanumān, having reflected thus upon many kinds of thoughts,
spoke these sweet words within the hearing of Vaidehī.
There was a king named Daśaratha, who possessed chariots, elephants, and horses; he was virtuous in character, of great renown, upright, and highly illustrious.
Born into a lineage of universal monarchs, he was equal to Indra in strength.
Delighting in non-violence, noble-minded, compassionate, and possessing the prowess of truth;
the foremost of the Ikṣvāku lineage, endowed with fortune and increasing prosperity; marked with the characteristics of a sovereign, possessed of vast glory, he was a bull among kings.
He was renowned throughout the earth bounded by its four oceans as a giver of happiness and one who himself lived in happiness.
His eldest son, dear to him, had a face like the lord of the stars;
named Rāma, he was a man of specialized knowledge and the best among all archers.
He is the protector of his own conduct, the protector of his kinsmen,
the protector of the world of living beings, and the scorcher of enemies of dharma;
[this was said] at the word of his father, who was truthful in his intent and advanced in years.
Accompanied by his wife and his brother, that hero went forth into the forest as an ascetic. While he was roaming about hunting in that great wilderness,
he heard of the slaughter at Janasthāna and that Khara and Dūṣaṇa had been killed.
Then, Janaki, having been carried off by Ravana out of his impatience—
exactly as she was described in her form, her complexion, and her splendor—
I heard of her from Raghava; here she is, found by me.
Having spoken these words, that bull among monkeys ceased;
and Janaki, having heard it, was filled with the utmost wonder.
Then she, whose hair-ends were curved and who possessed beautiful locks, [covered her face] with her hair.
Lifting up her face, the timid woman gazed at the śiṃśapā tree;
looking sideways, upwards, and likewise downwards,
she contemplated that inconceivable being.
He beheld the minister of the lord of the monkeys,
the son of the Wind, standing like the sun at its rising. Then, seeing him hidden within the branches, her mind was shaken.
5.030.001c There she saw the monkey, humble and speaking kindly;
5.030.002a but seeing that best of monkeys standing before her with humility,
5.030.002c the passionate Maithilī thought, "This is a dream."
Upon seeing him, Sītā became utterly unconscious, as if her life-breath had departed; and only after a long time did she regain consciousness.
The large-eyed woman reflected:
"Today I have seen this strange dream;
a monkey, which is forbidden by the collections of the scriptures."
"May it be well with Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
as well as with my father, King Janaka.
This is not even a dream, for I have no sleep."
For me, who am tormented by grief and sorrow because I am bereft of him whose face resembles the full moon, there is indeed no happiness.
For today my mind is tormented by love for him, and with all my being directed toward him, I am constantly thinking of nothing but him.
In that very way I see, in that way I hear,
and I think, "May this be my wish";
nevertheless, I deliberate upon it with my intellect.
"What is the reason that he has no form,
yet he speaks to me with a most distinct form? Homage be to Vācaspati, the wielder of the thunderbolt!"
And what has been spoken by this forest-dweller here before me regarding Svayambhū and Hutāśana— let that be so, and not otherwise.
5.031.001 The immensely radiant Hanumān, son of the Wind-god,
placed his joined palms to his head and addressed Sītā in a sweet voice: 5.031.002 "Who is this woman with eyes like lotus petals, dressed in soiled silk?"
"O blameless one, you stand there grasping the branch of a tree;
for what reason does water born of grief flow from your eyes,
like water scattered from the petals of two white lotuses?"
"O beautiful one, who are you among the gods, the asuras, the nāgas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas? Among the yakṣas and kinnaras, who are you?
O lady of lovely countenance, do you belong to the Rudras or the Maruts?"

"O lady of beautiful hips, you appear to me like one of the Vasu deities. Are you perhaps Rohiṇī— the best among the stars, endowed with every excellence— who has fallen from the abode of the gods, deprived of the Moon?"
"Whether out of anger or delusion, O dark-eyed one, you have provoked your husband Vasiṣṭha; you are not the auspicious Arundhatī.
Who is our son, father, brother, or husband to you, O slender-waisted lady?"
"You are grieving for one who has gone from this world to the next.
For by the secondary marks and primary characteristics that I perceive in you,
it is my opinion that you are a princess, the chief queen of a protector of the earth."
"If Sītā has been forcibly abducted from Janasthāna by Rāvaṇa— if you are she, may prosperity be yours— then tell me, who am asking you.
Having heard his words, she was delighted by the mention of Rāma.
5.031.011c Vaidehī spoke these words to Hanumān, who was perched upon a tree: 5.031.012a "I am the daughter of the high-souled Janaka of Videha;
5.031.012c I am known by the name Sītā, and I am the wife of the wise Rāma."
For twelve years there, in the residence of Rāghava,
I enjoyed human pleasures, with every desire fulfilled;
then, in the thirteenth year, [I shall see] the joy of the Ikṣvākus in his kingdom.
The king, together with his preceptor, proceeded to perform the consecration;
while the preparations for Rāghava’s consecration were being made,
the queen named Kaikeyī spoke these words to her husband.
"I shall neither drink nor eat my daily food;
this will be the end of my life if Rāma is consecrated. O best of kings, those words which were spoken by you out of affection—"
"If that [promise] must not be made false, let Rāghava go to the forest.
Remembering the boon granted by the queen, that king, being truthful in speech,
fell into a swoon upon hearing Kaikeyī’s cruel and unpleasant words.
Then the aged king, firmly established in truth and righteousness,
weeping, entreated his illustrious eldest son for the kingdom.
The glorious prince, regarding his father’s word as dearer than his own consecration, [complied].

Having first approached with his mind, he accepted with his speech; Rāma, whose prowess is truth, would give but not take back, and would never speak anything unpleasant even for the sake of his own life.
Having cast off his costly upper garments, that one of great renown mentally renounced the kingdom and entrusted me to his mother.
Then I, destined for the forest, quickly set out before him.
"For even in heaven, a life without him does not please me;
how much less so, O illustrious one, when the son of Sumitrā, the delighter of his friends,
has adorned himself with bark garments to follow in the wake of his elder brother."
"5.031.025a Firm in our vows and highly honoring our husband’s command, we have entered this forest of profound appearance that was previously unseen.
5.031.026a While he, of immeasurable prowess, dwells in the Daṇḍaka forest, I— "
My wife has been abducted by the evil-minded Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa.
He has granted me a period of two months as a favor for my life;
after those two months have passed, I shall then give up my life.

5.032.001 Having heard those words of hers, Hanumān, the leader of the monkey hosts, spoke a consoling reply to her who was overwhelmed by sorrow upon sorrow: 5.032.002 "O Goddess, I have come as a messenger to you by the command of Rāma."
"O Vaidehī, Rāma is well, and he has inquired after your welfare.
He who is the best among those who know the Vedas, knowing both the Brahma-weapon and the Vedas— he,
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, O Queen, has inquired after your welfare."
"And Lakṣmaṇa, of great splendor, your beloved attendant,
being consumed by grief, has offered his salutation with his head to you.
Having heard news of the welfare of those two lions among men, the queen—
With all her limbs thrilled with joy, she then spoke to Hanumān:
"Ah, how auspicious this worldly proverb appears to me:
'Joy comes to a living man even after a hundred years.'"
In that meeting of theirs, a wonderful affection was produced;
and having gained confidence in one another, the two of them engaged in conversation.
Having heard those words of hers, Hanumān, the leader of the monkey hosts, [replied].
He approached Sītā, who was wretched with grief;
the more Hanumān drew near to her,
the more Sītā became suspicious of Rāvaṇa.
"Alas! Fie, fie upon this deed that has been done by him to me! Having assumed another form, it is indeed that very Rāvaṇa himself!
Having said this, she, emaciated by grief, released that branch of the Aśoka tree.
On that very spot, she of faultless limbs sat down upon the ground.
Then the mighty-armed one paid homage to the daughter of Janaka;
but she, terrified with fear, did not look up at him again.
Seeing him bowing down, Sītā, whose face resembles the moon,
sighed deeply and spoke to the monkey in a sweet voice:
"If you are the illusory Rāvaṇa himself, who has entered into a magical disguise..."
"5.032.014c You cause me even greater anguish; that is not right.
5.032.015a Having abandoned your own form and assumed the guise of a wandering mendicant, you who were seen by me in Janasthāna—you are indeed that very Rāvaṇa."
"O night-stalker who can assume any form at will, you further torment me—who am already emaciated by fasting and miserable—with that heat; it is not fitting.
If you have come as a messenger from Rāma, may it be well with you."
5.032.017c I ask you, O best of monkeys, for stories of Rāma are indeed dear to me.
5.032.018a Tell me, O monkey, of the virtues of my beloved Rāma.
5.032.018c You steal my heart, O gentle one, just as a swift current sweeps away the riverbank.
"Oh, how pleasant is this dream, that I have been brought back after such a long time! To think that I now behold a forest-dweller sent by Rāghava!
Even in a dream, if I were to see the heroic Rāghava together with Lakṣmaṇa—
"May I see him and not despair; may even my dreams be free from envy.
I do not consider this a dream, for having seen a monkey in a dream, such prosperity cannot be attained—yet this prosperity has been attained by me."
"Could this be a delusion of the mind, or perhaps a movement of the wind? Or could it be a disorder born of madness, or a mirage?
Yet, this is not madness; nor is it a delusion possessing the symptoms of madness."
"I have recognized myself and this forest-dweller as well.
Having thus deliberated in many ways upon the relative strengths and weaknesses, Sītā, because of the demons' power to change their form at will, concluded that he was the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Having formed this thought, Sītā, the slender-waisted daughter of Janaka, did not then reply to the monkey.
Perceiving what Sītā was thinking, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, [reflected].
Then, with words pleasing to the ear, he gladdened her—
[he who was] radiant like the sun, beloved by the world like the moon,
and a king of all the world like the god Vaiśravaṇa.
Endowed with prowess like the highly illustrious Viṣṇu,
truthful in speech and sweet of voice like the god Vācaspati,
he was handsome, fortunate, and majestic like Kandarpa incarnate.
He who stands ready to strike with his wrath, the best great-charioteer (mahāratha) in the world,
under whose shadow of arms the entire world takes refuge— that high-souled one [was drawn away] from his hermitage by him in the form of a deer.
"You shall see the fruit of his actions— he by whom you were carried off from the empty place—
that powerful one who will soon slay Rāvaṇa in battle with arrows released in fury, like blazing fires."
"Sent by him as a messenger, I have come here to your presence.
Afflicted with grief due to separation from you, he has inquired after your welfare.
And so too does the highly energetic Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of Sumitrā’s joy."
Having offered his salutations, that mighty-armed one also inquired after her welfare:
"O Queen, there is a monkey named Sugrīva who is a friend of Rāma;
he is the king of the foremost of monkeys, and he has inquired after your well-being."
"Rāma, together with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa, remembers you constantly.
By good fortune you live, O Vaidehī, though fallen into the power of a Rākṣasī.
Before long, you shall see Rāma and the great chariot-warrior Lakṣmaṇa."
In the midst of ten million monkeys, [I saw] Sugrīva of immeasurable prowess.
I am a monkey named Hanumān, a minister of Sugrīva;
having leaped across the great ocean, I entered the city of Laṅkā.
Having placed my foot upon the head of the evil-minded Rāvaṇa,
I have come here relying on my own prowess to see you.
O Queen, I am not such a person as you imagine me to be.
"Let this doubt be abandoned; have faith in me as I speak.
Having heard that story from the bull among monkeys, Vaidehī spoke these consoling words in a sweet voice.
"Where was your association with Rāma? How do you know Lakṣmaṇa?
And how did the meeting between the monkeys and the men take place? O monkey, what are the distinguishing marks of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa?"
Tell me those things once more, so that grief may not overcome me. What was the stature of Rāma, and what was his appearance like?
Tell me how were the thighs and the arms of both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Thus addressed by Vaidehī, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god,
then began to relate the matter to Rāma exactly as it was.
"O Vaidehī, it is by good fortune that you, knowing me, inquire after me."
O lotus-petal-eyed one, listen as I describe to you the distinctive marks of your husband and of Lakṣmaṇa— those very signs of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa which have been observed by me, O large-eyed lady.

Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals and who is enchanting to all beings, was born to the daughter of Janaka, endowed with beauty and courtesy. In splendor he resembles the sun, and in forbearance he is equal to the earth.
Equal to Bṛhaspati in intelligence and like Vāsava in glory,
he was the protector of the world of living beings and the protector of his own kin;
that scorcher of foes was the guardian of his own conduct and of righteousness.

"O beautiful lady, Rāma is the protector of the four castes of the world; he is the establisher and the enforcer of the world's moral boundaries. Radiant and highly honored, he remains steadfast in the vow of celibacy."
He was grateful for the assistance of the virtuous and knew how to carry out his duties;
he was trained in the royal sciences and was a devotee of the Brahmins. He was learned in the scriptures, endowed with good character, disciplined, and a scorcher of his enemies.
Trained in the Yajurveda and highly honored by those who know the Vedas,
he was proficient in the science of archery (Dhanurveda), the Vedas, and the Vedāṅgas;
broad-shouldered, long-armed, with a neck like a conch shell and a handsome face.
O Queen, Rāma is known by the people as having hidden collarbones and beautiful copper-colored eyes;
he has a voice with the resonance of a drum, a glossy complexion, and great majesty. He is well-proportioned, with limbs symmetrically divided, and possesses a dark-hued skin.
He has three firm parts, three pendulous parts, three even parts, and is elevated in three places;
he possesses three folds, is depressed in three places, has four flawless limbs, and three heads;
he has four jars, four lines, four cubits, and is equal in four ways.
He has fourteen symmetrical pairs, fourteen teeth, and four modes of conduct;
he has large lips, jaws, and a nose; he is smooth in five places, possesses eight ridges, ten lotuses, ten broad features, is pervaded by three, and has two white [spots].
Rāghava has six prominent features and nine slender parts; he pervades all with his three qualities.
Devoted to truth and righteousness, glorious, and intent upon gathering and favoring others, he knows the distinctions of place and time and speaks kindly to all the world.
And his half-brother, the invincible son of Sumitrā,
is likewise endowed with such affection, beauty, and virtues;
the two of them are wandering the earth searching for you alone.

On the ridge of Mount Ṛśyamūka, thick with many trees, they saw the handsome Sugrīva sitting there, distressed for his brother’s wife, having been deposed by his elder brother. He was seated upon the back of the lord of beasts.

"We, however, serve that Sugrīva, the king of monkeys, who is true to his promise, after he was deposed from the kingdom by his elder brother. Then those two, dressed in bark garments and holding excellent bows in their hands—
Having arrived at a beautiful region of Mount Ṛśyamūka,
that bull among monkeys, seeing those two tigers among men armed with bows,
leaped to the summit of that mountain, bewildered by fear.
Then that lord of monkeys, stationed upon that peak,
quickly dispatched me alone to the presence of those two.
By the command of Sugrīva, I approached those two tigers among men.
Endowed with beauty and auspicious marks, they stood before me with palms joined in reverence. Having understood the true nature of reality, I, filled with joy,
placed those two bulls among men upon my back and brought them to that region.
And having been introduced in truth to the high-souled Sugrīva,
a great affection arose between them through their mutual conversation.
There, those two— endowed with fame, the lord of monkeys and the lord of men— [remained].
Having comforted one another with a conversation concerning their former history,
Lakṣmaṇa’s elder brother then consoled Sugrīva,
who had been driven out by his brother Vālin of great splendor on account of a woman.

Then Lakṣmaṇa reported to Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, the grief that Rāma— whose actions are effortless— felt arising from your disappearance. Having heard those words uttered by Lakṣmaṇa, the lord of monkeys [acted].

Then he became utterly lusterless, like the sun seized by a planet. Then, as she was being carried away by the Rākṣasa, those clusters of ornaments that had graced your limbs were cast down upon the surface of the earth.

Having brought all of those back to Rāma, the leaders of the monkey hosts joyfully showed them to him, yet they did not know your whereabouts. Those items were given to Rāma by me and presented by my own hand.
While his mind was thus distracted, those [ornaments] fell down making loud sounds; then,
having placed them upon his lap and gazed at them in many ways,
that god-like king lamented.
As he watched her, weeping and fainting again and again,
those [ornaments] further kindled the fire of grief within the son of Daśaratha;
and that high-souled one, afflicted by sorrow, lay there for a long time.
By me as well, he was raised up again with various words of encouragement after much difficulty.
Having seen those precious objects and having shown them to him again and again,
Rāghava, together with Saumitri, presented them to Sugrīva.
"O Noble Lady, because he no longer sees you, that descendant of Raghu suffers constantly with a great,
blazing fire, like a mountain of fire. On your account, sleeplessness, grief, and anxiety afflict that Raghava."
They torment that great-souled one, just as fires consume a fire-sanctuary;
by the grief of not seeing you, Rāghava is shaken,
like a massive mountain during a great earthquake.
"O daughter of a king, wandering through these most delightful forests, rivers, and waterfalls, he finds no pleasure because he does not see you.
That Raghava, a tiger among men, will soon find you."
O daughter of Janaka, having slain Rāvaṇa along with his friends and kinsmen,
both Rāma and Sugrīva then entered into an agreement to slay Vālī and likewise to search for you.
Then, having swiftly slain Vālin in battle,
Rāma made Sugrīva the lord of all the hosts of bears and monkeys;
thus was the alliance between Rāma and Sugrīva established by the Queen herself.
"Know me and Hanumān to be the messengers who have come here from those two.
Having regained his own kingdom, Sugrīva has assembled great monkeys and dispatched these mighty ones to the ten directions for your sake."
Commanded by Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, those of great prowess—
who resembled the king of mountains— set out from all sides across the earth.
Among them was the illustrious and mighty Aṅgada, the son of Vālin.
Having set out, that tiger among monkeys, accompanied by one-third of the army,
departed. While we were lost on the Vindhya, the best of mountains,
many days and nights passed as we were deeply overwhelmed with grief.
5.033.054a Because of our despair regarding the task, the passing of time, and fear of the king of monkeys, we have resolved to give up our lives.
5.033.055a Having searched the forest fastnesses, the mountains, and the waterfalls, [we found nothing].
"Unable to find the goddess, they have resolved to give up their lives.
Plunged deeply into an ocean of grief, Aṅgada lamented:
"O Vaidehī, there is both your disappearance and likewise the slaying of Vālī!"
Our fasting unto death and the passing of Jaṭāyu— while we were thus despondent over our master’s command and longing for death,
a great and powerful bird arrived as if for the sake of our mission.
The king of vultures named Saṃpāti, the uterine brother of the king of vultures,
having heard of his brother’s slaughter, spoke these words out of anger:
"By whom has my younger brother been killed, and where was he destroyed?"
"O best of monkeys, I wish for you to relate this. Aṅgada then recounted to him exactly how the great slaughter at Janasthāna had been carried out by the demon of fearsome form, directed against you.
Having heard of the slaughter of Jaṭāyu, that son of Aruṇa was deeply grieved;
O lady of excellent limbs, he spoke thus to you while you were dwelling in the abode of Rāvaṇa.
Having heard those words of Saṃpāti, which increased her joy—
Then, with Aṅgada at our head, we all set forth;
the monkeys were thrilled, satisfied, and filled with enthusiasm at the prospect of seeing you. Then, seeing the ocean, the monkey army despaired.
Having shaken off intense fear, I leapt across a hundred yojanas;
at night, I entered Laṅkā, which is teeming with Rākṣasas,
and there I beheld both Rāvaṇa and you, oppressed by grief.
"O blameless lady, all this has been related to you exactly as it happened. Speak to me, O Queen; I am the messenger of the son of Daśaratha.
You shall see me here, having come for your sake, with my efforts directed toward Rāma."
"O Queen, recognize the son of the Wind-god as Sugrīva’s minister. Your descendant of Kakutstha’s line, the best among all wielders of weapons, is well,
as is the auspicious Lakṣmaṇa, who is devoted to the service of his elder."
"O Goddess, devoted to the welfare of that heroic husband of yours, I alone have arrived here at the command of Sugrīva. By me,
moving about here without assistance and able to assume any form at will,"

The southern direction has been traversed by me in my search for your path. By good fortune, I shall dispel the grief of the monkey hosts who mourn your disappearance by announcing that I have found you.
"By good fortune, O Goddess, my crossing of the ocean has not been in vain;
by good fortune, I shall obtain this fame born of beholding you.
And the immensely heroic Rāghava will soon reach you."
Having slain Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, along with his friends and kinsmen,
O Vaidehī, the monkey Keśarin goes from there to Mount Kauraja, the highest of mountains,
and then to Mount Gokarṇa.
And that great monkey, my father, was seen by the divine sages as he was uprooting Śambasādana at the sacred ford of the lord of rivers. O Maithilī, I was born from Vāta in his field.
"He is renowned in the world as Hanumān by his own deeds alone;
O Vaidehī, I have described my master’s virtues for the sake of inspiring confidence in you.
Thus was Sītā, emaciated by grief, reassured by these arguments.
By means of her innate supernatural powers, she recognized that messenger;
and Janaki, having attained incomparable joy,
shed tears born of bliss from her eyes with their curved lashes.
That beautiful face of hers, with its large, copper-hued, white,
and long eyes, shone like the lord of stars released from Rāhu;
she clearly perceived Hanumān to be a monkey and nothing else.
Then Hanumān spoke this reply to that lovely-to-behold woman: "When the Asura Śambasādana had been slain in battle by the hero of monkeys at the urging of the great seer,"
Therefore, O Maithilī, I am indeed born of Vāyu; by my power, I am a monkey equal to him.
Once again, the highly energetic Hanumān, son of Māruta—
He spoke these humble words for the sake of inspiring confidence in Sītā:
"O illustrious lady, I am a monkey, a messenger of the wise Rāma. O Queen, behold this finger-ring engraved with Rāma's name."
"Take heart, may it be well with you; for the fruit of your suffering has been exhausted.
Taking hold of and gazing upon the ornament on her husband's hand, Janaki felt as if she had regained her husband himself, and she became joyful.
That beautiful face of hers, with its long eyes white and copper-hued at the corners,
became radiant with intense joy, like the lord of stars when released from Rāhu.
Then that modest young woman, gladdened by her husband’s message, [prepared to depart].
5.034.005c Delighted upon hearing what was pleasing, she praised the great monkey:
5.034.006a "You are valiant, you are capable, and you are wise, O best of monkeys,
5.034.006c since this abode of the Rākṣasas has been assailed by you alone."
The ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, extending for a hundred yojanas,
has been turned into a mere cow’s footprint by you as you strode across it with valor worthy of praise;
for I do not consider you to be an ordinary monkey, O bull among monkeys.
Since you have no terror of Rāvaṇa, nor even any agitation,
you are worthy, O best of monkeys, to converse with me,
provided that you have been sent by that Rāma who knows his own self.
The invincible Rāma will certainly not send [someone] to my presence without having tested [him],
especially without knowing his prowess;
and by good fortune, the righteous Rāma, who is devoted to dharma, is well.
And the highly resplendent Lakṣmaṇa, who increases the joy of Sumitrā—
if that descendant of Kakutstha is well, why then does he burn the earth, which has the ocean for its girdle, with his wrath like the fire risen at the end of an eon?
"Or rather, those two are capable of subduing even the gods;
yet I think there is no reversal of my own sorrows. Is Rāma indeed suffering? Is he not falling into despair?"
The Supreme Person performs even further duties;
is he not dejected or agitated, and does he not become confused in his tasks? Does the king’s son carry out the works that require human effort?
O scorcher of foes, does the seeker of victory employ the two-fold and three-fold means, as well as the [single] means, toward his friends? Does he acquire allies,
and is he also sought after by his allies?
Is he possessed of virtuous friends and honored by his companions? Does the prince hope for the favor of the gods?
And does he apply himself to both human effort and destiny?
I hope that Rāghava’s affection for me has not faded during our separation;
I hope that the monkey will deliver me from this calamity—
he who is always accustomed to comforts and unaccustomed to hardships.
Having encountered further suffering, I hope that Rāma does not despair.
Likewise, I hope that all is well with Kausalyā and Sumitrā,
and I constantly hear that Bharata is also doing well.
"Is Rāghava, who is worthy of honor, perhaps distressed on my account? Is Rāma not distracted by other thoughts? Will he rescue me?
And will Bharata, who is devoted to his brother, [lead] that formidable army of an akṣauhiṇī?"
Will the illustrious Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, come for my sake, sending forth his army protected by his ministers,
surrounded by heroic monkeys whose weapons are their teeth and claws?
And I trust that the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, the enhancer of Sumitrā’s joy,
skilled in weapons, will scatter the Rākṣasas with a net of arrows;
and I trust that they have been slain in battle by Rāma with the Raudra weapon.
In a short time, I shall behold Rāvaṇa along with his circle of friends.
Is it not that face of his, golden in color and possessing a fragrance like a lotus?
Without me, he withers, dejected by grief,
like a lotus at the exhaustion of water when scorched by the sun; and as for him who abandons the kingdom under the pretext of teaching dharma—
As he led me on foot into the forest,
there was no distress in him, nor fear, nor sorrow;
does he still maintain that fortitude in his heart?
Neither his mother, nor his father, nor anyone else possesses an affection for him that is superior to or even equal to mine; therefore,
O messenger, I wish to live.
"Until I hear news of my beloved"—
having spoken these words of great significance to that lord of monkeys with sweet meaning, the queen [departed].
Desiring once more to hear his delightful speech concerning Rāma, the beautiful woman ceased speaking.
Having heard Sītā’s words, Māruti, of fearsome prowess, [prepared to depart].
Placing his joined palms to his head, he spoke these further words:
"The lotus-eyed Rāma does not know that you are staying here;
as soon as he hears my message, Rāghava will come quickly."
Leading a vast army crowded with throngs of monkeys and bears,
and having paralyzed the unshakeable abode of Varuṇa with floods of arrows,
the descendant of Kakutstha will leave the city of Laṅkā devoid of Rākṣasas.
If there should be death in the interval, or if the gods together with the asuras should stand in Rāma’s path, he will slay them as well.
O noble lady, he is overwhelmed by the grief born of not seeing you.
Rāma finds no peace, like an elephant tormented by a lion. O Queen, I swear to you by the Dardara mountain, by its roots and fruits,
and by Malaya, Vindhya, Meru, and Mandara.
"O Vaidehī, you shall soon behold on Mount Prasravaṇa the face of Rāma— beautiful with its lovely eyes, its lips like the bimba fruit, and adorned with charming earrings, like the risen full moon."
He sat like Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, upon the summit of the vault of heaven. Rāghava eats no meat, nor does he indulge in honey;
he constantly eats well-prepared forest food at the fifth mealtime.
With his inner self absorbed in you, Rāghava does not even remove gadflies, mosquitoes, insects, or reptiles from his body;
Rāma is constantly intent on meditation and perpetually devoted to grief.
He thinks of nothing else, having fallen under the power of desire; Rāma, that best of men, remains perpetually sleepless, and even when asleep,
he awakens uttering the sweet words, "Sītā."
Upon seeing a fruit, a flower, or anything else that is pleasing to women,
he addresses you repeatedly while sighing, "O beloved!
O Queen, he is constantly consumed by the heat of longing.
Addressing you alone as "Sītā," that high-souled prince of firm vows has exerted every effort for your recovery.
Her grief dispelled by the chanting of Rāma’s name, yet sharing his sorrow through her own grief for him,
she was like the moon at the beginning of autumn when only a remnant of clouds remains.
Like night [to the moon], Sītā, the daughter of Videha, whose face resembles the full moon, having heard those words,
spoke these words consistent with dharma and artha to Hanumān.
"What you have spoken, O monkey, is like nectar mixed with poison; for Rāma is neither distracted by anything else nor is he overcome by grief,
whether in the midst of vast sovereignty or in the face of most terrible calamity."
As if binding a man with a rope, the Ordainer drags him away. O best of monkeys, destiny is surely irresistible for living beings;
behold Saumitri, myself, and Rāma, all bewildered by calamities.
"When will Rāghava reach the further shore of this grief—
like one who, exhausted and with his ship destroyed, is swimming in the ocean?
Having brought about the destruction of the Rākṣasas and having slain Rāvaṇa..."
"Having caused Laṅkā to be uprooted, when will my husband see me?
He must be told:
'Hurry! For my life shall last only as long as this year has not yet run its course."
"O monkey, ten months have passed and only two remain of the time limit that was set for me by the cruel Rāvaṇa,
as well as by my brother Vibhīṣaṇa regarding my restoration."
Though entreated with great effort, he does not set his mind upon doing that;
for the restoration of me to Rāvaṇa does not please him. Death, having come under the power of Time, seeks out Rāvaṇa in battle.
"O monkey, Jyeṣṭhā Kanyānalā, the daughter of Vibhīṣaṇa,
told this to me herself when she was sent by her mother.
There is a wise and learned bull among the Rākṣasas named Avindhya."
5.035.012c Steadfast, virtuous, and aged, he was highly esteemed by Rāvaṇa;
5.035.013a he urged him toward the destruction of the Rākṣasas at the hands of Rāma,
5.035.013c yet that evil-minded one would not listen even to his beneficial words.
"O best of monkeys, she hopes that her husband will soon regain me;
for my inner self is pure, and he possesses many virtues:
energy, manliness, courage, compassion, and gratitude."
Valour and majesty reside in the monkey and the descendant of Raghu;
he who slew fourteen thousand Rākṣasas in Janasthāna without his brother— who that is an enemy would not tremble before him?
5.035.017a That bull among men cannot be weighed down by calamities;
5.035.017c I am one who knows his majesty, just as Pulomajā knows that of Śakra.
5.035.018a O monkey, the heroic Rāma is like the sun, possessing rays in the form of a net of arrows.
"The waters consisting of enemies and Rākṣasas shall be brought to total desiccation"—
to her, who was speaking thus on account of Rāma, emaciated by grief and her face filled with tears, the monkey Hanumān spoke.
Upon hearing my words alone, Rāghava will swiftly arrive,
leading a vast army teeming with hosts of monkeys and bears;
or else, I myself shall liberate her this very day from the Rākṣasa.
"O blameless one, climb onto my back to escape this suffering;
for having placed you upon my back, I shall cross the ocean.
Indeed, I have the power to carry even Laṅkā together with Rāvaṇa."
"O Maithilī, today I shall deliver you to Rāghava as he stays at Prasravaṇa,
just as the fire delivers the oblation to Śakra.
This very day, O Vaidehī, you shall see Rāghava together with Lakṣmaṇa."
He was endowed with resolve like Viṣṇu for the slaying of the Daityas;
that mighty one, filled with enthusiasm at the sight of you, sat in his hermitage like Purandara seated upon the head of the king of serpents.
"Ascend my back, O Goddess; do not hesitate, O beautiful one.
Seek union with Rāma, as Rohiṇī does with the Moon.
She spoke thus, as if conversing with the Moon, like Suvarcalā with the Sun.
"Mounting my back, you shall cross the great ocean of the sky.
For when I have set out from here taking you with me, O lady, none of the inhabitants of Laṅkā will be able to follow my course."
"Just as I have arrived here, so shall I undoubtedly depart, O Vaidehī; behold me, lifting you up into the sky.
But Maithilī, having heard these extraordinary words from the best of monkeys, [was filled with wonder].
With all her limbs thrilled with wonder, she then spoke to Hanumān:
"Hanumān, how do you wish to carry me over such a long distance?
O leader of the monkey hosts, I consider that very thing to be your true monkey-nature."

"How can you, with such a small body, wish to lead me from here to the presence of my husband, the lord of men, O bull among monkeys? Having heard these words of Sītā, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, [replied].
The illustrious one reflected upon the new insult that had been committed:
"That dark-eyed woman does not know my true nature or my power;
therefore, let Vaidehī behold the form I can assume at will."
Having reflected thus, Hanumān,
the best of monkeys and crusher of enemies, then revealed his true form to Vaidehī.
That wise bull among monkeys leaped down from that tree.
Then, for the sake of inspiring confidence in Sītā, he began to grow;
resembling Mount Meru or the Mandara tree, he shone with the brilliance of a blazing fire.
And that bull among monkeys stood before Sītā.
Resembling a mountain, with a copper-colored face and great strength, the terrifying Hari,
whose teeth and claws were like thunderbolts, spoke thus to Vaidehī: "This city, together with its mountains, forests, and regions, along with its palaces, walls, and gateways— "
"I have the power to take this Laṅkā, with its protector, back [to Ayodhyā]. Therefore, O Queen, set aside that thought; enough with such longing.
O Vaidehī, bring freedom from grief to Rāghava along with Lakṣmaṇa."
Seeing him, who resembled a mountain, the daughter of Janaka, whose eyes were as broad as lotus petals, spoke to the legitimate son of the Wind-god:
"O great monkey, I know your courage and your strength."
"His movement is like that of the wind and his splendor is as wondrous as fire;
how could any other ordinary being deserve to come to this land? O bull among monkeys, he has reached the far shore of the immeasurable ocean."
"I know your power to travel and your ability to carry me;
however, you must quickly deliberate upon the certain success of your own mission here.
But it is improper, O best of monkeys, for me to go together with you."
The speed of you, who possess the force of the wind’s own velocity, might cause me to lose consciousness;
for I, clinging to the sky above the ocean,
might fall from your back out of fear as you travel with such speed.
"I have fallen into the ocean, which is teeming with whales, crocodiles, and large fish;
helpless, I shall quickly become the supreme food for the sea-monsters.
And I shall not be able to go with you, O destroyer of enemies."
"Even for you, who have a wife, there would undoubtedly be cause for suspicion;
moreover, seeing me being carried away, the Rākṣasas of terrible prowess,
commanded by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, would surely pursue me."
Surrounded by those heroes with spears raised in their hands, O hero, you, along with your wife, will fall into a state of peril;
for many armed Rākṣasas are in the sky while you are unarmed.
"How will you be able to proceed while protecting me as well,
while you are fighting with those Rākṣasas of cruel deeds? O best of monkeys, I might indeed fall from your back, afflicted by fear."
"O best of monkeys, if those terrifying, great, and powerful rākṣasas should somehow defeat you in combat;
or if I should fall while you are fighting with your back turned to them."
And having seized me when I have fallen, those wicked Rākṣasas might carry me away;
or they might snatch me from your hands, or even slaughter me.
For in battle, victory and defeat are seen to be unstable.
"Or else, being threatened by the rākṣasas, I might perish;
in that case, O best of monkeys, your effort would indeed be rendered fruitless.
Granted, you alone are capable of slaying all the rākṣasas."

5.035.057c Rāghava’s fame would surely suffer if the rākṣasas were slain by you. 5.035.058a Alternatively, having seized the rākṣasas, they might leave me behind in a secluded place, 5.035.058c where neither the monkeys nor Rāghava would recognize me.
But this undertaking is for my sake; therefore, it is useless for you.
For there is great merit in Rāma’s coming along with you, since the life of the high-souled Rāghava depends upon me.
O mighty-armed one, [your] brothers and your royal family will likewise be so;
deprived of hope on my account and emaciated by grief and torment, they,
along with all the bears and monkeys, will abandon their hold on life.

"O best of monkeys, placing devotion to my husband before me, I would not wish to touch the body of anyone other than Rāma even with my foot, O foremost of vanaras. As for the fact that I came into physical contact with Rāvaṇa by force,"
"Powerless, protectorless, and helpless as I am, what can I do?
If Rāma were to slay the ten-necked one here along with his rākṣasas,
and then take me from here and depart, that would be worthy of him."
For I have both heard of and seen the prowess of that great-souled one who crushes his enemies in battle;
neither gods, Gandharvas, serpents, nor Rākṣasas [can withstand him].
For they were indeed equal to Rāma in combat; having observed him in battle with his variegated bow,
he was possessed of great strength and prowess equal to Vāsava.
Who could withstand Rāghava together with Lakṣmaṇa, like a blazing fire fanned by the wind? [Rāghava],
the crusher of armies in battle, together with Lakṣmaṇa—
O leader of monkeys, who could withstand him in battle as he stands like a rutting elephant of the quarters, resembling the sun at the end of an eon with the rays of his arrows?
"O best of monkeys, quickly bring my husband here along with Lakṣmaṇa and the leaders of the troops—
he who has long been emaciated by grief for Rāma."
"O leader of monkeys, make me joyful.
Then that tiger among monkeys,
skilled in speech, having heard those words, was delighted by that speech and spoke to Sītā.
"O Goddess of auspicious appearance, what you have spoken is most fitting;
it is consistent with the nature of women and the modesty of virtuous wives.
Yet, womanhood itself is not capable of crossing over the ocean."

"O Jānakī, you who are endowed with discipline, regarding the second reason you have stated— that I ought not to touch anyone other than Rāma— having occupied this vast expanse extending for a hundred yojanas,"
"O Goddess, this is worthy of you, the wife of that great-souled one;
for who else but you, O Goddess, would speak such words?
And the descendant of Kakutstha shall hear everything without exception."

"O Queen, regarding this conduct of yours and these words you have spoken before me— O Queen, with a mind overflowing with affection and desiring to do what is pleasing to Rāma, I have uttered this for many reasons."
Because Laṅkā is difficult to enter and because the great ocean is difficult to cross,
and also out of my own capability, I have spoken thus.
I desire to bring you here this very day with the kinsman of Raghu.
"It was spoken thus out of deep affection and devotion, and not otherwise.
O blameless lady, if you do not venture to go with me,
then give me a token of recognition so that Raghava may indeed know [it is you]."
5.036.011a Thus addressed by Hanumān, Sītā, who resembled the daughter of a god,
5.036.011c spoke these words softly, her syllables choked with tears:
5.036.012a "You must speak this excellent token of recognition to my beloved."
At that time, at the north-eastern foot of Mount Citrakūṭa,
in that region of the Siddhāśrama not far from the Mandākinī, where roots, fruits, and water were abundant, she dwelt in the hermitage of an ascetic.
Having sported in his groves, which were fragrant with various flowers,
I sat upon your lap, my body drenched by the water. And in turn, Bharata’s elder brother fell fast asleep upon my lap.
Then a crow, filled with flesh, began to peck at me. Raising up a clod of earth, I warded off that crow;
yet that crow, tearing at me, continued to cling right there.
And yet, that eater of offerings, seeking meat for his food, did not desist;
and as I drew up my girdle in anger toward the bird,
while my garment was slipping down, I was indeed seen by you.

Laughed at by you, I was then filled with anger and shame; pursued by Time, greedy for prey, I was torn apart and came to you. And while you were sitting there, exhausted, I once again entered your lap.
Though I was angry, I was consoled by you with great joy; with my face filled with tears and gently wiping my eyes,
O Lord, I was noticed by you when I had been provoked by the crow.
Hissing like an enraged venomous serpent, you spoke these words: "O lady with thighs like an elephant's trunk, by whom has your breast been wounded? Who plays with a five-headed, wrathful serpent?"
Then, looking about, you indeed beheld that crow standing directly facing me with its sharp, blood-stained claws.
That crow was, it is said, the son of Śakra, the foremost among those who fly.
Moving through the air with great speed,
equal to the wind in its flight, the mighty-armed one, the best among the wise, then formed a cruel resolve toward the crow, his eyes rolling in anger.
Taking it from the bed of *darbha* grass, he joined it with the *astra* of Brahmā. Blazing like the fire of time (*kālāgni*), it flared up toward the twice-born one.
He then hurled that flaming blade of grass at the crow.
Then, having been cast out, Kāla went about in various ways;
desiring protection, he indeed wandered throughout this entire world.
He was abandoned by his father, by all the gods, and by the great ṛṣis.

Having wandered through the three worlds, he has come to you alone for refuge. O descendant of Kakutstha, you, who are the protector of those seeking shelter, have out of compassion protected him as he lay prostrate on the ground, even though he was worthy of death.
"Having found no refuge in the worlds, I have come to you alone for shelter. You spoke thus to me as I approached, distressed and despondent:
'It is not possible to make the Brahma-weapon futile; therefore, let it be commanded.'"
Then he struck out the right eye of that crow;
having paid homage to you and to King Daśaratha,
O hero, being dismissed by you, he returned to his own abode.
"O lord of the earth, for my sake you have discharged the Brahmā weapon even against a mere crow;
why then do you forgive him who would carry me away from you?
O bull among men, show great energy and have compassion for me."
5.036.034c Compassion is the supreme dharma; this I have heard from you alone.
5.036.035a I know you to be of great heroism, great energy, and great strength; 5.036.035c boundless on the further shore, unshakeable, and like the ocean in its profundity.

"O Raghava, why do you, the best among those skilled in weapons, endowed with courage and strength, not employ your missiles against the Rakshasas— the husband of the earth including its oceans, who is like Vasava himself?"
Neither the Nāgas, nor the Gandharvas, nor the Asuras, nor the hosts of Maruts are able to withstand the force of Rāma in battle.
If that powerful one has any regard for me, [let him show it].
Why does he not bring the Rākṣasas to destruction with his sharp arrows? Or why does Lakṣmaṇa, the scorcher of foes, not do so following his brother’s command?
For what reason does that hero of great strength not protect me?
"If those two tigers among men, whose splendor is equal to that of Vāyu and Indra, are unassailable even by the gods, for what reason do they disregard me?
Without a doubt, there must be some great evil deed of my own."
"Even though those two subduers of enemies are capable, they do not look after me.
Kausalyā, the high-minded lady, gave birth to the lord of the world;
inquire after his welfare on my behalf and pay him homage with your head bowed."
Garlands, all kinds of jewels, beloved and excellent women,
and even sovereignty over the vast earth which is difficult to attain—
having honored and propitiated both father and mother, [he gave them all].
Sumitrā, who has given birth to such noble sons, has followed Rāma into the life of a wandering mendicant;
thus that righteous-souled one, for the sake of his brother's favor, has renounced unsurpassed happiness and follows the descendant of Kakutstha into the forest to protect him.
With shoulders like a lion’s, mighty-armed, high-minded, and pleasing to behold,
he behaves toward Rāma as a father and treats me as a mother; yet,
O hero Lakṣmaṇa, he did not know that I was being carried away at that time.

"Attending upon the elders, fortunate, capable, and not a talkative man— Prince Lakṣmaṇa is my husband's dearest and best, and he is worthy of my father-in-law. Moreover, Rāma’s brother Lakṣmaṇa is always dearer to him than I am."
The valiant one who, when appointed to his station, upholds that burden—
whom Rāghava, upon seeing him, does not even remember as his aged elder—
he should be told of my welfare in my name for my sake.
Lakṣmaṇa is always gentle, pure, skillful, and dear to Rāma.
O Lord, speak these words again and again to the heroic Rāma:
"O son of Daśaratha, I shall sustain my life for one month."
"Beyond this month I shall not live; I tell you this in truth.
O Hero, you ought to rescue me, who have been held captive by the evil-doing Rāvaṇa through his deceit, just as Kauśikī was rescued from the netherworld."
Then, having removed the auspicious and divine crest-jewel from her garment, Sītā gave it to Hanumān, saying, "This is to be given to Rāghava. Thereupon,
the hero accepted that unsurpassed jewel.
He joined it with his finger, for his arm could not reach it;
having accepted the precious jewel and offered salutations, the best of monkeys circumambulated Sītā and stood respectfully by her side.
Filled with great joy born from the sight of Sītā, he went toward Rāma in his heart, while remaining stationary in his body; having taken hold of that most precious and highly valuable jewel.
Released by the power of Janaka’s daughter, who held him fast,
he was shaken off like a mountain peak by the wind;
with a joyful mind, he returned to his journey.
Having given the jewel, Sītā then spoke to Hanumān:
"This is a well-known token of recognition for Rāma in its true sense.
Indeed, upon seeing the jewel, Rāma will remember three things."
O best of monkeys, that hero has been further encouraged by my mother, by me, and by King Daśaratha;
therefore,
exert yourself in this undertaking and consider what the next step should be.
"O best of monkeys, you are the authority in this execution of the task;
consider what effort might bring about the destruction of his suffering.
Having promised "So be it," the son of the Wind-god, of formidable prowess, [prepared to act].
Having saluted Vaidehī with his head, he prepared to depart. Knowing that the monkey, the son of the Wind-god, was ready to set out,
the princess Maithilī spoke these words in a voice choked with tears.
"O Hanumān, you should say 'all is well' to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa together,
to Sugrīva along with his ministers, and to all the elder monkeys.
And tell them how that mighty-armed Rāghava will deliver me."
5.037.008c You ought to provide a remedy for this obstruction of the waters of sorrow.
5.037.009a [Act] so that the illustrious Rāma may recognize me as being alive;
5.037.009c that must be spoken by you, O Hanumān; through such speech, may you attain merit.

Having heard the words spoken by me, which are always full of encouragement, the prowess of the son of Daśaratha will increase for the sake of attaining me. Upon hearing from you these words joined with my message, Rāghava—
"The hero will duly carry out the plan of valor.
Having heard those words of Sītā, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god,
placed his joined palms upon his head and spoke this reply.
"Kākutstha, surrounded by the foremost of monkeys and bears, will arrive quickly;
having conquered your enemies in battle, he will dispel your grief.
Indeed, I see no one among mortals, nor among gods, nor among asuras," [who could do this].
Whoever dares to stand before him as he discharges his arrows—
even the sun, even Parjanya, or Yama, the son of Vivasvat—
is indeed capable of withstanding him in battle, especially for your sake.
"For he indeed seeks to rule the earth as far as the ocean;
for it is because of you, O daughter of Janaka, that Rāma’s victory has been achieved.
Having heard those words of his, which were perfectly true and well-spoken, [she was filled with joy].
Then Janaki highly esteemed those words and spoke this further:
"As he was about to depart, Sita, looking at him again and again,
spoke words imbued with affection for her husband, honoring him out of her deep friendship."
"Or if you think it right, O hero, subduer of enemies, stay for one day in some secluded place; having rested, you shall depart tomorrow.
For it is through the presence of me, a woman of little fortune, that you, O valiant one,"
"O tiger among monkeys, there might be a momentary release from this great sorrow once he has departed, but for me to return again,
there would be a risk even to my life; of this there is no doubt."
"O Vanara, the grief born of not seeing you would burn me even more, as if setting ablaze one already touched by sorrow upon sorrow. And this great uncertainty, O Hero, stands as it were before me."
"O Lord of Monkeys, among your great allies—
the monkeys and bears— how indeed will those armies of monkeys and bears, or those two sons of the best of men, cross the great ocean which is so difficult to traverse?"
"Only three beings here would have the power to leap across this ocean:
Vainateya, you, or Māruti.
Therefore, O hero, since this undertaking is so difficult to accomplish..."

"What solution do you perceive, for you are the best among those who know how to act? O slayer of enemy heroes, you alone are indeed sufficient to accomplish this task; the manifestation of your power will bring you glory."
If, having defeated Rāvaṇa in battle with all his forces,
he should go to his own city as a victor, that would bring me great renown. For the destroyer of enemy armies, having filled Laṅkā with his troops...
"If the descendant of Kakutstha were to lead me away,
that would be worthy of him; you must act in such a way that it may become a feat befitting that high-souled hero, a champion in battle."
Having heard those words, which were meaningful, coherent, and supported by reason, Hanumān spoke these further words in reply:
"O Queen, the lord of the armies of monkeys and bears, the foremost among leapers,"
Sugrīva, endowed with courage and firm in his resolve for your sake,
surrounded by tens of millions of thousands of monkeys,
will soon arrive, O Vaidehī, as the destroyer of the Rākṣasas.

34a. Endowed with prowess, courageous, and possessed of great strength, 34c. those monkeys stood ready to carry out his command, reaching their destination as soon as they formed it in their minds; 35a. whose movement was unimpeded—neither above, nor below, nor across.

Those of immeasurable splendor do not falter even in great undertakings. By those of great resolve, who follow the paths of the wind, this earth— with its oceans and mountain ranges— has been circumambulated many times.
"There are forest-dwellers there who are superior to me and some who are my equals;
however, there is no one at all inferior to me in the presence of Sugrīva. Since I have reached this place, how much more so must those of great strength?"
"For those who are eminent are not sent on errands; it is other people who are sent.
Therefore, enough with this distress, O Queen; let your grief depart.
With a single leap, these leaders of the monkey hosts shall reach Laṅkā."
"Mounted upon my back like the risen sun and moon,
those two beings of great power, lions among men, will come into your presence.
For those two heroes, the best of men, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, shall arrive together."
Having reached the city of Laṅkā, Rāghava, the joy of the Raghus, will destroy Rāvaṇa along with his hosts with his arrows; then,
O lady of beautiful hips, taking you with him, he shall return to his own city.
"Therefore, take heart—blessings be upon you—and wait for the appointed time;
before long, you shall behold Rāma blazing like a wind-fanned fire.
And when the lord of the Rākṣasas has been slain, along with his sons, ministers, and kinsmen,"
"You shall be reunited with Rāma, as Rohiṇī is with the Moon.
O Queen, O Maithilī, you will soon reach the further shore of your grief;
you shall see Rāvaṇa himself slain by Rāma before long."
Having thus comforted Vaidehī, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god,
resolved to depart and spoke again to Vaidehī:
"You shall soon behold that Rāghava, the slayer of foes, who has perfected his soul."

And you shall soon see Lakṣmaṇa standing at the gate of Laṅkā with bow in hand, along with those heroic monkeys who have claws and fangs for weapons, who possess the prowess of lions and tigers, and who resemble lordly elephants.

O Noble Lady, on the peaks of Mount Malaya and in Laṅkā, there are numerous troops of monkey leaders, resembling mountains and clouds, who are roaring aloud. But he has been struck in his vital organs by the terrible arrow of the God of Love.
Rāma finds no peace, like an elephant tormented by a lion.
Do not weep, O Queen, out of grief; let there be nothing unpleasant in your mind, for you have a protector in your husband, just as Śacī has in Śakra.
"Who else is superior to Rāma? Who is his equal to Saumitri?
Those two brothers, who are like Agni and Māruta, are your refuge.
O Queen, you shall not dwell long in this land."
In this most terrible place inhabited by hosts of Rākṣasas,
your arrival, my beloved, will not be long delayed;
wait only for the moment of my reunion with you.
Having heard those words of the high-souled son of the Wind,
Sītā, who resembled the daughter of a god, spoke these words for her own welfare:
"O Vanara, seeing you, who speak so kindly, I am filled with joy."
Just as the earth, when half its crops have grown, receives the rain,
so act with compassion toward me so that I, filled with longing, may touch that tiger among men with my limbs emaciated by grief.
And a token of recognition for Rāma was given, O best of the monkey hosts:
a stalk of grass, which when cast in anger had destroyed one eye of the crow,
and a piece of red arsenic placed upon the side of his cheek.

"Since your tilaka has been destroyed by him, you ought indeed to remember that [act]. O you who resemble Mahendra and Varuṇa, how can you, being so powerful, simply acquiesce to Sītā having been abducted while she dwells in the midst of the Rākṣasas?"
"This divine crest-jewel has been well preserved by me;
seeing it, O sinless one, I rejoice as if seeing you in the midst of calamity.
This glorious jewel, born of the waters, is now offered by me to you."
"Beyond this, I shall not be able to live, consumed as I am by grief.
I have endured these unbearable sorrows and the heart-piercing words of the most terrible Rākṣasīs for your sake."
"O slayer of enemies, I shall sustain my life for but one month;
beyond a month, O prince, I shall not live, deprived as I am of you.
This king of the Rākṣasas is terrible, and his very glance brings me no happiness."
"Having heard that you have met with calamity, I could not live for even a moment.
Having heard these piteous words spoken by Vaidehī, which were uttered with tears,
the highly resplendent Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, then replied:
"O Queen, I swear to you by the truth that Rāma has turned away from all else because of grief for you. While Rāma is overwhelmed by sorrow, Lakṣmaṇa suffers even more.
Since you have been found somehow, this is no time for lamentation."
"In this very moment, O beautiful lady, you shall see the end of your sorrows.
Those two blameless princes, tigers among men,
having been inspired by the sight of you, will reduce Laṅkā to ashes."
"O large-eyed lady, having slain the cruel Rāvaṇa along with his kinsmen in battle, the two descendants of Raghu will lead you back to their own city.
O blameless one, whatever token of recognition Rāma might require— "
"You ought to grant him even more that which produces joy.
She replied, "I have already given him the supreme token of recognition;
for it is by seeing this very ornament from my hair that Rāma [will recognize me]."
"O hero Hanumān, your words shall be worthy of trust. Taking that excellent jewel, the illustrious and best of monkeys bowed his head to the goddess and prepared to depart.
Beholding that bull among monkeys,
who was filled with the zeal to leap up and whose great momentum was increasing, the daughter of Janaka,
her face bathed in tears and distressed, spoke in a voice choked with sobs.
"O Hanuman, you must inquire after the welfare of all— the two brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who resemble lions—
and Sugrīva along with his ministers. And tell him how that mighty-armed Rāghava may deliver me."
Therefore, you ought to resolve this obstruction of the waters of sorrow,
as well as this intense surge of my grief and this intimidation by these rākṣasas.
"Having approached Rāma, you should say:
'May your path be auspicious, O hero among monkeys!
Once he has been informed of the matter by the princess,"
The monkey, his purpose accomplished and his heart overjoyed,
observed that only a small portion of the task remained and mentally set out toward the northern direction.
And having been honored by her with these commendable words, the monkey departed from that place and reflected:
"This task is nearly finished; this dark-eyed woman has been found."
5.039.002c Having bypassed the first three means, the fourth is seen here. 5.039.003a Conciliation is not effective against Rākṣasas; nor does bribery work upon those who have accumulated wealth.
People who are arrogant because of their strength cannot be subdued by means of dissension;
rather, it is through valor that this task of mine here appeals to me.
And for this undertaking, there is no way other than through valor.
Some certainty arises here:
for the Rākṣasas, whose heroes have been slain in battle,
have somehow today attained mildness.

5.039.005a He who, when assigned to a task, accomplishes even many things, 5.039.005c provided it does not conflict with the primary task, is worthy to perform that duty. 5.039.006a For there is not even a single means sufficient for the accomplishment of a minor task here in this world.
For he who knows a matter in its many aspects is capable of accomplishing that matter.
Having already reached a firm decision in this very matter, if I were to go to the abode of the Lord of the Monkeys, [I would be acting in vain].
He who knows the specific truth regarding the encounter between oneself and another—
by him my husband’s command would have been fulfilled.
How indeed might it now be that he has arrived safely?
The ten-faced one shall indeed bring forth a violent battle with me against the Rākṣasas,
