as well as his own substantial strength,
and challenge me to the fray.

"This supreme forest of that cruel man, which resembles the Nandana grove, is lovely to the eyes and the mind, and filled with various trees and creepers. I shall destroy it, just as fire consumes a dry forest."
When this is broken, that Rāvaṇa will then become enraged; thereafter,
the lord of the Rākṣasas will assemble a vast army consisting of horses, great chariots, and elephants.
Armed with tridents and iron spears,
a great battle will then ensue;
yet I shall face them in combat, they who possess fierce prowess.
Having encountered the rākṣasas with unimpeded prowess and having destroyed that army dispatched by Rāvaṇa,
I shall go happily to the abode of the lord of the monkeys.
Then Māruti, of terrifying prowess, enraged like the wind-god,
began to uproot trees with the great force of his thighs. Thereupon, the heroic Dhanuṃān destroyed that grove of women.
Resounding with the cries of intoxicated birds and filled with various trees and creepers,
that forest became unpleasant to behold as its trees were crushed, its pools of water shattered, and the mountain peaks pulverized.
With vine-cottages and painted chambers destroyed,
with great serpents and predatory beasts driven out,
and likewise with stone dwellings and houses overturned;
That great forest became shorn of its beauty,
for that great monkey had committed a grievous offense against the mind of that high-souled lord of wealth.
Desirous of battle, that lone monkey, blazing with splendor, took his stand at the gateway against many of great strength.
Then, there arose the sound of birds and the noise of trees being broken.
All the inhabitants of Laṅkā became agitated with terror;
fleeing in fear, the beasts and birds shrieked aloud,
and cruel omens appeared before the Rākṣasas.
Then, when sleep had departed, the rakshasis with distorted faces saw that forest laid waste and that heroic great monkey. Seeing them, the mighty-armed one of great being and great strength—
He assumed a truly massive form, terrifying to the rākṣasīs.
Then, seeing that monkey— who was like a mountain, possessed of a colossal body and great strength—
the rākṣasīs questioned the daughter of Janaka.
"Who is he, to whom does he belong, or from where has he come? For what reason has he arrived here?
And how was this conversation with him conducted by you?
Tell us, O large-eyed one; let there be no fear for you, O blessed lady."
"O lady with dark-cornered eyes, what conversation did he have with you?
Then the virtuous Sītā, beautiful in all her limbs, replied:
"What recourse do I have in discerning the intentions of Rākṣasas who can assume any form at will?"
"You yourselves must know who he is and what he will do;
for a serpent alone knows the tracks of a serpent, without a doubt.
I too am afraid of him; I do not know what his lineage may be."
"I know this one who has come to be a *rākṣasa* capable of assuming any form at will.
Having heard Vaidehī’s words, the *rākṣasīs* fled swiftly;
some stood still while others went to inform Rāvaṇa.
5.040.012 In the presence of Rāvaṇa, however, the rākṣasīs with deformed faces began to describe the terrifying, misshapen monkey.
5.040.013 "O King, in the midst of the Aśoka grove, there is a monkey of fearsome form."
Having conversed with Sītā, he of immeasurable prowess remains there;
yet Janaka’s daughter Sītā, though questioned by us in many ways, that fawn-eyed lady does not wish to reveal his identity.
He may be a messenger of Vāsava, or perhaps a messenger of Vaiśravaṇa;
or else he has been sent by Rāma with the desire to search for Sītā. By him, who possesses such a wondrous form, that which was so captivating to you—
The pleasure grove was crowded with various herds of deer and had been swept clean;
there was not a single spot there that had not been destroyed by him,
except for where Jānakī Sītā was, which he did not destroy.
Whether it was for the sake of protecting Jānaki or due to exhaustion, he could not be perceived;
or rather, what exhaustion could there be for him, since she herself was protected by him?
For Sītā had personally taken her stand upon that tree, which was rich with beautiful sprouts and leaves.
That large *śiṃśapā* tree was protected by him;
you ought to decree a severe punishment for that man of fierce appearance,
by whom Sītā was addressed and that grove was destroyed.

"O Lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas, who would speak to Sītā, who is protected by your mind, unless he were one who had renounced his life? Having heard the words of the Rākṣasa women, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas— "
With his eyes rolling in rage, he blazed like a sacrificial fire;
then the one of great splendor commanded the heroic Rākṣasas known as Kiṃkaras, who were his own equals, for the purpose of capturing Hanumān.
Eighty thousand of those swift *kiṃkaras* emerged from that palace, hammers and clubs in their hands;
they were pot-bellied, with great fangs, terrible in appearance, and possessed of great strength.
With their minds intent on battle and eager to seize Hanumān,
they all approached that monkey who stood stationed at the gateway;
with great speed, they rushed toward him like moths into a fire.
With various maces, iron clubs adorned with golden bands,
and arrows resembling the sun, they struck the best of monkeys;
yet the radiant and glorious Hanumān remained like a mountain.
Lashing his tail against the ground, he let out a great roar.
At the sound of that roar, they became filled with fear and apprehension;
and they beheld Hanumān, towering like a cloud at twilight.

5.040.030a Then those Rākṣasas, fearless because of their master’s command, rushed from every side at the monkey with various terrible weapons. 5.040.031a Surrounded on all sides by those heroes, that one of great strength—
He seized a formidable iron club resting against the gateway;
taking up that club, he struck down the night-stalkers,
just as the son of Vinatā seizes a writhing serpent.
The hero, the son of the Wind-god,
having seized [the enemy] and slain the *kiṃkara* rākṣasas, moved through the sky; desiring further combat, the hero once again approached the gateway.
Then, some of the *rākṣasas* there who had escaped from that danger reported to Rāvaṇa that all the *kiṃkaras* had been slain.
He [learned] that the great force of the *rākṣasas* had been destroyed.
Hearing this, the king, his eyes rolling,
commanded the son of Prahasta, who was peerless in prowess and exceedingly difficult to defeat in battle.
Then, having slain the *kiṃkaras*, Hanumān reflected:
"The grove has been destroyed by me, but the sanctuary temple (*caityaprāsāda*) was not demolished.
Therefore, I shall likewise destroy this temple as well."
Having thus reflected and displaying his strength with his mind, Hanumān,
the best of monkeys and son of the Wind-god, leaped upon the temple-palace as high as a peak of Mount Meru and ascended it.
Having violently assailed the lofty sanctuary-palace, the invincible Hanumān, blazing with splendor, became like Mount Pāriyātra. Then, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, assumed a massive body.
Boldly, he slapped his arms, filling Laṅkā with the sound.
By that great, ear-shattering noise of his arm-slapping,
birds fell from the sky, and he proclaimed this loudly:
Victorious is Rāma of exceeding strength, and victorious is the mighty Lakṣmaṇa;
victorious is King Sugrīva, protected by the descendant of Raghu. I am a servant of Rāma, the lord of Kosala, whose deeds are effortless.
Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god and destroyer of enemy armies,
would not have even a thousand Rāvaṇas as a match for him in battle as he strikes with thousands of rocks and trees.
"Having devastated the city of Laṅkā and paid homage to the daughter of Mithilā,
I shall depart with my purpose accomplished while all the rākṣasas look on.
Having spoken thus, the bull among monkeys remained seated in his celestial chariot at the sanctuary.
5.041.010c He roared with a terrifying sound, striking fear into the rākṣasas. 5.041.011a At that great noise, a hundred guardians of the shrine rushed forth,
taking up various weapons— javelins, swords, and battle-axes.
Discharging great destruction, they surrounded the son of the Wind;
like a vast and mighty whirlpool in the waters of the Gaṅgā,
that host of Rākṣasas shone as it hemmed in the best of monkeys.
Then the son of the Wind, filled with rage, assumed a terrifying form; Hanumān, the son of Māruta, having uprooted with great force a massive pillar of that palace adorned with gold, [hurled it].
Then the one of great strength whirled that hundred-edged [weapon],
and having slain a hundred rākṣasas like Indra with his thunderbolt against the asuras,
the glorious one, stationed in the sky, spoke these words.
Thousands of high-souled beings like me have been dispatched—
powerful lords of monkeys who remain under the command of Sugrīva—
in hundreds, hundreds of thousands, tens of millions, and even tens of billions.
"Sugrīva, the destroyer of you all, will arrive.
This city of Laṅkā shall no longer exist, nor you, nor Rāvaṇa,
because enmity has been established with that high-souled lord of the Ikṣvākus."
Commanded by the Lord of the Rākṣasas, the powerful Jambumālin, the son of Prahasta,
who possessed great tusks and carried a bow, went forth;
he wore red garlands and garments, was adorned with a wreath, and wore beautiful earrings.

5.042.002c He was massive, with rolling eyes, fierce, and difficult to conquer in battle. 5.042.003a Stretching with speed his great bow, which resembled Indra’s rainbow and was adorned with beautiful arrows, it produced a sound like a thunderbolt.
By the great sound of his bowstring being drawn, the cardinal directions,
the intermediate directions, and the sky were suddenly filled.
Beholding him approaching on a chariot yoked with donkeys, he—
5.042.005c Hanumān, endowed with great speed, rejoiced and let out a roar.
5.042.006a At that great monkey Hanumān, who was stationed upon the pinnacle of the archway,
the mighty-armed Jambumālin pierced him with sharpened arrows.
With a crescent-headed arrow in the face and a single barbed one in the head,
he pierced that lord of monkeys in the arms with ten iron shafts.
His copper-hued face, struck by the arrows, shone brilliantly.
Like a blooming lotus in autumn pierced by the rays of the sun,
the great monkey, struck by Bāṇa’s arrow, grew enraged;
then he saw a massive, exceedingly vast rock at his side.
5.042.010a The powerful and mighty one swiftly uprooted it and hurled it with great force.
5.042.010c Enraged, the Rākṣasa struck it with ten arrows.
5.042.011a Seeing that his effort had failed, Hanumān, of fierce prowess, [acted].
5.042.011c Having uprooted a massive *sāla* tree, the valiant one whirled it around.
5.042.012a Seeing the mighty monkey whirling the *sāla* tree,
the exceedingly powerful Jambumālin discharged a great many arrows.
With four arrows he cut down the *sāla* tree; with five he struck the monkey on the arm, with one arrow in the chest, and with ten between the breasts.
His body covered with arrows, he was overcome by great rage.
Seizing that very iron club, he whirled it with great speed; Ativega, fierce in his strength, having whirled it with exceeding force,
brought the club down upon the broad chest of Jambumali.
He had no head, no arms, and no knees;
neither bow, nor chariot, nor horses, nor arrows were seen there.
That great car-warrior Jambumālin was swiftly slain by him.
Slain, he fell to the ground with his limbs and ornaments crushed to powder. Hearing that Jambumālī and the mighty Kiṃkaras had been killed, Rāvaṇa grew furious, his eyes bloodshot with rage.
His eyes copper-red with rage at the slaying of the mighty Prahasta’s son,
he [sought] the sons of the ministers, who possessed exceeding heroism and prowess.

Then the lord of the night-stalkers quickly gave his command; thereupon, those seven ministers and sons, urged by the king of the rākṣasas, emerged from that palace, possessing a splendor like that of the seven-flamed fire.

Surrounded by a great force, armed with bows and possessing great strength, they were masters of weapons, the best among those skilled in arms, and each sought victory over the other; they were equipped with banners and flags, and their chariots were covered with nets of gold.
With great chariots yoked to horses that sounded like the roar of rain-clouds, those of immeasurable prowess, filled with joy, drew their bows variegated with refined gold,
appearing like clouds charged with lightning.
Then, having learned that their servants had been slain, those mothers,
along with their kinsmen and friends, became overwhelmed with grief. Adorned with ornaments of refined gold, they were consumed by mutual lamentation.
They rushed toward Hanumān, who stood stationed at the gateway;
emitting a rain of arrows with the roar of chariots,
those bulls among the Nairṛtas moved about like rain-bearing clouds.
5.043.008a Then Hanumān, being showered by those rains of arrows,
5.043.008c became obscured in form, like the king of mountains by torrents of rain.
5.043.009a That monkey, moving with great speed, eluded their arrows.
Moving through the stainless sky, he [overwhelmed] the force of the chariots of those heroes;
sporting with those archers, that hero shone in the firmament like the Lord Wind among the clouds in the sky.
Making a terrible roar and terrifying that great army,
the valiant Hanumān exerted his force against those rākṣasas.
The scorcher of enemies struck some with his palm and others with his feet.

With his fist he struck some, and with his claws he tore others; the monkey crushed some with his chest and others with his thighs. Some, by the very sound of his roar, fell right there upon the ground.
Then, when they had fallen down and collapsed upon the earth,
that entire army fled in the ten directions, afflicted by fear. The elephants trumpeted discordantly, and the horses fell to the ground.
The earth became strewn with chariots whose seats, banners, and umbrellas were shattered.
Having slain those powerful Rākṣasas,
the monkey of great strength and fierce prowess—
Desiring once more to fight with other rākṣasas,
that hero returned to that very gateway.
Having learned that the sons of his ministers had been slain by the high-souled monkey, [he set out].
5.044.001c Rāvaṇa, concealing his true intentions, formed an excellent plan.
5.044.002a He [dispatched] Virūpākṣa, Yūpākṣa, the Rākṣasa Durdhara, Praghasa, and Bhāsakarṇa— these five leaders of the vanguard armies.

5.044.003a Daśagrīva commanded the heroes, experts in policy, 5.044.003c who were intent on capturing Hanumān and equal to the wind in speed in battle: 5.044.004a "Go, all you leaders of the army, accompanied by great forces!"
"Let that monkey, along with his horses, chariot, and elephants, be punished.
Having encountered that forest-dweller, he must indeed deal with him as he deserves;
furthermore, the task at hand must be accomplished in accordance with the requirements of place and time.
Judging by his deeds, I do not consider him to be a mere monkey;
in every respect, he must be a great being endowed with immense power,
created perhaps by Indra himself through the force of asceticism for our sake.
5.044.007a The nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, gods, asuras, and great ṛṣis,
5.044.007c all together with you, were utterly defeated by me.
5.044.008a They must certainly have devised some kind of deception against us.
"There is no doubt that this very thing must be accepted by force; you must not disregard Hari, whose prowess is fierce,
for I have seen monkeys who are swift and possess immense valor."
Vālin along with Sugrīva, the mighty Jāmbavat,
Nīla the commander-in-chief, and others such as Dvivida—
neither their terrifying movement, nor their splendor, nor their prowess was lacking.
There is no intelligence, no strength or energy, nor any calculation of form [to be found in him].
This must be known as a great being established in the form of a monkey. Exerting a great effort, let his restraint be carried out.
Granted, the three worlds— including Indra, along with gods, asuras, and humans—
would not be sufficient to stand before you on the field of battle;
nevertheless, one who knows the way of policy and desires victory in war [should act accordingly].
"One must protect oneself with great effort, for success in battle is fickle. Having received these words of their master,
all those of great energy sprang up with immense speed, possessing a splendor equal to that of fire.
With chariots, rutting elephants, and horses of great speed,
and with all kinds of sharp weapons, they were equipped with every force.
Then those heroes beheld that great monkey blazing with splendor.
Like the sun rising with its rays, garlanded by the beams of its own brilliance—
standing at the gateway, possessed of great speed, a great being, and great strength;
of great intelligence, great energy, a great body, and great power.
Upon merely beholding him, all those stationed in every direction then rushed forward from here and there with their various terrifying weapons.
His [five] arrows were made of iron, sharp, white, and yellow-tipped.
5.044.020c Struck on the head by Durdhara with arrows resembling blue lotus petals,
5.044.021a that monkey, pierced in his head by those five shafts,
leapt up into the sky, roaring and making the ten directions resound.
Then the heroic and mighty Durdhara, mounted on his chariot with his bow ready,
advanced while scattering hundreds of various arrows.
That monkey warded him off in the sky as he rained down shafts.
Like a wind driving a rain-cloud at the end of the monsoon,
he was then tormented by that irresistible one; yet the son of the Wind-god let out a roar once more and increased his speed.

5.044.025a That monkey, having suddenly leapt a great distance, alighted upon Durdhara’s chariot with great speed, like a mass of lightning falling upon a mountain. 5.044.026a Then he [crushed] that chariot whose eight horses were churned to pieces and whose axle and pole were broken.
Having abandoned [his chariot], Durdhara fell to the ground, deprived of life.
Seeing him fallen upon the earth, Virūpākṣa and Yupākṣa—
those two invincible subduers of enemies— were filled with rage and sprang forward.
5.044.028a Having suddenly leaped up with those two, he stood in the stainless sky;
5.044.028c the long-armed monkey was struck on the chest by their two mallets. 5.044.029a Having warded off the force of those two swift ones, the one of great strength—
5.044.029c He, whose prowess was equal to that of Suparṇa, fell back upon the ground once more.
5.044.030a Having reached a *sāla* tree and uprooted it, that monkey,
the son of the Wind, 5.044.030c slew both those heroic Rākṣasas.
Then, knowing those three to have been slain by the swift monkey,
the highly impetuous Praghasa violently attacked the monkey;
and the valiant Bhāsakarṇa, filled with rage, took up a spear.
Standing on one side of the illustrious tiger among monkeys,
Praghasa struck him with a sharp-edged spear,
and the Rākṣasa Bhāsakarṇa struck that best of monkeys with a trident.
With his limbs mangled by those two and his body hair smeared with blood,
the monkey became enraged, possessing a radiance like that of the rising sun; he uprooted a mountain peak together with its deer, serpents, and trees.
The heroic Hanumān, that elephant among monkeys, slew the two Rākṣasas. Then, when those five generals had fallen,
the monkey destroyed whatever force remained.
With horses against horses, elephants against elephants, warriors against warriors, and chariots against chariots,
that monkey destroyed them like the thousand-eyed Indra destroying the asuras;
the field was strewn with slain elephants and horses, and great chariots with broken axles.
The ground was covered on all sides with slain rākṣasas whose paths were blocked.
Then the monkey, having struck down those heroic commanders of the army in battle along with their forces and their mounts, [proceeded].
Having seized that very gateway, the hero stood there like Time itself, having made its moment, at the destruction of all creatures;
he then caused those five generals to be slain.
Having observed Hanūmat along with his followers and mounts, the king, eager for battle,
gazed intently at Prince Akṣa, who stood unharmed and ready for combat.
Urged on by the casting of his gaze,
that powerful hero, whose variegated golden bow was drawn,
then leapt up as he was incited in the assembly.
Then, like a fire fed with oblations by the foremost of the twice-born,
[he appeared] with the great splendor of the rising sun,
covered with a network of refined gold.
Mounting his chariot,
that heroic bull among the Nairṛtas set out toward Mahāhari.
Then [he beheld] that which was earned through the accumulation and gathering of ascetic penance.
It was adorned with a network of refined gold,
possessed banners, and a flagstaff decorated with jewels;
it was well-yoked to eight excellent horses swift as thought.
Unassailable by gods or asuras, moving without attachment, radiant as the sun, traversing the sky, and composed;
equipped with a quiver and adorned with eight fastened swords.
With his javelins and spears inserted in their proper order,
he shone brilliantly with his full array of weapons,
which were adorned with golden chains and possessed the luster of the moon and the sun.
Then, mounted upon a chariot with the brilliance of the sun,
he who possessed valor equal to that of the immortals went forth;
filling both the sky and the earth with its mountains.
Accompanied by forces resounding with the noise of horses, elephants, and great chariots, he approached the monkey who was seated at the gateway, ready and waiting.
Having encountered that Hari,
who stood like the fire at the end of an eon at the destruction of all creatures, the tawny-eyed one was struck with wonder and seized by agitation.
The prince gazed upon that great-souled monkey with eyes full of high esteem, observing both his speed and his prowess against the enemies.
Reflecting upon his own power and the void,
the one of great strength flourishes like the sun at the end of winter; having observed that prowess, he was filled with wrath.
Firmly stationed in the battle, his mind composed, he urged Hanumān on in the fray with three sharp arrows that were difficult to ward off.
Then, having observed that monkey— who was full of pride,
whose fatigue was overcome, and who had triumphed over his enemies— Akṣa, his mind agitated, gazed upon him.
With arrows in hand and his bow grasped, adorned with golden neck-ornaments, armlets, and beautiful earrings,
that valiant one quickly approached the monkey.
The encounter between those two was peerless,
causing even the gods and asuras to tremble with awe; the earth resounded and the sun did not scorch.
The wind did not blow and the mountains did not tremble; seeing the combat between the monkey and the prince,
the heavens roared and the ocean was agitated.
Then that hero [discharged] well-feathered arrows with golden shafts, like venomous serpents,
he who was a knower of the truth regarding the application and release of meditative concentration.
Then he struck three arrows into the head of the monkey; with those arrows falling simultaneously upon his head,
blood flowed from him and his rolling eyes were smeared with gore.
Resembling the newly risen sun and possessing arrows for its rays,
he shone like the sun encircled by a garland of light.
Then that best of ministers to the lord of the Piṅgas—
Beholding that son of the best of kings in battle—
possessing uplifted and variegated weapons and a wonderful bow—
he rejoiced and was filled with zeal, facing toward the fray.
Like the sun-garlanded one standing upon the peak of Mount Mandara,
his anger increased, endowed with strength and heroism,
[he confronted] Prince Akṣa along with his army and his mounts.
Then, with the rays of fire from his eyes, he scorched [them];
thereafter, that cloud of Rākṣasas, possessing a bow like Indra’s rainbow, rained down a shower of arrows in battle.
He swiftly loosed arrows at the lord of monkeys on the mountain,
like a rain-cloud pouring down upon a great peak. Then the monkey [assailed] him, whose prowess was fierce in battle.
Beholding the youth Akṣa in battle, whose arrows possessed increased splendor, strength, and vigor, he—
whose prowess was equal to that of a thundercloud— roared with joy.
Out of youthful impetuosity, proud of his prowess in battle,
with his fury intensified and his eyes like blood,
he approached the incomparable monkey in combat.
Like an elephant encountering a great pit covered with grass, he,
whose roar was like the sound of a thundercloud, let out a cry as those arrows were forcibly struck down by him.
5.045.021c That son of the Wind-god quickly leapt into the sky,
appearing terrible as he tossed his arms and thighs about.
5.045.022a As he was leaping up, the powerful [Hanuman] rushed toward him.
That powerful and preeminent Rākṣasa,
a charioteer who was the very best of car-warriors,
scattered arrows like a rain-cloud showering stones upon a mountain.
Warding off those arrows of his,
the heroic monkey moved along the path frequented by the wind, darting forth like the Maruts between the volleys of shafts.
Swift as thought in battle and possessing fierce prowess,
he stood with his bow grasped,
intent on combat and covering the sky with various excellent arrows.
He gazed at Akṣa with eyes full of great respect,
and that son of the Wind-god fell into deep thought.
Then, his chest pierced by arrows, the monkey—
Roaring, the great-armed one, that best of princes and high-souled hero who knew the true nature of specific deeds,
reflected upon his prowess in battle.
Though he possesses the splendor of the rising sun, he does not act like a child;
this one of great strength performs mighty deeds,
yet he is not [satisfied] with all his deeds in battle, which are so resplendent.
My mind is set upon his destruction here;
for this high-souled one is great in prowess, composed, and exceedingly enduring in combat.
Without doubt, through the arising of the excellence of his past deeds,
he is honored by sages along with nāgas and yakṣas;
his mind is expanded by valor and energy.
Standing before me, he gazes at me;
for the prowess of this swift-acting one would cause even the gods and asuras to tremble in their hearts.
"Indeed, he will not fail to overcome me if he is merely disregarded;
for his prowess increases in battle. However, his total destruction is what I prefer."
"A fire that is growing cannot be ignored," thinking thus of the enemy's momentum,
the valiant one prepared his own application of action.
Then the mighty great monkey exerted his full force and set his mind upon slaying him;
he [struck] those eight horses of his, which were possessed of great speed.

On the path frequented by the wind, the heroic monkey, the son of the Wind-god, struck down those who were composed and capable of bearing great burdens during the cosmic dissolution with blows from his palms.
Then that great chariot-warrior was struck by the palm of his hand;
defeated by the minister of Piṅgādhipa,
its seat shattered and its pole broken loose, it fell.
His horse having been slain, he fell from the sky to the earth;
then that great car-warrior, abandoning the chariot,
rose into the air equipped with his bow and wielding a sword.
Through the intensity of his asceticism, the rishi of fierce power cast off his body like a residence for the Maruts;
then the monkey [beheld] him moving through the sky.
In that place frequented by the king of birds, the wind, and the siddhas,
he who possessed the speed and prowess of the wind approached him and firmly seized him by the feet in succession.
Whirling him around a thousand times, the monkey—
whose prowess was equal to his father’s— seized the great serpent like the Lord of Birds and released it with force.
On the surface of the earth in that battle, that best of monkeys—
his arms, thighs, hips, and neck broken, his bones crushed and his eyes gouged out— was shedding blood.
With his joints shattered and his tendons torn asunder,
that Rākṣasa was slain by the son of the Wind on the earth;
the great monkey, having crushed him against the surface of the ground—
He caused great fear for the lord of the Rākṣasas,
having assembled with great seers who wander on wheels and observe great vows, as well as with spirits, yakṣas, and pannagas.
When Kumāra had been slain, that monkey was gazed upon by the gods, including Indra, who were filled with intense wonder;
having struck down him whose splendor was like the son of Vajrin (Indra).
The hero went to that very same gateway, where the prince Akṣa stood with eyes like blood,
as if Time itself had paused for a moment while intent upon the destruction of all creatures.
Then, when the prince Akṣa had been slain by Hanumān, the high-souled lord of the rākṣasas composed his mind and, equal to Indra himself—
Out of rage, he commanded Indrajit:
"You are skilled in weapons and the foremost among those who bear arms; you are one who brings grief even to the gods and the asuras."
Having witnessed his deeds among the gods, including Indra,
and having acquired weapons through the propitiation of the Grandfather (Brahmā),
neither the Asuras nor the hosts of Maruts can prevail once they have encountered the power of your weapons.
5.046.003c There is no one in the three worlds who has not experienced exhaustion in battle.
5.046.004a You alone are protected by the strength of your arms and preserved by ascetic power; you are the knower of the distinctions of place and time, O best of the wise.

There is no deed that is impossible for you to perform in battles by means of your action; there is nothing that cannot be accomplished by you through deliberation and counsel. Indeed, there is no one at all among the three types of assemblies who is not subject to your influence.

He who does not know your power of weapons and your strength— your strength which is commensurate with my ascetic power, as well as your prowess and your mastery of weapons in combat— [does not truly know you].
Having encountered you in the crush of battle, my mind— its purpose now certain— feels no further fatigue.
All the *iṅkara* demons have been slain, as has the *rākṣasa* Jambumālin.
The heroic sons of your ministers, those five leaders of the army,
and your beloved uterine brother Prince Akṣa have been slain; yet, O slayer of enemies, my reliance was not placed in them alone, but in you.
O wise one, having seen this great strength of the monkey,
as well as his power and prowess, and having also considered your own inherent strength;
Exert your strength according to your own power; for when you have approached, the crushing of the enemy's force will subside once the foe has been pacified.
"Having thus considered your own strength and that of the enemy, O best among those skilled in weapons, begin your endeavor. Indeed,
it is not the superior course of action for me to send you away."

5.046.011 This is considered the wisdom regarding the duties of kings and the nature of the kṣatriya. 5.046.012 O subduer of enemies, one must certainly master proficiency with various weapons in battle; victory in war is indeed desirable.
Then, having heard those words of his father,
he whose prowess was like that of the son of Dakṣa, being of undepressed spirit, performed a circumambulation of his lord.
His mind resolved upon battle, the hero Indrajit was then honored by his beloved followers; roused with enthusiasm for the fight, he set out for the conflict.
The illustrious son of the lord of the Rākṣasas, whose eyes were like lotus petals and who possessed great splendor, went forth like the ocean on the days of the moon's change;
he was equal in speed to the king of birds.
Indrajit, who was equal to Indra himself, mounted the chariot that was yoked with four beasts of prey having white, sharp fangs and possessed of unimpeded speed.
That charioteer, the best among archers, skilled in weapons and foremost among those who know missiles,
swiftly pursued Hanumān in his chariot to where he was.
He [heard] the rattling of that chariot and the sound of the bowstring upon the bow.
Upon hearing this, that hero among monkeys became exceedingly joyful;
taking up his great bow and sharp-pointed arrows, he,
skilled in battle, set out toward Hanumān.
Then, as he went forth for battle with arrows in hand, his joy having arisen from that conflict,
all the quarters of the sky became turbid.
And fierce deer howled in many ways,
while the nāgas and yakṣas, great ṛṣis, and siddhas who wander through the air gathered there.
And flocks of birds, covering the sky, cried out loudly, exceedingly delighted,
upon seeing Indrajit approaching swiftly on his chariot. The monkey [beheld him].
He let out a great roar and increased his speed with force. Indrajit, however, mounted upon his divine chariot and holding a variegated bow,
drew it with a sound as powerful as a flash of lightning.
Then those two, endowed with extreme speed and great strength, fearless in battle—
the monkey and the son of the lord of the Rākṣasas— encountered one another.
Like the lords of the gods and asuras locked in enmity,
he [fought] against that hero, a great car-warrior skilled with the bow, who was highly esteemed in battle.
The immensely powerful and immeasurable one struck down Śarapravega and proceeded along the path of his father.
Then [he discharged] arrows with long and sharp points.
The hero, slayer of enemy warriors, released well-feathered arrows with variegated golden shafts, which were discharged in rapid succession with the force of a thunderbolt's fall.
He heard that sound of his chariot,
the resonance of the mṛdaṅga, bherī, and paṭaha drums,
and the twang of the bow being drawn.
Hearing the sound, the great monkey leaped up once more; amidst the showers of arrows, the monkey swiftly maneuvered,
evading the aim of his opponent as he sought to release his shafts.
As those arrows came toward him once more,
Hanumān, the son of the Wind, stretched out his arms and leapt up.
Both of them were endowed with great speed and were experts in the arts of war.
Captivating the minds of all beings, the two of them waged a supreme battle.
The Rākṣasa could find no opening in Hanumān, nor could the son of the Wind-god find any opening in that great-souled one.
5.046.031c Those two, whose prowess was equal to that of the gods, having encountered one another, became incapable of enduring each other;
5.046.032a then, as that target was being struck down;
As the arrows fell in vain,
the high-souled one, whose self was composed through the practice of meditative absorption, fell into deep reflection.
Then the son of the Rākṣasa king formed a plan toward that chief of the monkey heroes,
having observed the invincibility of that ape.

Thinking, "How shall I bring him under control? for the sake of subduing him, that hero, the best among those skilled in weapons and possessed of great splendor, then aimed the weapon of his grandfather at that foremost of monkeys.
Knowing "he is not to be slain," Indrajit, who knew the true nature of weapons, bound that son of the Wind with a weapon, O mighty-armed one.
Then, by that weapon, the monkey was bound by the Rākṣasa.
He became motionless and fell to the surface of the earth.
Then, having realized that he was bound by the weapon,
his slight momentum was brought to an end through the power of the Lord.
The hero among monkeys reflected upon the favor shown by his grandfather and his own [merit];
then, with the mantras of Svāyambhuva, he consecrated the Brahmāstra.
Hanumān reflected upon the boon granted by the Grandfather:
"By the power of the Teacher of the World, I do not possess the ability to release myself from this bond of weapons."
"Thus, this binding by means of weapons has been ordained; I must comply with it, for it originates from my own self. Having considered the power of the weapon, the monkey—
Reflecting upon the favor of the Grandfather and his own power of liberation,
he followed the command of the Grandfather.
"Even though I am bound by a weapon, no fear arises in me, for I am protected by the Grandfather, Mahendra, and Anila. Furthermore,
I perceive great merit in being captured by the Rākṣasas."
"Since there was a conversation with the lord of the Rākṣasas, let my enemies seize me. Having thus resolved upon his purpose, that slayer of enemy heroes,
like an elephant, withdrew from his exertion after due reflection.
Having been forcibly approached and seized by his enemies,
he roared while being reviled by them in various ways.
Then, the Rākṣasas saw that subduer of foes lying motionless.
They bound him with hemp-fibers and with strips of tree-bark woven together.
He accepted that binding by his enemies and the forceful suppression by those heroes.
"If the Lord of the Rākṣasas, having resolved upon this matter, should endeavor to see me out of curiosity," [thinking thus],
that powerful one was released from the bark-fiber by which he had been bound by means of a divine weapon (astra).
"That weapon-binding does not yield to any other binding.
Then the hero Indrajit, having observed that best of monkeys bound with the bark of trees, [reflected].
Once released from the weapon, it fell into reflection:
"For a weapon follows one who is bound by another.
Alas! A great deed has been performed in vain."
The Rākṣasas did not consider the course of their mantras; furthermore, when one weapon was neutralized by another, no further weapon could be discharged,
and we were all thrown into doubt.
Bound by the *astra* weapon, Hanumān did not realize his own condition; though being dragged by those Rākṣasas and tormented by those bonds,
he was then struck by the cruel Rākṣasas with sticks and fists.
That monkey was dragged into the presence of the lord of the rākṣasas.
Then Indrajit, seeing that he had been released from the weapon but was bound with cords of tree bark, [acted accordingly].
There he showed that mighty hero among monkeys to the king and his retinue— him,
the best of monkey chiefs, bound like an elephant in rut.

5.046.052c The Rākṣasas reported [the matter] to Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas. 5.046.053a "Who is this? Whose is he? From where has he come? What is his purpose? Who is his protector?"—such were the discussions that arose there among the Rākṣasa heroes.
"Let him be slain! Or let him be burned! Or let him be devoured!"—thus other Rākṣasas there, filled with rage, spoke to one another.
Then the high-souled one suddenly passed by that path.
There, at the feet of the lord of the Rakshasas,
he saw the aged attendants of the king,
as well as a residence adorned with great jewels.
5.046.056a That one of great splendor, Rāvaṇa, saw the best of monkeys being dragged here and there by demons of hideous form. 5.046.057a And the best of monkeys also beheld the lord of the rākṣasas.
Endowed with splendor and strength, blazing like the sun,
Daśānana, his copper-red eyes rolling with rage, gazed upon that monkey.
Then, to those eminent counselors who were seated there— men advanced in lineage, character, and age— he gave instructions regarding him;
and in due order, that monkey was questioned by them.
For the sake of the task at hand, he first informed the Lord of the Monkeys of the root of the matter:
"I have come here as a messenger from his presence."
Then Hanumān, of terrifying prowess, amazed by that deed, gazed upon the lord of the Rākṣasas with eyes copper-red with rage; he was resplendent,
shining with a magnificent and radiant golden [garland].
Then [he saw him] of great splendor, wearing a crown covered with a net of pearls;
adorned with various golden ornaments set with diamonds and composed of precious gems, as if fashioned by the mind itself.
It was clothed in highly precious silk, smeared with red sandalwood paste,
and anointed with various and diverse unguents;
it was further adorned with large, beautiful, yet terrifying protective eyes.
With ten heads, each possessing blazing, sharp, great fangs and protruding lips,
he shone with immense power like Mount Mandara with its peaks teeming with various serpents.
Resembling a mass of blue collyrium, he shone with a necklace upon his chest;
with a face like the full moon, he was like a cloud accompanied by cranes.
With arms adorned with bound bracelets and smeared with the finest sandalwood paste, [he stood there].

Seated upon an excellent throne— vast, variegated with crystal, refined by an array of jewels, and spread with a superb carpet— he was adorned with thick, radiant armlets that resembled five-headed serpents.
It was attended on all sides from nearby by women who were exceedingly adorned,
holding yak-tail fans in their hands;
it was guarded by Durdhara, Prahasta, and the Rākṣasa Mahāpārśva.
He was seated with his ministers who were experts in the principles of counsel, and with the minister Nikumbha, surrounded by four demons arrogant in their strength,
as if the entire world were encompassed by the four oceans.

Hanumān beheld the lord of the Rākṣasas, possessed of exceeding splendor, seated among his ministers who were conversant with the essence of counsel and others of auspicious intellect, like the Lord of the Gods surrounded by the deities.
Stationed upon the peak of Mount Meru like a rain-bearing cloud,
though being tormented by those demons of terrifying prowess,
he was filled with supreme wonder and gazed upon the lord of the rākṣasas.
Then, seeing the lord of the rākṣasas shining so brightly, Hanumān, bewildered by his splendor, reflected in his mind:
"Oh, what beauty! Oh, what fortitude! Oh, what strength! Oh, what radiance!"
"Oh, how the king of the Rākṣasas is endowed with every auspicious mark! If unrighteousness were not so powerful,
this lord of the Rākṣasas would be the protector even of the world of the gods, including Śakra himself."
"Indeed, the worlds, including the gods and the dānavas, tremble before him;
for when enraged, he is capable of turning the entire universe into a single ocean.
Thus did the wise monkey engage in various reflections.
Having witnessed the power of the king of the rākṣasas, who possessed immeasurable energy—
Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the worlds cry out— beholding that tawny-eyed one standing before him, the mighty-armed one was overcome with great wrath.
5.048.002 With eyes copper-red with rage, the king spoke these words—timely, extensive, and full of meaning—to Prahasta, his most excellent minister:
5.048.003 "Let this evil-souled one be questioned: from where does he come, and what is his purpose?"
"What is the purpose of this destruction of the grove and this threatening of the rākṣasīs?
Having heard Rāvaṇa's words, Prahasta spoke these words:
"Take heart; may it be well with you; you need have no fear, O monkey."
5.048.005a "If you have been sent by Indra to Rāvaṇa’s abode, 5.048.005c then tell the truth; let there be no fear for you, O monkey, and you shall be released.
5.048.006a Whether you belong to Vaiśravaṇa, or to Yama, or to Varuṇa..."
Having assumed this beautiful form of Yama and Varuṇa,
you have been sent as a messenger by Viṣṇu, who desires victory;
for your splendor is not that of a monkey, though your form alone is that of a monkey.
"O monkey, tell me the truth now, and then you shall be released;
for if you speak a falsehood, your life will be difficult to preserve. Or rather, tell me the reason for which you have entered Rāvaṇa’s abode."
Thus addressed, the best of monkeys then spoke to the lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas: "I am not [the servant] of Śakra, nor of Yama, nor of Varuṇa;
I have no friendship with the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), nor have I been dispatched by Viṣṇu."
"This is merely my birth; I am a monkey who has come here.
Because the sight of the Lord of the Rākṣasas was difficult to obtain, I have destroyed this grove of the King of the Rākṣasas for the purpose of seeing him."

Then those powerful Rākṣasas arrived, desiring battle; and for the sake of protecting my body, I fought them back in the fray. Even by the gods or the Asuras, I cannot be bound with the nooses of missiles.
"Even from my grandfather, this very boon has come to me:
that when I desired to see the king, I employed the weapon;
yet I was released by the weapon, while the Rākṣasas were excessively tormented."
"Know me to be the messenger of Rāghava, who possesses immeasurable power.
O Lord, hear also these beneficial words of mine.
Having observed that being of great courage, the courageous and best of monkeys [spoke].
5.049.001c With an attentive mind, he spoke these meaningful words to the ten-faced one:
5.049.002a "O Lord of Rākṣasas, I have arrived here at your abode by the command of Sugrīva; 5.049.002c your brother, the lord of monkeys, has inquired after your welfare."
"Listen to the command of your brother, the high-souled Sugrīva— a speech endowed with righteousness and purpose, beneficial both in this world and the next.
There was once a king named Daśaratha, who possessed chariots, elephants, and horses."
He was a kinsman to the world like a father, possessing a splendor equal to that of the Lord of the Gods.
His eldest son, mighty-armed and a lord who acted for his father's pleasure,
departed at his father’s command and entered the Daṇḍaka forest.
Accompanied by his brother Lakṣmaṇa and his wife Sītā,
the one named Rāma, possessed of great splendor, has taken recourse to the path of righteousness. His devoted wife Sītā, who follows her husband, was lost in the forest.
The daughter of the high-souled King Janaka, the ruler of Videha— searching for that queen, the prince, accompanied by his younger brother,
reached Mount Ṛśyamūka and was united with Sugrīva.
By him, the search for Sītā was promised;
and by Rāma, the sovereignty over the monkeys was bestowed upon Sugrīva. Then, having slain Vālin in battle, that prince—
Sugrīva, the lord of the hosts of monkeys and bears, was established in the kingdom.
That Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys who was true to his promise, being intent on searching for Sītā,
dispatched the monkeys in all directions.
Hundreds, thousands, and millions of monkeys searched for her in all directions— below,
above, and in the sky; some among them were equal to Vainateya, while others there were like the wind.
The heroic monkeys are of great strength, swift, and possess unimpeded movement.
I, however, am named Hanumān, the legitimate son of the Wind-god;
for the sake of Sītā, I have quickly crossed this expanse of a hundred yojanas.

Having crossed the ocean itself, I have come here desiring to see her. Therefore, O highly wise one, you who have perceived the goals of this life and have mastered the power of asceticism ought not to detain another's wife.

For wise men like you do not become attached to actions that are contrary to dharma, fraught with many calamities, and destructive to one's very roots. And who, indeed, would endure the arrows released by Lakṣmaṇa, which follow the course of Rāma’s wrath?
"Even among the gods and asuras, no one would be able to stand before his arrows; O King, there is no one to be found in the three worlds who,
having caused offense to the descendant of Raghu, could obtain happiness."
"5.049.019a These words are beneficial for the three times, righteous, and conducive to worldly prosperity;
5.049.019c consider this, O god among men: let Janaki be restored to him.
5.049.020a For this goddess has been seen by me, and that which is difficult to obtain here has been attained."
The remaining subsequent action, which is the cause in this matter, O Rāghava,
has been observed by me: that Sītā is thus devoted to grief,
whom you do not recognize when seized, like a five-headed female serpent.
This [resolve] cannot be worn down even by the Asuras or the immortals,
like food excessively mixed with poison that has been consumed with vigor;
it is this very acquisition of dharma which you have obtained through the heat of your asceticism.

It is not right to destroy him who has taken up his own life; for even that immunity from death which you perceive as yours through your ascetic powers— attained by both gods and asuras— is due to this great cause.
5.049.025a This Sugrīva is indeed neither a god, nor an asura, nor a human;
5.049.025c neither a rākṣasa, nor a gandharva, nor a yakṣa, nor a serpent.
5.049.026a O King, Rāghava is human, and Sugrīva is the lord of the monkeys.
"Therefore, O King, how will you bring about the preservation of life?
For one does not achieve the accumulation of righteousness when it is joined with the fruit of unrighteousness;
rather, that very fruit follows [the action], and righteousness is the destroyer of unrighteousness."
"You have already obtained the fruit of righteousness; of this there is no doubt.
Yet, you shall very soon experience the fruit of this unrighteousness as well—having considered the slaughter at Janasthāna, and likewise the slaying of Vālin."

Understand that the alliance between Rāma and Sugrīva is for your own benefit. Indeed, I alone am certainly capable of destroying Laṅkā along with its horses, chariots, and elephants; however, this is his firm resolve.
For Rāma has indeed vowed, in the presence of the hosts of monkeys and bears,
the extermination of those enemies by whom Sītā was violated;
for even Purandara himself, if he were to do harm to Rāma, [would be destroyed].
No other person would find happiness, much less one such as you.
Know that this woman whom you recognize as Sītā and who stands under your control is actually Kālarātri, the destroyer of all Laṅkā.
"Enough with this noose of Time, Sītā personified, which you have yourself slung around your neck; consider what is truly beneficial for yourself,
for she will be consumed by Sītā’s splendor and tormented by Rāma’s wrath."

"Behold this city, with its towers and gateways, being consumed by fire. Having heard these unpleasant words from the monkey, who spoke without dejection and with great eloquence, that peerless man [Rāma]—
5.049.036c Daśānana, his eyes rolling with rage,
ordered the execution of that great monkey.
5.050.001a Having heard those words of the high-souled monkey, [he gave the command].
Overwhelmed with rage, Rāvaṇa ordered his execution. When the wicked-souled Rāvaṇa had thus commanded his death,
Vibhīṣaṇa did not approve of it, for he had reported that [the captive] was a messenger.
Knowing that the lord of the Rākṣasas was enraged and that the task at hand had arrived,
he who was established in the knowledge of how to perform duties reflected upon what must be done. Then,
having determined his course of action, the conqueror of enemies honored his elder brother with conciliatory words.

5.050.004c Skilled in speech, he spoke words that were exceedingly beneficial. 5.050.005a "O King, this killing of the monkey is contrary to dharma, despised by the ways of the world, and unworthy of you, O hero."
Without doubt, this enemy has grown powerful,
for he has committed immeasurable harm.
The virtuous do not advocate for the execution of a messenger.
Indeed, many punishments for a messenger have been seen: disfigurement of the limbs, flogging with whips,
shaving of the head, as well as branding with a mark.
"For these punishments, they say, are for messengers;
but the execution of a messenger has never even been heard of among us. And how could one whose intellect is disciplined by dharma and artha [act otherwise]?"
One who has ascertained the truth regarding higher and lower matters,
such as you, would not remain under the sway of anger;
for those possessed of inner strength restrain their anger.
Neither in the discourse on Dharma, nor in worldly conduct,
nor even in the mastery of the intellect regarding the sciences, shall there be found anyone equal to you, O hero.
For you are indeed the supreme among all gods and asuras;
yet I see no merit whatsoever in the killing of this monkey.
Let this punishment be inflicted upon those by whom this monkey was sent.

Whether he be virtuous or unvirtuous, this messenger has been dispatched by others; speaking for the sake of another and being dependent on them, a messenger does not deserve death. Moreover, O King, if he is slain, I see no other bird remaining.
"If the great ocean were to come back here to the further shore,
O conqueror of enemy cities, then no effort should be made to slay him; rather,
you ought to apply your effort against the gods, including Indra."
Now that he is lost, I see no other messenger who can go to those two ill-behaved princes, so fond of battle, for the sake of war.
He should rouse those obstructed on the long journey,
as well as the valor, energy, and spirit of the high-minded,
even against that which is difficult for both gods and demons to conquer.
"O delighter of the mind, it is not fitting for you to destroy the prospects of war with the Nairṛtas;
for they are well-disposed, heroic, and disciplined."
Born into families of great virtue,
these high-minded men are the best among weapon-bearers; these warriors, numbering in the tens of millions, are well-supported.
Let that much of the army depart as a single division;
let some of them go forth at your command,
having seized those two foolish princes.
Having heard those words of his, which were beneficial for the time and place and most excellent, the mighty Ten-necked one spoke to his brother regarding how he might exert his power over others.
"What you have said is indeed correct; the execution of a messenger is censured.
However, some form of restraint other than death must certainly be imposed upon him.
For it is said that the tail is a cherished ornament for monkeys."
"Let it burn him quickly; let him go forth consumed by that fire.
Then let all his friends, kinsmen, relatives, and well-wishers behold him in this wretched state, emaciated and disfigured in limb."
5.051.005a The Lord of the Rākṣasas commanded the entire city, including its courtyards:
5.051.005c "Let him be led around by the Rākṣasas with his tail set ablaze.
5.051.006a Having heard those words of his, the Rākṣasas, harsh with anger, [set about their task].
They wound his tail with worn-out cotton cloths;
as his tail was being bound, the great monkey grew in size like a fire in the forests that has found dry fuel.
Then, having sprinkled him with oil, they cast him into the fire.
With his blazing tail, he struck down those Rākṣasas;
his soul overcome by rage and impatience, his face was like the rising sun.
5.051.010a Bound once more by those cruel rākṣasas who had gathered together, that best of monkeys,
the hero, formed a resolve appropriate for the occasion. 5.051.011a "Granted, these rākṣasas are indeed not capable of restraining me even when I am bound."
Having severed their bonds and leaped up, I shall slay them once again;
I am indeed a match for all these rākṣasas in battle.
However, for the sake of pleasing Rāma, I will endure such [an ordeal].
"I must explore Laṅkā once again;
for it was not clearly seen by me at night due to the layout of its fortifications.
Therefore, Laṅkā must certainly be inspected by me at the end of the night."
"Let the Rākṣasas at will bind me again with fetters and cause me pain by fanning my tail; yet there shall be no weariness in my mind.
Then they [beheld] that great monkey, who possessed great courage and whose outward appearance was concealed.
Having seized that elephant among monkeys, the Rākṣasas went forth joyfully,
proclaiming their own deeds with the sounds of conchs and kettledrums;
those Rākṣasas of cruel deeds paraded him through the city.
Hanumān patrolled the great city of the Rākṣasas;
then the great monkey beheld various celestial palaces,
as well as enclosed grounds and well-laid-out courtyards.
The monkey searched the streets crowded with houses and the crossroads;
likewise, at the squares, the four-way junctions, and along the royal highway, all the rākṣasas shouted, "The spy! The spy! regarding the monkey.
Then, while the tip of Hanumān’s tail was burning,
those hideous-eyed Rākṣasīs reported that unpleasant news to the Queen:
"O Sītā, that copper-faced monkey with whom you conversed— "
"He is being led away, encircled by his blazing tail.
Hearing those cruel words, which were like the news of her own abduction,
Vaidehī, consumed by grief, approached the sacrificial fire.
At that time, the large-eyed lady, facing the auspicious fire, approached it with self-restraint, like one attending upon the bearer of oblations; for that great monkey, she thought:
"If there is devotion to the service of my husband, and if there is the practice of austerity..."
5.051.024c If there is the state of being his sole wife, then be cool for Hanumān;
5.051.025a If that wise one has any compassion for me,
5.051.025c Or if there remains any portion of my good fortune, then be cool for Hanumān.
If that righteous-souled one knows me to be endowed with virtuous conduct and longing for reunion with him, then be cool toward Hanumān.
If the noble Sugrīva, who is true to his promise, delivers me, [then be cool toward Hanumān].
"O mighty-armed one, become cool for Hanumān out of this suffering. Then the fire, with its sharp flames and steady, clockwise-turning crest,
blazed up as if foretelling auspiciousness for the monkey to that fawn-eyed woman.
While his tail was burning, the monkey thought:
"Why does this blazing fire not burn me on all sides?
It appears with great flames, yet it causes me no pain."
5.051.030c It was like the onset of winter, fixed upon the tip of his tail.
5.051.031a Or rather, this is clearly what was seen by me while leaping: 5.051.031c By the power of Rāma, a miracle occurred on the mountain as it stood in the lord of rivers.
5.051.032a If even the ocean and the wise Maināka mountain displayed such agitation for the sake of Rāma, what will Agni not do?
5.051.033a Through his compassion for Sītā and through the fiery splendor of Rāghava.
"Because of my friendship with my father, the fire does not burn me.
Then that elephant among monkeys reflected further for a moment;
thereafter, the great monkey leapt up with speed and let out a roar.
Then the illustrious son of the Wind-god reached the city gate, which was as high as a mountain peak and crowded with stationed Rākṣasas;
becoming like a mountain for a moment, he then regained his self-control.
Having reached his ultimate diminution, he cast off his bonds;
and being liberated, the glorious one became once again like a mountain.
And as he looked about, he saw an iron bar resting against the gateway.
Seizing that [mace] adorned with black iron, the mighty-armed son of the Wind-god slaughtered all those guards once more. Having slain them, he whose prowess was fierce in battle—
Gazing once more upon Laṅkā,
he, whose tail-tip produced garlands of flames,
shone like the sun with its garland of rays.
Then, gazing upon Laṅkā, the monkey, his desire fulfilled and his enthusiasm increasing, reflected on what remained to be done:
"What indeed remains for me to accomplish here at this time?"
"That which would cause even greater torment to these Rākṣasas has been achieved:
first, the forest has been devastated, the foremost Rākṣasas have been slain, and a portion of their army has been destroyed; what remains is only the destruction of the fortress."
"If the fortress is destroyed, my labor will result in ease;
with little effort, my exertion in this task shall be fruitful. For this fire that blazes upon my tail—"
"It is right to satisfy him with these finest houses.
Then, with his tail ablaze like a rain-cloud charged with lightning,
the great monkey roamed across the rooftops of Laṅkā.
Hanumān released the fire,

which resembled the crest of the fire of cosmic destruction; through its union with the wind, that immensely powerful and exceedingly swift conflagration blazed like the fire of time and grew ever greater.
The wind drove the blazing fire through those dwellings;
those great mansions, adorned with golden lattices and made of pearls and gems, crumbled away along with their precious jewels.
5.052.011a Those shattered palaces fell upon the surface of the earth,
5.052.011c like the mansions of the Siddhas falling from the sky when their merit is exhausted; 5.052.012a [palaces] constructed with diamonds, coral, lapis lazuli, pearls, and silver.
He beheld various elements flowing forth from the palace;
just as fire is never satiated with wood and grass,
so too Hanumān was not at all satiated with the slaughter of the lords of the Rākṣasas.
Enveloped by the flames of the fire,
with its foremost heroes slain and its warriors turned back,
she was overcome by the power of Hanumān’s wrath.
Lanka became as if struck by a curse, filled with agitated, terrified, and dejected Rākṣasas,
and marked by a blazing fire with its rising flames.
The high-minded Hanumān beheld Laṅkā,
which appeared like the earth struck down by the wrath of the Self-born One;
having slain those many Rākṣasas, he [proceeded].
Having destroyed that forest with its many trees and having set fire to the rakṣasa dwellings,
the high-souled one went to Rāma in thought.
Having set all of Laṅkā ablaze with the fire from his tail, that great monkey,
the best of monkeys, then extinguished it in the ocean. He saw the city burning, devastated, and its hosts of rākṣasas terrified.
5.053.001 Having gazed upon Laṅkā, the monkey Hanumān began to reflect.
5.053.002 A very great terror came over him, and self-reproach arose within him:
"What deed have I done here by burning down Laṅkā?"
"Blessed are those best of men, O Great-Souled One, who by their wisdom restrain rising anger, just as one quenches a blazing fire with water.
If this Laṅkā were thus consumed, surely the noble Jānakī would have been burned as well."

5.053.004c By burning that city, I have, through ignorance, destroyed my master’s purpose. 5.053.005a That task for which this undertaking was begun has been brought to ruin by me; 5.053.005c for while burning Laṅkā, I failed to protect Sītā.
"This task was one that could have been accomplished with little effort; there is no doubt it was already done.
Overcome by anger, I have brought about the destruction of the very root. Janaki is clearly lost, for she is not seen without having been consumed by fire."
If some part of Laṅkā has been reduced to ashes and the entire city destroyed by me through a lapse of wisdom,
then even the relinquishing of my own life right here seems preferable to me.
"Shall I throw myself today into the fire, or rather into the mouth of the submarine mare?
Or shall I give my body to the creatures dwelling in the ocean?
For how could I possibly look upon the Lord of Monkeys while still alive?"
Indeed, it was by me— by a destroyer of the very essence of all that must be done— that those two tigers among men were shown this very thing out of the fault of anger;
thus was my unstable wrath made manifest throughout the three worlds.

"Fie upon this passionate state of being, which is powerless and unstable, since even though I am a lord, Sītā was not protected by me out of passion! When Sītā is lost, however, both of them will perish."

Upon their destruction, Sugrīva, along with his kinsmen, will perish. Having heard these very words, how will the righteous Bharata, who is devoted to his brother, be able to live, together as he is with Śatrughna?
"When the most righteous Ikṣvāku dynasty has undoubtedly met its destruction,
all subjects will be tormented by grief and anguish. Therefore, I am bereft of fortune, having lost the accumulation of both dharma and worldly purpose."
"His soul overwhelmed by the fault of wrath, he will clearly be the destroyer of the world"—
as he was thinking this, omens appeared;
and having perceived them as before, he reflected once more.

Or rather, this auspicious woman, whose every limb is beautiful and who is protected by her own splendor, shall not perish; for fire does not burn within fire. Indeed, the mind of that one of immeasurable luster never deviates from dharma regarding his wife.
The purifier (Agni) deserves to touch her, who is protected by her own virtuous conduct;
surely it is through the power of Rāma and the merit of Vaidehī that this carrier of oblations,
whose function is burning, did not consume me.
How could she— the deity of the three brothers beginning with Bharata,
and the beloved of Rāma’s heart— ever perish?
Or rather, this imperishable Lord, whose function is burning, is sovereign over all.

"My tail does not burn; how then could it consume my noble lady? By virtue of her ascetic power, her truthful speech, and her undivided devotion to her husband—even if she were to consume the fire itself, the fire shall not consume her."
While he was thus reflecting there upon the queen’s adherence to dharma, Hanumān heard the words of the high-souled Cāraṇas:
"Aha! Truly, an unbearable deed has been performed by Hanumān!"
"By repeatedly releasing the terrible fire into the abode of the Rākṣasas, this city of Laṅkā—with its palaces, ramparts, and gateways—has been consumed by flames;
yet Jānaki has not been burnt. This is truly a source of great wonder to us."
Through omens that revealed the truth, through reasons of great merit,
and through the words of the sages, Hanumān became joyful in heart.
Then the monkey, having attained the object of his desire, [proceeded].
Knowing that the princess was unhurt and seeing her again before his very eyes,
he set his mind on returning.
Then, having saluted Jānaki as she sat at the foot of the *śiṃśapā* tree, he said: "By good fortune, I see you here unharmed.
Then Sītā, looking again and again at him as he was about to depart, [gazed after him].
5.054.002c She addressed these words, imbued with affection for her husband, to Hanumān:
5.054.003a "O slayer of enemy heroes, you alone are certainly sufficient to accomplish this task; glorious indeed is the manifestation of your strength."
If that descendant of Kakutstha, the crusher of enemy forces, having overwhelmed Laṅkā with his armies, were to lead me away, that would be worthy of him;
for such is the valor of that great-souled one.
"Bring about the very truth for one who is a hero in battle.
Having heard those words of hers— words imbued with purpose, humble, and supported by reason— Hanumān spoke this reply.
"Kakutstha, surrounded by the foremost of monkeys and bears, will arrive quickly;
he who, having conquered your enemies in battle, will dispel your grief.
Having thus comforted Vaidehī, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, [continued].
Having resolved to depart, he paid his respects to Vaidehī.
Then that tiger among monkeys, the crusher of enemies, eager for the sight of his master,
ascended Ariṣṭa, the best of mountains.
It was graced by dark-blue forest ranges filled with towering *padmaka* trees,
and it was surrounded by many *sāla*, *tāla*, and *aśvakarṇa* trees, as well as bamboos;
it was further adorned by widespread canopies of flowering creepers.
It was crowded with various herds of wild animals, adorned with the outpourings of mineral ores,
endowed with many springs, and dense with heaps of rocks;
it was frequented by great ṛṣis, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and uragas.

That best of monkeys, possessed of exceeding strength, ascended that mountain, which was thick with creeping vines and trees, its caves infested by lions, crowded with packs of tigers, and filled with trees bearing succulent roots and fruits.
Urged on by the intense joy of the imminent sight of Rāma,
he trampled with the soles of his feet upon the lovely mountain ridges; consequently,
the rocks were shattered and reduced to powder with a great roar.
Having ascended that lord of mountains, the great monkey grew in size,
seeking the northern shore from the southern side of the salt ocean.
Then the heroic son of the Wind-god climbed the mountain.
He beheld the formidable ocean, inhabited by fish and serpents;
like the wind traversing the sky, that tiger among monkeys, the son of the Wind-god, proceeded from the southern direction toward the north.
Then that best of mountains, oppressed by that monkey,
roared along with those spirits and sank into the surface of the earth,
its peaks trembling and its trees falling.
By the force of his thighs, the flowering trees were crushed and fell broken upon the earth like those struck by Indra’s weapon; likewise,
the mighty beings dwelling within the depths of the caves were tormented.
The terrifying roar of lions, as if splitting the sky, was heard;
then the Vidyādharīs, their garments slipping and disarrayed and their ornaments thrown into confusion, suddenly flew up from the mountain.
Exceedingly large, powerful, with flaming tongues and potent venom,
the great serpents writhed about with their heads and necks crushed.
Likewise, the kinnaras, uragas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and vidyādharas [were likewise afflicted].
Leaving that best of mountains, which was being oppressed, they took their stand in the sky.
And that glorious mountain, pressed down by that powerful one,
entered the subterranean realm (rasātala) along with its trees and towering peaks.
Ten *yojanas* in width and thirty *yojanas* in height,
that mountain became a supporter of the earth, reaching level with the ground.
It was beautiful with its moon-like white lotuses and auspicious with its sun-like *kāraṇḍava* birds.
With Tiṣya as its śrāvaṇa-kadamba tree, with clouds for its moss and grassy meadows;
with Punarvasu as its great fish, and the red-limbed planet (Mars) as its mighty crocodile; with Airāvata as its great island, it was stirred by the swan of Svātī.
With waves produced by the gathering of winds, its waters cooled by the rays of the moon,
and its lotuses and water-lilies awakened by *bhujaṅga*, yakṣas, and gandharvas,
it seemed as if swallowing the sky and scraping the lord of the stars.
As if carrying away the sky along with its stars and the orb of the sun,
the glorious and great monkey Hanumān, a traveler of the air, moves along like the abode of the wind-god, dragging the masses of clouds behind him.
Clouds of great size shone forth, colored pale-red, blue, madder-red, and greenish-orange;
they entered the masses of clouds and emerged from them again and again.
Like the moon, he appeared both hidden and manifest;
roaring with a great roar, possessing a sound as vast as the thundering of clouds,
the one of great splendor returned once more through the middle of the ocean.
Having touched the lord of mountains, Sunābha,
the valiant one approached with great speed like an iron arrow released from a bowstring;
having reached it for a short distance, he beheld the great mountain.
Resembling a great Indra-cloud, the bull among monkeys let out a roar.
Hearing that roar as he cried out, all those monkeys from every side became eager, longing for the sight of their friend.

5.055.012a Jāmbavān, the best of monkeys, his mind thrilled with joy, 5.055.012c addressed all the monkeys and spoke these words: 5.055.013a "In every way, Hanumān has accomplished his task; there is no doubt about this."
For such a roar could not have come from one who had not accomplished his task.
Hearing the force of that great-souled one’s arms and thighs and his roar,
the monkeys leapt up here and there in joy.
5.055.015a Delighted and desiring to see Hanumān, they moved from mountain peak to mountain peak and from summit to summit.
5.055.016a Full of joy, they grasped the well-flowered branches at the tops of the trees.
The monkeys scattered like bright garments.
Seeing that great monkey approaching, resembling a dense mass of clouds,
all those monkeys then stood with their palms joined in reverence.
Then the swift monkey, who resembled a mountain,
descended upon the peak of Mount Mahendra, which was thick with trees.
Thereupon, all those foremost of monkeys were delighted in their hearts.
They stood surrounding the high-souled Hanumān;
and having surrounded him, they all attained supreme joy,
their faces beaming with delight as he returned free from ailment.
Taking gifts of roots and fruits,
the monkeys honored the best of monkeys, the son of the Wind-god; some rejoiced and shouted, while others made sounds of "kila-kilā."
And the bull-like monkeys, filled with joy, brought branches of trees. Then the great monkey Hanumān paid homage to the venerable elders headed by Jāmbavān, as well as to Prince Aṅgada.
Honored by those two and gratified by the monkeys,
he who was himself worthy of worship reported briefly that he had seen the Queen;
then, taking the son of Vālin by the hand, he sat down.
Then, in a delightful region of the Mahendra mountain,
Hanumān, feeling confident, spoke to those bulls among monkeys:
"That daughter of Janaka has been seen, residing in the Aśoka grove."
Guarded by most terrible ogresses,
the blameless young woman wore her hair in a single braid; longing for the sight of Rāma,
she was exhausted from fasting, soiled, with matted hair, and emaciated.
Then, having heard those words of the son of the Wind-god— words of great significance that were like nectar— all the monkeys became joyful.
Some roared, others shouted, and other mighty ones bellowed.
Some let out shouts of "kila-kilā," while others roared back in response.
Some of those elephant-like monkeys were overjoyed, raising their tails high;
they brandished their long, curved, and extended tails.
But other monkeys, leaping from the mountain peaks, joyfully touched Hanumān, who resembled an elephant. Then Aṅgada spoke to Hanumān, who had already delivered his message.
5.055.032c Among all the heroic monkeys, you have spoken words that are unsurpassed. 5.055.033a In terms of courage and prowess, no monkey is found to be your equal,
since you have leaped across the vast ocean and returned once more.
"By good fortune, you have seen the illustrious queen, the wife of Rāma;
by good fortune, that descendant of Kakutstha will now cast off the grief born of separation from Sītā.
Then the monkeys [honored] Aṅgada, Hanumān, and Jāmbavān.
Surrounding him with great joy, those excellent monkeys took their places upon vast rocks, desiring to hear of the crossing of the ocean,
and to see Laṅkā, Sītā, and Rāvaṇa.
All stood with palms joined in reverence, their faces turned toward Hanumān. There stood the illustrious Aṅgada, surrounded by many monkeys,
like the Lord of the Gods attended by the deities in heaven.
That lofty and great mountain was then joyfully occupied by the famous and illustrious Hanumān, as well as by Aṅgada, whose arms were adorned with armlets.
The peak of that mountain blazed with splendor;
then, upon the summit of Mount Mahendra,
the mighty monkeys, led by Hanumān, experienced supreme joy.
Then, greatly delighted,
Jāmbavān questioned the joyful great monkey, the son of the Wind, regarding the progress of his mission:
"How was the Goddess seen by you, and how does she fare there?"
"How did that Daśānana of cruel deeds behave toward her?
O great monkey, tell us all of this in truth;
having heard its meaning, we shall further deliberate upon the determination of our course of action."
"Whatever matter must be addressed there by us who have gone,
and whatever is to be protected there— may your lordship explain that to us.
Then, having been thus commissioned by him, his hair stood on end with joy.
Bowing his head in reverence to the goddess Sītā, he replied:
"In your very presence, I leapt from the summit of Mount Mahendra into the sky,
with a concentrated mind, desiring to reach the southern shore of the ocean."
As I was going along, something terrible appeared like an obstacle;
I saw a divine, golden peak, most enchanting,
standing there blocking my path, and I considered that mountain to be an impediment.
Having approached that divine, golden, and most excellent of mountains,
I resolved in my mind, "This must be split by me. And so,
I struck that great mountain with my tail.
The peak, resembling the sun, shattered into a thousand pieces.
And perceiving my resolve, that great mountain spoke these sweet words, as if gladdening my heart: "O son!"
"Know me also as your paternal uncle, a friend of Mātariśvan,
known as Maināka, dwelling in the great ocean. O son, in ancient times, the best of mountains possessed wings."
At will, they roamed across the earth, harassing it on all sides.
Having heard of the conduct of these mountains, the blessed Mahendra, the subduer of Pāka,
severed their wings by the thousands with his thunderbolt.
"But I was rescued from that by your high-souled father;
O child, I was then cast into the great ocean by Māruta.
And I must provide assistance to Rāma, O subduer of enemies."
"Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma, possesses prowess equal to that of Mahendra.
Having heard this from the high-souled Maināka,
and having informed him of my mission, my mind was uplifted by the mountain.
Permitted by that high-souled Maināka, I set out upon the remainder of the journey, employing my greatest speed; then,
for a very long time, I proceeded along the path with great velocity.
Then I beheld the goddess Surasā, the mother of the *nāgas*.
In the midst of the ocean, that goddess addressed these words to me:
"O best of monkeys, you have been designated as my food by the immortals."
"Then I shall devour you; you have been ordained for me after a long time.
Thus addressed by Surasā, he stood with palms joined in reverence and bowed down;
then, his face turning pale, he uttered these words.
The illustrious Rāma, son of Daśaratha and scorcher of his foes, has entered the Daṇḍaka forest together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā;
yet his wife Sītā has been abducted by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa.
"I am a messenger going to her presence by the command of Rāma.
You ought to provide assistance to Rāma, O dweller of this realm;
or else, having seen Maithilī and Rāma, whose actions are effortless,"
"I shall enter your mouth; this is my solemn promise.
Thus addressed by me, Surasā, who can assume any form at will, replied: "No one shall ever pass through this; this is my boon."
Thus addressed by Surasā, I instantly became ten yojanas in length and twice that in width;
and she opened her mouth to a size corresponding to my proportions.
Seeing that his mouth was opened wide, I made my body small; in that very moment, I became the size of a thumb. Having quickly entered that mouth, I emerged from it in an instant.
The goddess Surasā spoke to me again in her own form: "O best of monkeys, O gentle one, go as you please for the accomplishment of your purpose;
and bring back Vaidehī to the high-souled Rāghava."
"Be happy, O mighty-armed one; I am pleased with you, O monkey.
Then I was praised by all beings, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!
Thereupon, I leaped into the vast sky like Garuḍa.
My shadow was seized, yet I could not see anything at all. Then, my speed gone, as I looked toward the ten directions,
I saw nothing there by which my movement had been taken away.
Then this thought arose in me: "What indeed is the purpose of my going, when such an obstacle has arisen that her form cannot be seen? As I grieved, I cast my gaze downward.
Then I saw a terrifying rākṣasī lying in the water;
and having laughed with a great roar, she spoke these unseemly words to me as I stood there unperturbed.
"Where are you going, O large-bodied one? You are desired by me, who am hungry. Satisfy my body, which has long been deprived of food.
"Very well," I replied, and then I accepted her words.
Her body did not fill up even when I expanded it beyond its natural proportions;
her vast and terrifying mouth grew ever larger as she devoured me,
yet she remained unaware of me or of the transformation I had wrought.
