Then, contracting my vast form within the blink of an eye,
I seized her heart and leapt up into the sky.
With her arms flung wide, that terrifying woman fell into the salt waters.
"I have heard from the sky-dwellers— the Siddhas together with the Cāraṇas— that the terrible Rākṣasī Siṃhikā, who resembled a mountain,
has been swiftly slain by Hanumān after her heart was torn out."
Having slain her, and remembering once more my urgent duty,
I traveled a great distance and beheld the southern shore of the ocean, adorned with mountains,
where that city of Laṅkā stands.
When the sun had set, I entered the city, the abode of the rākṣasas, unobserved by the demons of terrible prowess; there,
throughout the entire night, I searched for the daughter of Janaka.
Having entered Rāvaṇa’s inner apartments, I did not see that woman of slender waist.
Then, not seeing Sītā in Rāvaṇa’s residence,
I encountered an ocean of grief from which I could perceive no further shore.
And while I was grieving, I saw an excellent grove of houses surrounded by a magnificent golden wall;
having leaped over that wall, I beheld it filled with many trees.
In the midst of the Aśoka grove stands a great śiṃśapā tree;
having climbed it, I see a grove of golden plantain trees.
Not far from that śiṃśapā tree, I behold the woman who has the complexion of the forest.
She was dark-complexioned with eyes like lotus petals, her face emaciated by fasting;
she was surrounded by hideous and cruel ogresses who subsisted on flesh and blood, like a doe hemmed in by tigresses.
Having seen that blameless woman, the wife of Rāma, in such a state, I remained right there, watching her from within a *śiṃśapā* tree. Then,
a tumultuous sound arose, mingled with the tinkling of waist-bands and anklets.
"In Rāvaṇa’s residence, I heard an exceedingly deep sound;
thereupon, being greatly agitated, I withdrew my true form and remained hidden in the thick foliage of the śiṃśapā tree like a bird."
Then Rāvaṇa’s wives and the mighty Rāvaṇa himself arrived at that place where Sītā was staying. Upon seeing the lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas, Sītā, who possessed beautiful limbs, [beheld him].
With her thighs pressed together and her full breasts, she was embraced by his arms;
then the ten-necked Rāvaṇa spoke to Sītā, who was in extreme distress, as he fell with his head bowed: "Hold me in high esteem."
"O proud Sītā, if out of arrogance you do not welcome me,
then after two months have passed, I shall drink your blood.
Having heard these words of that evil-minded Rāvaṇa, [she was filled with fear].

5.056.060c Utterly enraged, Sītā spoke these supreme words: 5.056.061a "O lowest of Rākṣasas, [you who have seized] the wife of Rāma of immeasurable splendor, 5.056.061c the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha, the lord of the Ikṣvāku lineage!"

"How has your tongue not fallen out for speaking what should not be spoken? What kind of valor do you possess, O ignoble one, you who have come here having abducted me from the absence of my husband? O sinner, you were not seen by that great-souled one."
"You are not the equal of Rāma; you are not even fit for his service. The descendant of Raghu is worthy of sacrifice, truthful in speech, and one who delights in battle.
Having been addressed with these harsh words by Jānaki, the ten-faced one—
He suddenly blazed with rage like a fire upon a funeral pyre. Rolling his cruel eyes and raising his right fist,
he began to strike Maithilī, while the women there cried out in lamentation.
Rising up from the midst of the women, his wife named Mandodarī, who was excellent, restrained that evil-minded one;
and though he was afflicted by passion, he was addressed with sweet words by her.

"O you whose prowess is equal to that of Mahendra, what business have you with Sītā? Delight yourself today with me; Jānaki is not my superior. [Enjoy yourself] with the daughters of the gods and Gandharvas, and even with the daughters of the Yakṣas."
"O Lord, enjoy yourself here together with Sītā; what else will you do?
Then, by those women gathered together, that night-stalker of great strength was suddenly raised up and led to his own palace.
When that ten-necked one had departed, the Rākṣasa women, with their deformed faces,
began to revile Sītā with cruel and most dreadful words. Jānakī, however, regarded their speech as if it were mere straw.
Having encountered Sītā, their threats then became useless;
rendered motionless by their futile roaring, those flesh-eating Rākṣasīs reported to Rāvaṇa Sītā’s great resolve.
Then all of them together, their hopes shattered and their efforts abandoned, surrounded her on every side and fell under the power of sleep.
While they were thus fast asleep, Sītā remained devoted to the welfare of her husband.
Lamenting piteously, the wretched woman, deeply afflicted by grief, mourned. Seeing Sītā in such a dreadful state, I, though weary, reflected upon it; my mind found no peace.
And for the purpose of conversing with Jānakī, I devised this plan;
therefore, the lineage of the Ikṣvāku family was placed by me at the forefront.
Having heard these words, which are honored by the assembly of royal sages—
The goddess, her eyes veiled by tears, replied to me:
"Who are you, O bull among monkeys? By what means and how have you arrived here?
And what is your friendship with Rāma? You ought to tell me this."

Having heard those words of hers, I also spoke these words: "O Queen, there is a lord of monkeys named Sugrīva, of great strength and terrible prowess, who shall be the companion of your husband Rāma."
"Know me to be his servant, Hanumān, who has come here.
I have been sent to you by my master, Rāma, whose actions are effortless.
And this [message] was spoken personally by that illustrious son of Daśaratha, a tiger among men."
"O illustrious lady, he gave you this ring as a token of recognition.
O Queen, I wish to be commanded by you: what shall I do?
Shall I lead you to the side of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, or what is your further command?"
Having heard and understood this, Sītā, the daughter of Janaka,
said, "May Rāghava, having destroyed Rāvaṇa, take me away.
Having bowed my head to the noble and blameless lady, I—
"I requested this token of recognition, which brings joy to Rāghava’s heart.
Thus addressed, that woman of noble form, deeply distressed, gave me that most excellent and supreme jewel and entrusted me with her message.
Then, having bowed down to that princess with a composed mind, I circumambulated her clockwise, my heart uplifted; and then,
having resolved it in my mind, I spoke again to Uttara.
"O Hanuman, you ought to relate my story to Rāghava,
so that upon hearing it, those two heroes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, together with Sugrīva, may come here without delay. Act in such a way."
"If this should turn out otherwise, my life shall last but two months;
the descendant of Kakutstha will not see me, and I shall die like one who is helpless.
Hearing those piteous words, anger overcame me.
And immediately thereafter, I beheld the remaining task that lay ahead;
then my body grew like a mountain, and,
longing for battle, I began to destroy that forest.
Then those hideous-faced rākṣasīs, having awakened, beheld that grove devastated, with its deer and birds wandering in terror;
and seeing me there in the forest, they gathered together from here and there.
5.056.093c Having arrived together, they quickly reported it to Rāvaṇa:
5.056.094a "O King, this impenetrable forest of yours has been destroyed by a wicked-minded monkey, 5.056.094c who, O mighty one, did not recognize your prowess."
"O Indra among kings, quickly order the execution of that evil-minded man who acts against your will, so that he may meet his destruction.
Having heard this, the exceedingly invincible [messengers] were dispatched by the lord of the Rākṣasas.
There were eighty thousand *rākṣasas* named Kiṃkaras, who followed the will of Rāvaṇa; with a club, I slaughtered them all in that forest region as they held spears and mallets in their hands.
Of those [demons], the survivors who remained fled with swift strides;
they reported to Rāvaṇa that the army had been slaughtered by me.
Then, a thought arose in me, and I ascended the temple-palace.
Having slain the hundreds of rākṣasas stationed there with my pillar once more,
I, having become the ornament of Laṅkā, destroyed him in my wrath. Then he dispatched Jambumālin, the son of Prahasta.
"I shall slay that Rākṣasa, endowed with great strength and skilled in battle,
along with his followers, using my most terrible iron club.
Having heard this, the lord of the Rākṣasas [summoned] the exceedingly powerful sons of his ministers.
Rāvaṇa dispatched those who were well-equipped with infantry forces.
"With my iron club alone, I shall send them all to the abode of Yama," he thought,
having heard that the sons of his ministers, swift in their prowess, had been slain in battle.
Rāvaṇa dispatched five heroic leaders of his armies;
I indeed destroyed all of them along with their troops.
Then the Ten-necked one [sent] his son Akṣa, who possessed great strength.
Together with many *rākṣasas*, he dispatched him into the fray.
But Mandodarī suddenly seized by the feet her son, the prince who was skilled in battle, as he sprang up into the sky.
Having whirled that leather-clad weapon a hundred times and hurled it, I crushed him.
Hearing that the axle had arrived there broken,
Rāvaṇa then dispatched his second son, named Indrajit.
Highly incensed, he commanded the mighty one who was fierce in battle;
having deprived even that bull among Rākṣasas of all his strength and his prowess in combat, I attained supreme joy.
For this mighty-armed and immensely powerful one was dispatched by Rāvaṇa with great confidence, accompanied by heroes intoxicated with pride;
he has bound me with extreme speed using the Brahmā weapon.
Then the Rākṣasas bound me there with ropes;
having seized me, they brought me into the presence of Rāvaṇa.
Upon seeing me, I was addressed by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa.
When questioned regarding my arrival in Laṅkā and the slaughter of the Rākṣasas,
I explained everything there that had occurred for the sake of Sītā. O Lord, desiring a sight of her, I have come to your abode.
"I am Hanumān, the son born of the Maruts, a monkey.
Know me to be a messenger of Rāma, a kapi and minister of Sugrīva.
As such, I have come here to your presence on a mission for Rāma."

5.056.115a Listen also to the command which I proclaim to you; 5.056.115c O Lord of Rākṣasas, the Lord of Monkeys has addressed these words to you with focused intent— 5.056.115e Consistent with virtue, wealth, and pleasure, beneficial and wholesome like nourishing food.
"While I was dwelling on Mount Ṛṣyamūka, which is filled with vast trees,
Rāghava, who is valiant in battle, entered into friendship with me.
He told me, O King, that my wife had been abducted by a rākṣasa."
"Therefore, for the sake of my assistance, you ought to make an agreement with me.
The Lord Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, made an alliance with Sugrīva— whose kingdom had been seized by Vālin— with fire as witness."
By him, having destroyed Vālin with a single arrow in combat,
he was made the great king of the monkeys and the lord of those who leap; therefore,
we must provide him assistance here with our whole being.
He has been dispatched by him to your presence here in accordance with righteousness. Let Sītā be brought quickly and given back to Rāghava,
before the heroic monkeys destroy your army.
"Indeed, who among us has not known from of old the origin of the monkeys,
who go to the presence of the gods when invited?
Thus did the king of the monkeys speak to you, as he was addressed by me.
Then he looked at me, as if burning me with his angry gaze.
By that Rākṣasa of fierce deeds, I was ordered to be killed.
Then his high-minded brother, named Vibhīṣaṇa, [intervened].
"Therefore, that king of the rākṣasas was entreated by me for your sake:
'O Rākṣasa, the killing of an envoy is not seen in the royal treatises;
rather, an envoy who speaks for the welfare of others must understand the truth as it is.'"
"Even for a very great offense, the mutilation of a messenger is seen as the punishment for one of incomparable prowess; according to the scriptures, there is no execution here.
When Vibhīṣaṇa had spoken thus, Rāvaṇa gave his orders to them.
"Let this very tail of mine be burned today by the Rākṣasas. Then,
having heard his words,
my tail was wrapped all around with hempen fibers, as well as with cloth made of cotton.
Then those Rākṣasas, equipped with the gear of Siddhas and possessing fierce prowess,
began to set my tail ablaze while striking it with sticks and fists. I was bound by many snares and held fast by the Rākṣasas.
"May no suffering whatsoever befall me as I desire to see the city by day.
Then those heroic Rākṣasas proclaimed me, bound and enveloped in fire,
along the royal highway as they arrived at the city gate.
Then, contracting my own immense form once again and releasing that bond, I stood restored to my natural state;
seizing an iron club, I slaughtered those Rakshasas.

Then I leaped with great speed toward that city gate; and with my blazing tail, I, unperturbed, burned that city along with its palaces and towers, just as the fire at the end of an eon consumes all living beings.
Having burned Laṅkā, doubt again overcame me:
"By my burning Laṅkā, Sītā has undoubtedly been burned.
Then I heard the auspicious words of the Cāraṇas.

When those speaking of the news in wonder said, "Jānakī has not been burned," my mind was awakened upon hearing that marvelous speech; and Vaidehī was seen by me once more, and I was sent away by her again.
"By the power of Rāghava and by your own splendor,
and for the sake of Sugrīva’s purpose, everything has been accomplished by me. All of this has been duly performed by me there."
"Whatever remains here that has not been done, let all of that be performed.
Having heard this entire narrative, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god,
once again proceeded to speak further words in reply.

5.057.002a The exertion of Rāghava and the zeal of Sugrīva have borne fruit, 5.057.002c having encountered the character of Sītā and my own great leap. 5.057.003a O bulls among monkeys, the character of Sītā is worthy of her noble lady.
By his ascetic power he can sustain the worlds, or if enraged, he could even consume them with fire.
In every respect, this Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, has grown excessively powerful;
for when he touched her body, she was not destroyed by his ascetic power.
The flame of fire, even when touched by the hand,
could not do what the daughter of Janaka would do when defiled by the fury of Rāvaṇa, that evil-minded one, in the midst of the Aśoka grove.
Beneath a *śiṃśapā* tree, that virtuous woman stood piteously,
surrounded by ogresses, emaciated by the torment of grief,
and lusterless like a crescent moon enveloped by a streak of clouds.
Vaidehī, devoted to her husband, possessed of beautiful hips, and held fast by Janaka’s daughter, did not think of Rāvaṇa, who was arrogant in his strength;
for the auspicious Vaidehī was devoted to Rāma with her whole being.
With her mind fixed on no one but Rāma, as Paulomī is devoted to Purandara, Sītā—
clad in that same single garment, likewise covered in dust,
her limbs distressed by the torment of grief— remained intent on the welfare of her husband.

5.057.011a That woman was seen by me in the forest, being repeatedly threatened in the midst of hideous ogresses; 5.057.011c indeed, that beautiful lady was there with her hair in a single braid, dejected, and wholly devoted to thoughts of her husband.
5.057.012a She wore a single braid, miserable, and entirely absorbed in anxiety for her husband.
Sleeping on the ground, her limbs pale like a lotus at the onset of winter,
having turned away from Rāvaṇa’s advances and resolved to die—
how was that fawn-eyed woman somehow brought to feel confidence?
Then, having been addressed and shown the entire matter,
she attained great joy upon hearing of the friendship between Rāma and Sugrīva;
her conduct was disciplined and her devotion to her husband was supreme.
"That great-souled ten-headed one whom no one can slay— Rāma shall be merely the instrument for his destruction. Thus remains the highly fortunate Sītā, wholly devoted to her grief.
"Whatever must be done here, let all that be prepared.
Having heard those words of his, the son of Vālin spoke,
after having obtained the permission of all the great monkeys headed by Jāmbavān.
5.058.002a Since this matter has thus come to pass and has been reported to you, it is right that we should go together with Vaidehī to see those two sons of the king.
5.058.003a Even I alone am sufficient to overcome the city along with its hosts of rākṣasas.
"To destroy that Laṅkā by force and the exceedingly powerful Rāvaṇa—
how much more so, O heroes, when accompanied by you monkeys who are strong, self-disciplined, skilled in weapons, capable, and desirous of victory?"

But I shall destroy Rāvaṇa in battle, along with his army, his attendants, his sons, and his brothers in combat. [I shall employ] the Brahma, Aindra, Raudra, Vāyavya, and likewise the Vāruṇa [weapons].
"If the weapons of Śakrajit are difficult to behold in combat,
I shall scatter them and slay the Rākṣasas;
permitted by you, my prowess shall restrain him."
For this incomparable, continuous rain of rocks has been unleashed by me;
it could slay even the gods in battle, let alone those night-stalkers. Even the ocean might overstep its shore, and even Mount Mandara might tremble.
The enemy host could not shake Jāmbavān in battle; indeed,
the heroic monkey, the son of the Wind, alone is sufficient to destroy all the gathered hosts of Rākṣasas, both those of the present and those of the past.
5.058.011 Even Mount Mandara would be shattered by the great force of the thighs of Panasa and the high-souled Nila; how much more so, then, the Rākṣasas in battle?
[This holds true] even among the wars of gods and Asuras, and among Gandharvas, Uragas, and birds.
"Name a warrior to oppose Mainda or Dvivida;
these two best of monkeys, sons of the Aśvins, possess great speed and have attained supreme arrogance through the pride of their grandfather’s boon."
Indeed, in order to honor the Aśvins, the Grandfather of all the worlds formerly granted them incomparable invulnerability from all beings; yet,
intoxicated by the pride of that boon, they [the Aśvins] crushed a vast army.
"O heroes, those two monkeys have drunk the nectar of the gods.
For these two alone, when enraged, are capable of destroying Laṅkā along with its horses, chariots, and elephants— let all the other monkeys stand aside."
"But it is improper for us, O monkeys, who have seen the goddess, to go into the presence of the high-souled Rāghava without her;
our report there would be: 'The goddess was seen, yet she was not brought back.'"

O best of monkeys, I perceive this as something incongruous with you who are renowned for your prowess; for among the gods and daityas in all the worlds, there is none of you who cannot leap, nor any who is your equal in valor.
"When the rākṣasas have thus had their heroes slain by Hanumān, what else remains to be done here? Let us take Jānakī and depart.
To him who had thus formed this resolution, Jāmbavān, the best of monkeys, [spoke].
5.058.021c Being exceedingly pleased, he who knew the meaning spoke these meaningful words: 5.058.022a "O prince, this resolve of ours is not yet lacking in endurance, just as you perceive it."
"However, since Rāma’s mind is firmly resolved,
you should see that the success of the task will follow accordingly.
Then the forest-dwellers accepted the words of Jāmbavān.
Then all those heroes, headed by Aṅgada and the great monkey Hanumān, filled with joy and led by the son of the Wind,
abandoned the summit of Mount Mahendra and leaped away, those bulls among monkeys.
Resembling Mount Meru and Mount Mandara, like great elephants in rut,
those of massive body and great strength seemed to cover the very sky;
they honored that self-possessed one of mighty power as he was being celebrated by the spirits.
As if carrying the immensely swift Hanumān with their very glances, they—
having achieved their purpose and elevated by the success of their tasks— fixed their minds upon Rāghava’s fulfillment of his objective and his supreme glory.
All were eager to deliver the pleasant news; all rejoiced at the prospect of battle; all were high-minded and resolute in their determination to counter Rāma.
Then those forest-dwellers leaped into the sky and began to soar.
They reached a forest filled with trees and creepers that resembled the Nandana grove; it was the one known as Madhuvana, protected by Sugrīva,
unassailable by all beings, and enchanting to the hearts of all creatures.
5.059.009a Since the immensely powerful monkey Dadhimukha always protects it—
5.059.009c he who is the maternal uncle of the high-souled Sugrīva, the leader of the monkeys—
5.059.010a having reached that forest, they became exceedingly exultant.
5.059.010c The monkeys [prepared] a great [feast] most pleasing to the mind of the lord of monkeys.
5.059.011a Then those monkeys, seeing the great Madhuvana, were delighted;
5.059.011c Those monkeys, tawny as honey, entreated the prince for honey.
Then the prince, having paid his respects to those aged monkeys headed by Jāmbavān,
granted them permission to consume the honey.
Thereupon, all the forest-dwellers, being thus permitted, were filled with great joy.
Then, filled with joy, they danced here and there; some sang, some bowed down,
some danced, and some laughed.
Some fall, some wander about;
some float, and some lament. Some take refuge in one another.
Some call out to one another,
some leap from tree to tree,
and some fall from the tops of the trees onto the ground.
Some, with great speed, rise from the surface of the earth and fly toward the tops of massive trees;
another approaches one who is singing while laughing at him.
One approaches another who is laughing by laughing; one approaches another who is weeping by weeping;
one approaches another who is pushing away by pushing away.
That monkey army became completely agitated,
its conduct driven by the intense impulse of having drunk the honey-wine;
and there was not a single one among them who was not intoxicated.
And there was no one there who was not satisfied as that forest was being devoured,
while the trees were stripped of their leaves and flowers.
Beholding them, the monkey named Dadhivaktra, out of anger,
restrained those monkeys;
though he was being reviled by those enraged ones.
The protector of the forest, aged among the monkey heroes and possessed of fierce splendor, again set his mind upon the protection of the grove from the monkeys.
He spoke harsh words to some with boldness, struck others incessantly with his palms,
and having approached some, he engaged them in quarrels.
In that same manner, he approached some with conciliation;
yet they, out of intoxication, did not restrain their impetuous force,
and he was not restrained by them through force.
Assailed by those who have cast off all fear, he is dragged away by them in a crowd, disregarding his own faults,
as they gore him with their claws and bite him with their teeth.
Attacking that monkey with their palms and feet out of intoxication, all those monkeys rendered that great forest devoid of its inhabitants.
Hanumān, the best of monkeys and a bull among vanaras, said to them:
"O vanaras, partake of the honey with unperturbed minds.
Having heard Hanumān’s words, Aṅgada, the foremost of the monkeys, [spoke].
With a serene mind, he replied: "Let the monkeys drink the honey.
Even an improper act must certainly be performed by me at the word of Hanumān who has accomplished his task; how much more so, then, such a thing?"

Having heard these words from the mouth of Aṅgada, the bull-like monkeys, greatly rejoiced, honored him, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! Having thus paid homage to Aṅgada, the bull among monkeys, all the monkeys [prepared for action].
They went to Madhuvana as swiftly as the current of a river;
having attacked the guardians of Madhuvana with valor,
they were emboldened by the permission [of their leader] and by seeing and hearing of Maithilī.
Then, having all flown up together from there, they attacked the forest guards by the hundreds as they were stationed in Madhuvana;
seizing many jars of honey, each measuring a *droṇa*, they carried them off.
Some, all together, were killing one another, while others were devouring them;
some, honey-colored as bees, drank the honey and spat it out,
and others, intoxicated, struck each other with the dregs of the honey.
Others stood at the roots of trees, grasping branches;
others, utterly exhausted by intoxication, lay down after spreading out leaves. The monkeys, like those possessed by madness, were joyful, being intoxicated with honey.
Some threw things at one another, while others stumbled; some let out shouts of defiance, and others warbled joyfully. Intoxicated by honey, some of the monkeys slept upon the ground.
Even those who were the honey-keepers there, the servants of Dadhimukha,
were driven away in all directions by those fearsome monkeys;
they were dragged along on their knees and shown the path to heaven.
Extremely agitated, they went to Dadhimukha and spoke these words:
"The Madhuvana has been forcibly destroyed by those who were granted boons by Hanumān;
we too were dragged on our knees and shown the path of the gods."
Then the monkey Dadhimukha, the forest-dweller, became enraged upon hearing that Madhuvana had been destroyed; he then consoled those monkeys, saying:
"Come here, let us go to those excessively arrogant monkeys!"
"We shall stop by force those who are eating the honey. Having heard these words of Dadhimukha, those heroic bulls among monkeys went once again to Madhuvana together with him.
And in their midst, Dadhimukha, seizing a massive tree,
rushed forward with speed; and all those monkeys likewise [seized] boulders, trees, and even rocks.
Taking [the weapons], those enraged elephant-like monkeys arrived where their leaders were;
having fastened the words of their masters to their hearts,
those heroes rushed forward with speed, armed with *sāla* trees, *tāla* trees, and rocks.
Those heroes, the Pālas, by the thousands, assailed the monkeys who were arrogant in their strength, whether they were perched in the trees or standing on the ground. Then,
seeing Dadhimukha enraged, the bulls among the monkeys—

Then, led by Hanumān, they rushed forward with great speed. As that mighty-armed and exceedingly powerful Āryaka was charging toward them with a tree, the enraged Aṅgada struck him there with his two arms.
Blinded by intoxication, he did not realize, "This is my noble kinsman.
Then he swiftly crushed him upon the surface of the earth with great force.
With his arms broken, turned away, overwhelmed, and drenched in blood, [he lay there].

For a moment, that heroic elephant among monkeys suddenly lost consciousness. Having with great difficulty escaped from those monkeys, that bull among monkeys went to a secluded spot and spoke to the servants who had gathered there.
"Let these remain; let us go where our lord, the monkey Sugrīva of the broad neck, stays together with Rāma.
And I shall report every fault of Aṅgada to you, O King."
5.060.029c Having heard these words, the indignant one will cause the monkeys to be slain.
5.060.030a For this Madhuvana is the cherished grove of the high-souled Sugrīva; 5.060.030c it is divine, inherited from his father and grandfather, and difficult even for the gods to approach.

"Sugrīva will cause all these monkeys— who are greedy for honey and whose lives are now forfeit— to be slain with punishment, along with their friends and kinsmen. For these evil-minded ones deserve death, as they have shown contempt for the king’s command."
"Anger born of indignation shall not be fruitless for us. Having spoken thus, the mighty Dadhimukha sprang up suddenly and departed, accompanied by the forest guards.

In the mere twinkling of an eye, that wise forest-dweller, the son of the Thousand-rayed Sun, Sugrīva the monkey, arrived at the place where Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sugrīva were. Having seen both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, as well as Sugrīva, [he approached].
From the sky, he descended upon the level ground. Having alighted, that one of great prowess, Hari Dadhimukha— the supreme lord of the cowherds— was surrounded by all those guardians of the cowherds.
With a dejected face and placing his joined palms upon his head,
he pressed Sugrīva’s auspicious feet with his own head.
Then, the bull among monkeys [perceived] the monkey fallen prostrate before him.
Upon seeing him, his heart was filled with agitation, and he spoke these words:
"Arise, arise! Why have you fallen at my feet?
O hero, let there be no fear for you; let the truth be told."
5.061.003a But once he had been inspired with confidence by that high-souled Sugrīva,
5.061.003c the highly wise Dadhimukha rose up and spoke these words:
5.061.004a "O King, neither by Ṛkṣarajas, nor by you, nor even by Vālin—
For this forest was previously abandoned and was indeed devoured by monkeys;
yet these [monkeys] were attacked and driven off by the forest guards,
and disregarding them, they continue to eat and drink the honey.
Some there cast away what remained, while others devoured it;
though they were being restrained, they all indeed knit their brows.
For these [others] were even more enraged and were thus provoked by them.
5.061.007c While they were being held back from that forest by the enraged leaders of the monkeys,
5.061.008a then those bulls among monkeys, by means of those many heroic monkeys with eyes bloodshot with rage, 5.061.008c were violently shaken by the forest-dwellers.
Some were struck with hands, some were beaten with knees;
they were dragged about at will and shown the path of the gods.
Thus were these heroes slain while you stood as their protector.
"The entire Madhuvana grove shall be devoured by them to their heart's content.
While Sugrīva, that bull among monkeys, was being addressed in this manner,
the highly wise Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, questioned him.
"O King, why has this monkey, the guardian of the grove, appeared before us?
And with reference to what matter did he speak these words in such distress?
Thus was Sugrīva addressed by the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa.
5.061.013c Skilled in speech, he replied these words to Lakṣmaṇa:
5.061.014a "Noble Lakṣmaṇa, the heroic monkey Dadhimukha has reported:
5.061.014c 'The honey has been consumed by the heroic monkeys, led by Aṅgada.'"
Such an undertaking would not have been possible for those who had not yet accomplished their task,
as was achieved by those monkeys who entered the forest;
the Queen has been seen, there is no doubt, and by none other than Hanumān.
For there is indeed no other means for accomplishing this task than Hanumān;
O bull among monkeys, the success of the mission, wisdom, resolve, valor, and learning are all firmly established in Hanumān.
Where Jāmbavān, the lord of the host, is the leader of Aṅgada,
and Hanumān is the supervisor, there his course cannot be otherwise. Indeed, Madhuvana has been ravaged by heroes headed by Aṅgada.
Having reflected upon this, the bull-like monkeys returned from the southern quarter;
they recounted how they had entered Madhuvana and how that entire grove was plundered and consumed by the vanaras.
"The Pālas have been restrained together and likewise struck upon their knees;
for this purpose, this sweet-spoken monkey named Dadhimukha, renowned for his prowess, has arrived here to speak."
"O mighty-armed Saumitri, Sītā has been seen; look at this according to the truth.
Once we have approached her, let all the monkeys drink the honey as they please, O bull among men, for they will not do so without having seen Vaidehī."
"Let them venture into this excellent, divine forest granted by you, O forest-dweller.
Then the righteous Lakṣmaṇa, together with Rāghava,
was filled with joy upon hearing those words, pleasant to the ear, issuing from the mouth of Sugrīva.
Rāma and the highly illustrious Lakṣmaṇa rejoiced greatly upon hearing this from Dadhimukha; and Sugrīva, being delighted,
spoke these words again to the forest-guardian.
"I am pleased, gentle one, that the forest was enjoyed by those who have accomplished their task; I have forgiven what was forgivable and observed the conduct of those who have fulfilled their duty.
I desire to see them quickly, with Hanumān as their leader."
He went with the two Raghavas to see those monkeys— who had attained their purpose after overcoming the pride of the king of beasts—
and to hear of their efforts in recovering Sītā.
5.062.001a Thus addressed by Sugrīva, the monkey Dadhimukha was delighted;
5.062.001c he paid his respects to Rāghava, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sugrīva.
5.062.002a Having bowed down to Sugrīva and the two mighty Rāghavas, he—
Accompanied by the heroic monkeys, he leapt straight up into the sky.
Just as he had previously come, so did he depart with great speed;
descending from the heavens to the earth, he entered that forest.
5.062.004a Having entered Madhuvana, he saw the leaders of the monkey troops, 5.062.004c all of whom were intoxicated and arrogant, urinating honey-water.
5.062.005a Joining his palms in reverence, the hero approached them.
He spoke these gentle words with a joyful countenance to Aṅgada:
"O gentle one, you should not feel anger because you were obstructed by them;
out of ignorance and in their wrath, the guards prevented you."
"O mighty one, you are the crown prince and the lord of this forest;
therefore, you ought to forgive the fault previously committed out of folly.
For just as your father was formerly the lord of the hosts of monkeys,"

"In the same way, O Sugrīva, you alone and no other among the best of monkeys [are my refuge]. For, O sinless one, I went and reported to your paternal uncle the arrival here of all these forest-dwellers."
5.062.010a Having heard of your arrival along with these leaders of the monkey troops,
he was delighted and not at all angry upon hearing that the forest had been violated.
5.062.011a Your paternal uncle Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, is overjoyed at me.
"Send them all here quickly," the king said.
Hearing these gentle words of Dadhimukha, Aṅgada,
the best of monkeys and skilled in speech, addressed those [monkeys] with these words.

"O leaders of the monkey hosts, I suspect this news has been heard by Rāma; therefore, O harassers of foes, it is no longer fitting for us to remain here once our task is accomplished. Having drunk the honey to our heart's content, we forest-dwellers are now rested."
"What remains? My departure for that place where Sugrīva, my superior, resides.
Whatever all the leaders of the monkey hosts shall tell me when they have assembled, that I shall do in what must be done; I am dependent upon you."
"Although I am the crown prince and thus not authorized to issue commands,
you have performed such improper deeds that you cannot withstand me.
Even as Aṅgada was speaking these imperishable words, they heard his speech."
With joyful minds, the forest-dwellers spoke these words:
"O King, O bull among monkeys, who, being a lord, would speak thus?
For everyone, intoxicated by the pride of power, thinks only of himself."
This speech is most worthy of you and of no one else;
for your humility proclaims your future auspicious fortune.
We too have all made preparations to go there.

5.062.020c Where Sugrīva, the imperishable lord of the heroic monkeys, resides— 5.062.021a for without being commanded by you, O best of monkeys, it is not possible for those monkeys to move even a single step anywhere; we tell you this as the truth.
While they were speaking thus, Aṅgada replied to them:
"Very well, let us go! Having said this, he leapt up from the surface of the earth;
and as he was leaping up, all those leaders of the monkey hosts followed after him.
Having rendered the sky devoid of space, like fires cast upward by a sacrifice,
those impetuous monkeys suddenly leapt into the air,
roaring with a great clamor like clouds driven by the wind.

5.062.025 While Aṅgada had not yet arrived, Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, spoke to the lotus-eyed Rāma, who was overwhelmed by grief: 5.062.026 "Take heart; may prosperity be yours! The queen has been seen; of this there is no doubt."
"It would not have been possible for them to come here, for they were beyond our reach long ago;
indeed, he would not have come into my presence had his mission failed. Yet here is the mighty-armed Prince Angada, the foremost among leapers."
Even if such an undertaking were possible for those who have not yet accomplished their task,
he would instead become dejected in countenance, his mind wandering and agitated;
for this [kingdom] belongs to his father and grandfather, and was protected by his ancestors.
"O Lord of Monkeys, had the Lord of Monkeys not been delighted, he would not have destroyed Madhuvana for me.
O Rāma of noble vows, take heart; Kausalyā has given birth to a worthy son.
The Queen has been seen by Hanumān, and by no one else—of this there is no doubt."
5.062.030e For there can be no other cause for the accomplishment of an action than one of that same nature.
5.062.031a O best of the wise, success and intelligence reside in Hanumān;
5.062.031c as well as resolve and valor, which are as firmly established in him as radiance is in the sun.

Where Jāmbavān is the leader, Aṅgada the commander of the forces, and Hanumān the presiding authority, there is no other outcome for him. O you of immeasurable prowess, do not be filled with anxiety now.
Then, indeed, he heard the sound of "kila-kila" nearby in the sky,
from the forest-dwellers who were roaring, proud of Hanumān’s deed,
as they approached Kiṣkindhā as if announcing their success.
Then, having heard that roar of the monkeys, the best of monkeys,
with his long tail extended and curved, became joyful in spirit;
those monkeys also arrived, longing for a sight of Rāma.
Placing Aṅgada and the monkey Hanumān at their head,
those heroes led by Aṅgada, joyful and filled with delight,
fell down near the king of monkeys and Rāghava.
Then the mighty-armed Hanumān, having bowed his head in salutation,
reported to Rāghava that the lady was self-restrained and unhurt.
Then, as the son of the Wind-god had thus ascertained the facts regarding Sugrīva, [Rāma spoke].
5.062.039c Lakṣmaṇa, full of joy, gazed upon the delighted [Hanumān] with great respect.
5.062.040a And then Rāghava, the slayer of enemy heroes, delighting in his affection,
gazed upon Hanumān with immense honor.
Then, having gone to Mount Prasravaṇa with its variegated forests,
they bowed their heads to Rāma and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa;
and placing the crown prince in front, they paid homage to Sugrīva.
Then they began to relate what had happened regarding Sītā:
her confinement in Rāvaṇa’s inner apartments, her threats by the rākṣasīs,
her deep devotion to Rāma, and the agreement she had made.
5.063.004 All those monkeys related this in the presence of Rāma;
having heard that Vaidehī was unharmed, Rāma spoke this reply:
5.063.005 "Where is the goddess Sītā? And how does she behave toward me?"
"O monkeys, tell me all this concerning Vaidehī. Having heard Rāma’s words in his presence, the monkeys urged Hanumān, who was well-acquainted with Sītā’s circumstances.
Having heard their words, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god and an expert in speech,
spoke concerning his discovery of Sītā:
"I have leaped across the ocean, which extends for a hundred yojanas."
Seeking Janaki Sita and desiring to see her, I went there; there lies the city named Lanka belonging to the evil-minded Ravana,
situated on the southern shore of the southern ocean.

There, in the inner apartments of Rāvaṇa, I beheld the virtuous Sītā; though living there, that beautiful woman had set her heart’s desire upon you, O Rāma. I saw her in the midst of the ogresses, being threatened again and again.
Guarded by hideous ogresses in the pleasure grove,
the queen— though she is undeserving of suffering— is enduring misery,
confined within Rāvaṇa’s inner apartments and closely watched by the rākṣasīs.
Wearing her hair in a single braid, dejected, and wholly intent on thoughts of you,
she sleeps upon the ground with pale limbs like a lotus at the onset of winter;
having turned away from Rāvaṇa’s advances, she is resolved to die.
"O Kākutstha, that queen was somehow discovered by me with my mind fixed on you,
O sinless one, as I gradually proclaimed the fame of the Ikṣvāku lineage. O tiger among men, she was inspired with confidence by me."
Then the queen was addressed, and the entire matter was explained to her;
having heard of the friendship between Rāma and Sugrīva, she attained great joy. Her conduct is disciplined, and her devotion toward you is likewise firm.
Thus, O bull among men, have I beheld the highly fortunate daughter of Janaka, endowed with fierce asceticism and devotion to you;
and she has given me a token of recognition regarding what occurred in your presence.
"O highly wise son of the Wind, on Mount Citrakūṭa, you must inform Rāma— that tiger among men—
concerning the crow; tell him everything that has been seen by you here," so Janakī said to me.
"And this must be given to him with great care, having been well preserved,
while you speak these words within the hearing of Sugrīva:
'This glorious crest-jewel was guarded by me with great effort for you.'"
He said, "Remember this piece of red arsenic (*manaḥśilā*) as a token; 'Remember me' is what he told you.
"O sinless one, this glorious jewel born of water has been sent by me to you; seeing it, I shall rejoice in you even in my calamity."
"O son of Daśaratha, I shall sustain my life for one month;
beyond that month, having fallen into the power of the rākṣasas, I shall not live.
Thus spoke Sītā, the slender-limbed lady who walks the path of dharma.
Confined within Rāvaṇa’s inner apartments, her eyes wide like those of a doe;
this is everything that has been told by me exactly as it happened, O Rāghava. By all means, let a crossing over the waters of the ocean be prepared.
Knowing that the two princes had been restored to confidence,
and having given that token of recognition to Rāghava,
she related everything concerning the Queen in its proper sequence.
The son of Vāyu related this in full with his speech.
Thus addressed by Hanumān, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha,
placed that jewel upon his heart and wept along with Lakṣmaṇa.
But seeing that most excellent jewel, Rāghava, emaciated by grief,
spoke these words to Sugrīva with eyes filled with tears:
"Just as a cow, out of affection for her calf, lets milk flow from her udder out of love,"

In the same way, my heart is filled with joy at the sight of this jewel. This jewel was given to Vaidehī by my father-in-law at the time of her marriage; when fastened upon her head, it shines most brilliantly.
For this gem, born of water and honored by the most excellent,
was given by the wise Śakra, who was highly gratified during the sacrifice.
Upon seeing this best of gems, it is as if one has seen my father.
"O gentle one, today I have come to understand the situation regarding the powerful King of Videha.
For this jewel shines upon the head of that beloved woman of mine;
by seeing it today, I feel as though I have recovered her."
"O gentle one, tell me again and again what Sītā, the princess of Videha, said— she who,
as if sprinkling one whose life-breath has departed with water, drenched me with the water of her words.
But what could be more painful than this, that this [child] was born from water?"
"O Saumitri, I see the jewel, yet Vaidehī has not arrived. If Vaidehī lives for long, she might endure for a month;
but, O gentle one, I could not live for even a moment without that dark-eyed woman."
"Lead me also to that place where my beloved was seen;
having obtained news of her, I would not remain even for a moment. O lady of beautiful hips, how could she—being so timid—remain fearless at that time?"
She stands in the midst of terrifying and formidable *rākṣasa*s,
like the autumn moon, freed from darkness, obscured by clouds; her face, covered by the *rākṣasa*s, does not shine.
"O Hanumān, tell me truly what Sītā said;
indeed, by this I shall live, just as a sick man lives by medicine. What did my beautiful lady say, she who speaks so sweetly?"
"O Hanumān, tell me how Jānakī, that woman of noble form, continues to live when separated from me— having encountered sorrow after sorrow. Thus was Hanumān addressed by the high-souled Rāghava.
He reported everything Sītā had said to Rāghava:
"O bull among men, the lady Jānaki has spoken these words regarding the past events at Citrakūṭa exactly as they occurred."
Previously, while Janaki was sleeping happily with you, she rose first;
then a crow suddenly flew up and pecked her between the breasts.
And in turn, O elder brother of Bharata, you slept upon the lap of the queen.
And again, it is said, that bird caused pain to the queen;
then, having returned once more, he reportedly tore her severely.
Thereupon you were awakened by her, drenched in her blood.
O scorcher of enemies, you were awakened from your deep sleep by that very crow which was constantly harassing her;
and upon seeing her, O mighty-armed one, crying out between her breasts—
Sighing like an enraged venomous serpent, you spoke:
"O timid one, by whom has the space between your breasts been torn with the tips of its claws?
Who is playing with an angry, five-headed serpent?"
Looking about, he suddenly beheld a crow standing directly in front of me with its sharp claws smeared with blood. That crow was indeed the son of Śakra, the best among those who fly.
Moving swiftly through the interior of the earth, he was equal to the wind in speed.
Then, O mighty-armed one, best among the wise, his eyes rolling with rage, he formed a cruel intent toward the crow.
5.065.012a Taking a blade of darbha grass from the sacrificial seat, you charged it with the Brahmā weapon.
5.065.012c Blazing like the fire of cosmic destruction, it flared up toward the bird.
5.065.013a You then hurled that blazing blade of darbha at the crow.
Then that blazing blade of darbha grass pursued the crow.
Abandoned by his father, by all the gods, and by the great seers,
it wandered through the three worlds but found no protector.
"O Raghava, descendant of Kakutstha, you who are a refuge, protect with compassion this one who has fallen to the ground seeking your protection— even though he deserves death—
for it is not possible to render a weapon's power in vain."
Then he struck the right eye of that crow;
having paid homage to you, O Rāma, and to King Daśaratha,
the crow was then dismissed and returned to his abode in the sky.
"O Rāghava, why do you, who are the best among those skilled in weapons, endowed with courage, and possessed of virtue, not employ your weapons against the rākṣasas?
Neither the nāgas, nor the gandharvas, nor the asuras, nor the hosts of maruts [are a match for them]."
O Rāma, they are able to stand before you and counter-attack;
if you, the heroic one, have any concern for me,
let Rāvaṇa be swiftly slain in battle with your well-sharpened arrows.
Or has Lakṣmaṇa, that scorcher of enemies, taken his brother’s command? For what reason does Rāghava, that best of men, not protect me?
Those two tigers among men are capable, possessing a splendor equal to wind and fire.
"Why do these two, who are invincible even to the gods, neglect me?
There is no doubt that some great evil deed of my own exists,
since these two subduers of foes, though capable together, disregard me."
Having heard Vaidehī’s piteous words spoken with tears,
I again addressed these words to that noble lady:
"O Queen, I swear to you by the truth that Rāma is turned away from all else by grief for you."
While Rāma is overwhelmed by grief, Lakṣmaṇa also suffers deeply. You have somehow been found; this is no time for lamentation.
O beautiful lady, in this very moment you shall see the end of your sorrows.
Those two tigers among men, the princes and subduers of enemies,
emboldened by the sight of you, shall reduce Laṅkā to ashes;
and having slain the fierce Rāvaṇa along with his kinsmen in battle.
"The mighty-armed Rāghava will surely lead you back to his own city. O blameless lady, you ought to give him a token of recognition that he would recognize,
which will produce joy in him."
Having surveyed all the directions, O one of great strength, she untied this supreme jewel from her braid and gave it to me from her garment for your sake,
O best of the Raghus; having accepted that divine jewel.
Having prostrated with my head before her,
I was eager to return; and seeing me thus resolved upon going and observing my increasing enthusiasm, the daughter of Janaka, that woman of excellent complexion, spoke to me.
With her face filled with tears, distressed, and speaking with a voice choked by sobs, she said:
"O Hanumān, you must inquire after the welfare of both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who resemble lions,
as well as Sugrīva along with his ministers."
And you ought to arrange it so that the mighty-armed Rāghava may deliver me from this obstruction of the waters of sorrow,
and [quench] this intense surge of my grief.
And having gone into the presence of Rāma, you should report this threat from these rākṣasas;
may your path be auspicious, O hero among monkeys!
"O lion among kings,
this is the speech that the noble Sītā spoke to you with sorrow;
having understood this, I have related it to you."
"Have faith that Sītā is safe and sound. Then, O tiger among men, out of affection for you and out of friendship, I was addressed again by the Queen with great agitation.
"In this way, O hero, you must speak to Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, in many such ways so that he may quickly reach me after slaying Rāvaṇa in battle. Or,
if you think it best, O subduer of enemies, stay for one day."
"O monkey, having rested in some secluded place, you shall depart tomorrow. O vanara, by your presence, may there be for a moment a release from this ripening of grief for me, who am so unfortunate."
"For once you, the valiant one, have departed for your return, there will be a threat even to my life; of this there is no doubt. The grief born of not seeing you will torment me all the more."
She is overcome by sorrow after sorrow, fallen into misfortune, and destined for suffering;
yet this great mass of heroic troops stands as if before me— there is no doubt that it consists of monkeys and bears who are your allies.
"How indeed will those armies of monkeys and bears, or those two sons of the best of men, cross the great ocean which is so difficult to traverse?
For only three kinds of beings are capable of leaping across this sea."
"O sinless one, whether it be the power of Vainateya, of Vāyu, or yours,
in this undertaking which is so difficult to accomplish, O hero, what solution do you perceive? Speak, O best among those who know how to act."

"O slayer of enemy heroes, you alone are certainly sufficient to accomplish this task; indeed, the manifestation of your strength will bring you glory. Even if, with all your forces, you were to kill Rāvaṇa in battle after killing me..."

If the victorious Rāma were to lead his own city back, that would bring him glory; yet Rāghava does not deserve to do so in the same manner as I was carried away from that hero’s forest by a *rākṣasa* through deception, out of sheer fear.
If that descendant of Kakutstha, the crusher of enemy forces, having overwhelmed Laṅkā with his armies, were to lead me away, that would be worthy of him;
for such is the valor of that great-souled one, befitting his nature.
"Act in such a way that you may become a hero in battle. Having heard those words, which were meaningful, humble, and supported by reason,
I then spoke these further words in reply.
"O Queen, Sugrīva— the lord of the armies of monkeys and bears, the best among leapers, endowed with courage, and firm in his resolve for your sake—
is there. His followers are likewise endowed with prowess, full of spirit, and possessed of great strength."
5.066.018c At the mere thought and resolve of his mind, the monkeys stood ready at his command;
5.066.019a their movement was unimpeded— neither above, nor below, nor across—
and those of immeasurable splendor did not falter even in great tasks.
5.066.020a Many times over, by those illustrious monkeys endowed with great strength,
5.066.020c this earth was circumambulated while following the path of the wind.
5.066.021a Among them, there are forest-dwellers who are superior to me, and others who are my equals.
"In the presence of Sugrīva, there is no one inferior to me. Since I have already arrived here, what need is there to mention those of great strength?
For the most distinguished are not sent on errands; it is others who are sent."
"Therefore, enough of this lamentation, O Queen; let your grief depart.
With a single leap, the leaders of the monkey hosts shall reach Laṅkā, and those two [Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa] shall follow upon my back like the rising sun and moon."
"O highly fortunate lady, two lions among men will come into your presence;
you shall soon behold Rāghava, the slayer of enemies who resembles a lion,
and Lakṣmaṇa with bow in hand, stationed at the gate of Laṅkā."
"You shall soon behold those heroes who have claws and fangs as their weapons, possessing the prowess of lions and tigers, monkeys with the splendor of monkey-lords,
gathered together upon the peaks of Mount Malaya in Laṅkā, which resemble mountains and clouds."
"Before long, you shall hear the roar of the monkey leaders as they cry out;
and you shall soon see Rāghava, the subduer of foes, returned from his forest exile and consecrated in Ayodhyā along with you."
Then, with words that were auspicious, pleasing, and spoken without dejection, I pacified the daughter of the King of Mithilā; she attained peace.
She was likewise tormented by grief for you.
